# 1.3. Terms and Definitions

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-1/AA-1.3.mdx

sidebar_position:  7

# 1.3. Terms and Definitions

<MarginText>1/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00415-01", "AI12-0443-1"]} />
<p>Terms are defined throughout this document, indicated by <i>italic</i> type. Terms explicitly defined in this document are not to be presumed to refer implicitly to similar terms defined elsewhere. Mathematical terms not defined in this document are to be interpreted according to the <i>CRC Concise Encyclopedia of Mathematics, Second Edition</i>. Other terms not defined in this document are to be interpreted according to the <i>Webster's Third New International Dictionary of the English Language</i>. Informal descriptions of some terms are also given below. <br /></p>

<MarginText>1.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The index contains an entry for every defined term.<br />

<MarginText>1.b/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00415-01"]} />
The contents of the <i>CRC Concise Encyclopedia of Mathematics, Second Edition</i> can be accessed on <a href="http://www.mathworld.com">http://www.mathworld.com</a>. The ISBN number of the book is ISBN 1584883472.<br />

<MarginText>1.c/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0443-1"]} />
The definitions found in this subclause are short, descriptive definitions. These are most useful for comprehension when an exact meaning is not needed. More formal, detailed definitions are found in the body of the Reference Manual; these are needed to determine the exact application of rules to constructs and entities.<br />

<MarginText>1.d/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0443-1"]} />
To see the difference, consider &ldquo;aliased view&rdquo;. The descriptive definition is &ldquo;a view of an object that can be designated by an access value&rdquo;. The formal definition is a lengthy paragraph in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10">3.10</a> that defines 10 separate constructs as aliased views. In order to reason about a language rule that requires an aliased view in a particular context, one needs to look at the list of constructs in order to determine if the object in hand is actually an aliased view. The descriptive definition is no help in this case. <br />

<MarginText>1.e/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0443-1"]} />
<b>Term entry: </b>Each term defined in this subclause is marked like this in the body of the AARM near its detailed formal definition. <br />

<MarginText>1.f/5</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Here are some AARM-only definitions: The Ada Rapporteur Group (ARG) interprets the Ada Reference Manual. An Ada Issue (AI) is a numbered ruling from the ARG. Ada Issues created for Ada 83 are denoted as "AI83", while Ada Issues created for Ada 95 are denoted as "AI95" in this document. Similarly, Ada Issues created for Ada 2005 are denoted as "AI05", Ada Issues created for Ada 2012 are denoted as "AI12", and Ada Issues created for Ada 2022 are denoted as "AI22". The Ada Commentary Integration Document (ACID) is an edition of the Ada 83 RM in which clearly marked insertions and deletions indicate the effect of integrating the approved AIs. The Uniformity Rapporteur Group (URG) issued recommendations intended to increase uniformity across Ada implementations. The functions of the URG have been assumed by the ARG. A Uniformity Issue (UI) was a numbered recommendation from the URG. A Defect Report and Response is an official query to WG9 about an error in the standard. Defect Reports are processed by the ARG, and are referenced here by their ISO numbers: 8652/nnnn. Most changes to the Ada 95 standard include reference(s) to the Defect Report(s) that prompted the change. The <i>Ada Conformity Assessment Test Suite (ACATS)</i> is a set of tests intended to check the conformity of Ada implementations to this standard. This set of tests was previously known as the Ada Compiler Validation Capability (ACVC). <br />

<a id="Subclause_1.3.1"></a>

## 1.3.1  Types, Objects, and their Properties

<MarginText>1/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>abstract type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>tagged type intended for use as an ancestor of other types, but which is not allowed to have objects of its own<br /></dd>
<MarginText>2/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>access type</b></dt>
<dd>type that has values that designate aliased objects<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>3/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Access types correspond to &ldquo;pointer types&rdquo; or &ldquo;reference types&rdquo; in some other languages.<br />

<MarginText>4/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>accessibility level</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>representation of the lifetime of an entity in terms of the level of dynamic nesting within which the entity is known to exist<br /></dd>
<MarginText>5/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>aliased view</b></dt>
<dd>view of an object that can be designated by an access value<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>6/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Objects allocated by allocators are aliased. Objects can also be explicitly declared as aliased with the reserved word aliased. The Access attribute can be used to create an access value designating an aliased object.<br />

<MarginText>7/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>ancestor of a type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>type itself or, in the case of a type derived from other types, its parent type or one of its progenitor types or one of their ancestors<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>8/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Ancestor and descendant are inverse relationships.<br />

<MarginText>9/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>array type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>composite type whose components are all of the same type<br /></dd>
<MarginText>10/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>aspect</b></dt>
<dd>specifiable property of an entity<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>11/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code> on the declaration of the entity. Some aspects can be queried via attributes.<br />

<MarginText>12/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>attribute</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>characteristic or property of an entity that can be queried, and in some cases specified<br /></dd>
<MarginText>13/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>category of types</b></dt>
<dd>set of types with one or more common properties, such as primitive operations<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>14/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: A category of types that is closed under derivation is also known as a class.<br />

<MarginText>15/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>character type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>enumeration type whose values include characters<br /></dd>
<MarginText>16/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>class of types</b></dt>
<dd>set of types that is closed under derivation, which means that if a given type is in the class, then all types derived from that type are also in the class<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>17/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: The set of types of a class share common properties, such as their primitive operations.<br />

<MarginText>18/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>composite type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>type with components, such as an array or record<br /></dd>
<MarginText>19/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>controlled type</b></dt>
<dd>type that supports user-defined assignment and finalization<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>20/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Objects are always finalized before being destroyed.<br />

<MarginText>21/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>default initial condition</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>property that holds for every default-initialized object of a given type<br /></dd>
<MarginText>22/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>derived type</b></dt>
<dd>type defined in terms of a parent type and zero or more progenitor types given in a derived type definition<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>23/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note 1: A derived type inherits properties such as components and primitive operations from its parent and progenitors.<br />

<MarginText>24/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note 2: A type together with the types derived from it (directly or indirectly) form a derivation class.<br />

<MarginText>25/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>descendant of a type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>type itself or a type derived (directly or indirectly) from it<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>26/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Descendant and ancestor are inverse relationships.<br />

<MarginText>27/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>discrete type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>type that is either an integer type or an enumeration type<br /></dd>
<MarginText>28/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>discriminant</b></dt>
<dd>parameter for a composite type, which can control, for example, the bounds of a component that is an array<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>29/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: A discriminant for a task type can be used to pass data to a task of the type upon its creation.<br />

<MarginText>30/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>elementary type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>type that does not have components<br /></dd>
<MarginText>31/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>enumeration type</b></dt>
<dd>type defined by an enumeration of its values, which can be denoted by identifiers or character literals<br /></dd>
<MarginText>32/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>full type</b></dt>
<dd>type that defines a full view<br /></dd>
<MarginText>33/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>full view</b></dt>
<dd>view of a type that reveals all of its properties<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>34/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: There can be other views of the type that reveal fewer properties.<br />

<MarginText>35/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>incomplete type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>type that defines an incomplete view<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>36/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Incomplete types can be used for defining recursive data structures.<br />

<MarginText>37/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>incomplete view</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>view of a type that reveals minimal properties<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>38/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: The remaining properties are defined by the full view given elsewhere.<br />

<MarginText>39/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>indexable container type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>type that has user-defined behavior for indexing, via the Constant{"_"}Indexing or Variable{"_"}Indexing aspects<br /></dd>
<MarginText>40/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>integer type</b></dt>
<dd>type that represents signed or modular integers<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>41/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: A signed integer type has a base range that includes both positive and negative numbers, and has operations that can raise an exception when the result is outside the base range. A modular type has a base range whose lower bound is zero, and has operations with &ldquo;wraparound&rdquo; semantics. Modular types subsume what are called &ldquo;unsigned types&rdquo; in some other languages.<br />

<MarginText>42/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>interface type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>abstract tagged type that has no components or concrete operations except possibly null procedures<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>43/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Interface types are used for composing other interfaces and tagged types and thereby provide multiple inheritance. Only an interface type can be used as a progenitor of another type.<br />

<MarginText>44/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>invariant</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>assertion that is expected to be True for all objects of a given private type when viewed from outside the defining package<br /></dd>
<MarginText>45/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>iterable container type</b></dt>
<dd>type that has user-defined behavior for iteration, via the Default{"_"}Iterator and Iterator{"_"}Element aspects<br /></dd>
<MarginText>46/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>limited type</b></dt>
<dd>type for which copying (such as in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>) is not allowed<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>47/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: All types are either limited types or nonlimited types.<br />

<MarginText>48/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>needed component</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>component of a record type or record extension that is required to have its value specified within a given aggregate<br /></dd>
<MarginText>49/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>nominal subtype</b></dt>
<dd>subtype specified when a view of an object is defined<br /></dd>
<MarginText>50/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>nonlimited type</b></dt>
<dd>type for which copying is allowed<br /></dd>
<MarginText>51/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>object</b></dt>
<dd>entity that contains a value, and is either a constant or a variable<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>52/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#S0032">object_declaration</a></code> or by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code>. A formal parameter is (a view of) an object. A subcomponent of an object is an object.<br />

<MarginText>53/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>operational aspect</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>aspect that indicates a logical property of an entity, such as the precondition of a subprogram, or the procedure used to write a given type of object to a stream<br /></dd>
<MarginText>54/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>parent of a derived type</b></dt>
<dd>first ancestor type given in the definition of the derived type<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>55/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: The parent can be almost any kind of type, including an interface type.<br />

<MarginText>56/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>partial view</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>view of a type that reveals only some of its properties<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>57/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: The remaining properties are defined by the full view given elsewhere.<br />

<MarginText>58/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>primitive operations of a type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>operations (such as subprograms) declared together with the type declarations<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>59/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Primitive operations are inherited by other types in the same derivation class of types.<br />

<MarginText>60/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>private extension</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>type that extends another type, with the additional properties hidden from its clients<br /></dd>
<MarginText>61/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>private type</b></dt>
<dd>type that defines a partial view<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>62/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Private types can be used for defining abstractions that hide unnecessary details from their clients.<br />

<MarginText>63/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>progenitor</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>type given in the interface list, if any, of an interface, task, protected, or derived type definition<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>64/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: A progenitor is always an interface type.<br />

<MarginText>65/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>protected type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>composite type whose components are accessible only through one of its protected operations, which synchronize concurrent access by multiple tasks<br /></dd>
<MarginText>66/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>real type</b></dt>
<dd>type that has values that are approximations of the real numbers<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>67/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Floating point and fixed point types are real types.<br />

<MarginText>68/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>record extension</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>type that extends another type optionally with additional components<br /></dd>
<MarginText>69/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>record type</b></dt>
<dd>composite type consisting of zero or more named components, possibly of different types<br /></dd>
<MarginText>70/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>reference type</b></dt>
<dd>type that has user-defined behavior for &ldquo;.all&rdquo;, defined by the Implicit{"_"}Dereference aspect<br /></dd>
<MarginText>71/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>representation aspect</b></dt>
<dd>aspect that indicates how an entity is mapped onto the underlying hardware, for example the size or alignment of an object<br /></dd>
<MarginText>72/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>scalar type</b></dt>
<dd>either a discrete type or a real type<br /></dd>
<MarginText>73/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>stable property</b></dt>
<dd>characteristic associated with objects of a given type that is preserved by many of the primitive operations of the type<br /></dd>
<MarginText>74/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>storage pool object</b></dt>
<dd>object associated with one or more access types from which the storage for objects created by allocators of the access type(s) is obtained<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>75/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Some storage pools can be partitioned into subpools in order to support finer-grained storage management.<br />

<MarginText>76/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>stream</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>sequence of elements that can be used, along with the stream-oriented attributes, to support marshalling and unmarshalling of values of most types<br /></dd>
<MarginText>77/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>subtype</b></dt>
<dd>type together with optional constraints, null exclusions, and predicates, which constrain the values of the type to the subset that satisfies the implied conditions<br /></dd>
<MarginText>78/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>synchronized</b></dt>
<dd>can be safely operated on by multiple tasks concurrently<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>79/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Synchronized is used to qualify entities, as in a synchronized interface.<br />

<MarginText>80/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>tagged type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>type whose objects each have a run-time type tag, which indicates the specific type for which the object was originally created<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>81/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Tagged types can be extended with additional components.<br />

<MarginText>82/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>task type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>composite type used to represent active entities which execute concurrently and that can communicate via queued task entries<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>83/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: The top-level task of a partition is called the environment task.<br />

<MarginText>84/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>type</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>defining characteristic of each object and expression of the language, with an associated set of values, and a set of primitive operations that implement the fundamental aspects of its semantics<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>85/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: Types are grouped into categories. Most language-defined categories of types are also classes of types.<br />

<MarginText>86/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>view of an entity</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>representation of an entity that reveals some or all of the properties of the entity<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>87/5_1.3.1</MarginText>
Note: A single entity can have multiple views.<br />

<a id="Subclause_1.3.2"></a>

## 1.3.2  Subprograms and their Properties

<MarginText>1/5_1.3.2</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>function</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>form of subprogram that returns a result and can be called as part of an expression<br /></dd>
<MarginText>2/5_1.3.2</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>overriding operation</b></dt>
<dd>operation that replaces an inherited primitive operation<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>3/5_1.3.2</MarginText>
Note: Operations can be marked explicitly as overriding or not overriding.<br />

<MarginText>4/5_1.3.2</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>postcondition</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>assertion that is expected to be True when a given subprogram returns normally<br /></dd>
<MarginText>5/5_1.3.2</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>precondition</b></dt>
<dd>assertion that is expected to be True when a given subprogram is called<br /></dd>
<MarginText>6/5_1.3.2</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>procedure</b></dt>
<dd>form of subprogram that does not return a result and can only be invoked by a statement<br /></dd>
<MarginText>7/5_1.3.2</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>subprogram</b></dt>
<dd>unit of a program that can be brought into execution in various contexts, with the invocation being a subprogram call that can parameterize the effect of the subprogram through the passing of operands<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>8/5_1.3.2</MarginText>
Note: There are two forms of subprograms: functions, which return values, and procedures, which do not.<br />

<a id="Subclause_1.3.3"></a>

## 1.3.3  Other Syntactic Constructs

<MarginText>1/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>aggregate</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>construct used to define a value of a composite type by specifying the values of the components of the type<br /></dd>
<MarginText>2/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>compilation unit</b></dt>
<dd>program unit that is separately compiled<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>3/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code> contains either the declaration, the body, or a renaming of a program unit.<br />

<MarginText>4/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>construct</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>piece of text (explicit or implicit) that is an instance of a syntactic category defined under Syntax<br /></dd>
<MarginText>5/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>container</b></dt>
<dd>structured object that represents a collection of elements all of the same (potentially class-wide) type, such as a vector or a tree<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>6/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note: Several predefined container types are provided by the children of package Ada.Containers (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-A/AA-A.18#Subclause_A.18.1">A.18.1</a>).<br />

<MarginText>7/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>container aggregate</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>construct used to define a value of a type that represents a collection of elements, by explicitly specifying the elements in the collection<br /></dd>
<MarginText>8/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>core language</b></dt>
<dd>clause or annex in which are defined language constructs or capabilities that are provided by all conforming implementations<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>9/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note: A construct is said to be part of the core language if it is defined in a core language clause or annex.<br />

<MarginText>10/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>declaration</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>language construct that associates a name with (a view of) an entity<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>11/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note: A declaration can appear explicitly in the program text (an explicit declaration), or can be supposed to occur at a given place in the text as a consequence of the semantics of another construct (an implicit declaration).<br />

<MarginText>12/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>generic instance</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>nongeneric unit created by the instantiation of a generic unit<br /></dd>
<MarginText>13/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>generic unit</b></dt>
<dd>template for a (nongeneric) program unit<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>14/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note 1: The template can be parameterized by objects, types, subprograms, and packages.<br />

<MarginText>15/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note 2: Generic units can be used to perform the role that macros sometimes play in other languages.<br />

<MarginText>16/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>iterator</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>construct that is used to loop over the elements of an array or container<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>17/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note: Iterators can be user defined, and can perform arbitrary computations to access elements from a container.<br />

<MarginText>18/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>iterator filter</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>construct that is used to restrict the elements produced by an iteration to those for which a boolean condition evaluates to True<br /></dd>
<MarginText>19/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>library unit</b></dt>
<dd>separately compiled program unit, which is a package, a subprogram, or a generic unit<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>20/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note: Library units can have other (logically nested) library units as children, and can have other program units physically nested within them. A root library unit, together with its children and grandchildren and so on, form a subsystem.<br />

<MarginText>21/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>master construct</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>one of certain executable constructs for which there can be objects or tasks whose lifetime ends when the construct completes<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>22/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note: Execution of a master construct is a master, with which objects and tasks are associated for the purposes of waiting and finalization.<br />

<MarginText>23/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>needed compilation unit</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>compilation unit that is necessary to produce an executable partition, because some entity declared or defined within the unit is used elsewhere in the partition<br /></dd>
<MarginText>24/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>package</b></dt>
<dd>program unit that defines the interface to a group of logically related entities, along with their implementation<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>25/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note: Typically, a package contains the declaration of a type (often a private type or private extension) along with the declarations of primitive subprograms of the type, which can be called from outside the package, while their inner workings remain hidden from outside users.<br />

<MarginText>26/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>parallel construct</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>executable construct that defines multiple activities of a single task that can proceed in parallel, via the execution of multiple logical threads of control<br /></dd>
<MarginText>27/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>partition</b></dt>
<dd>part of a program, which consists of a set of interdependent library units<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>28/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note: Each partition can run in a separate address space, possibly on a separate computer. A program can contain just one partition, or it can be distributed across multiple partitions, which can execute concurrently.<br />

<MarginText>29/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>pragma</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>compiler directive to provide control over and above that provided by the other syntactic constructs of the language<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>30/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note: There are language-defined pragmas that give instructions for optimization, listing control, etc. An implementation can support additional (implementation-defined) pragmas.<br />

<MarginText>31/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>program</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>set of partitions, each of which can execute in a separate address space, possibly on a separate computer<br /></dd>
<MarginText>32/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>program unit</b></dt>
<dd>language construct that is a package, a task unit, a protected unit, a protected entry, a generic unit, or an explicitly declared subprogram other than an enumeration literal<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>33/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
Note: Certain kinds of program units can be separately compiled. Alternatively, they can appear physically nested within other program units.<br />

<MarginText>34/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>reduction expression</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>expression that defines how to map or transform a collection of values into a new set of values, and then summarize the values by applying an operation to reduce the set to a single value<br /></dd>
<MarginText>35/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>renaming</b></dt>
<dd>declaration that does not define a new entity, but instead defines a new view of an existing entity<br /></dd>
<MarginText>36/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>specialized needs annex</b></dt>
<dd>annex in which are defined language constructs or capabilities that are not necessarily provided by all conforming implementations<br /></dd>
<MarginText>37/5_1.3.3</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>subunit</b></dt>
<dd>body of a program unit that can be compiled separately from its enclosing program unit<br /></dd>
<a id="Subclause_1.3.4"></a>
</dl>

## 1.3.4  Runtime Actions

<MarginText>1/5_1.3.4</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>assertion</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>boolean expression that is expected to be True at run time at certain specified places<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>2/5_1.3.4</MarginText>
Note: Certain pragmas and aspects define various kinds of assertions.<br />

<MarginText>3/5_1.3.4</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>elaboration</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>process by which a declaration achieves its run-time effect<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>4/5_1.3.4</MarginText>
Note: Elaboration is one of the forms of execution.<br />

<MarginText>5/5_1.3.4</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>evaluation</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>process by which an expression achieves its run-time effect<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>6/5_1.3.4</MarginText>
Note: Evaluation is one of the forms of execution.<br />

<MarginText>7/5_1.3.4</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>execution</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>process by which a construct achieves its run-time effect<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>8/5_1.3.4</MarginText>
Note: Execution of a declaration is also called elaboration. Execution of an expression is also called evaluation.<br />

<MarginText>9/5_1.3.4</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>logical thread of control</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>activity within the execution of a program that can proceed in parallel with other activities of the same task, or of separate tasks<br /></dd>
<MarginText>10/5_1.3.4</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>master</b></dt>
<dd>execution of a master construct<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>11/5_1.3.4</MarginText>
Note: Each object and task is associated with a master. When a master is left, associated tasks are awaited and associated objects are finalized.<br />

<a id="Subclause_1.3.5"></a>

## 1.3.5  Exceptional Situations

<MarginText>1/5_1.3.5</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>check</b></dt>
<dl>
<dd>test made during execution to determine whether a language rule has been violated<br /></dd>
<MarginText>2/5_1.3.5</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>exception</b></dt>
<dd>kind of exceptional situation<br /></dd>
<MarginText>3/5_1.3.5</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>exception occurrence</b></dt>
<dd>run-time occurrence of an exceptional situation<br /></dd>
<MarginText>4/5_1.3.5</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>handle an exception</b></dt>
<dd>perform some actions in response to the arising of an exception<br /></dd>
<MarginText>5/5_1.3.5</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>raise an exception</b></dt>
<dd>abandon normal program execution so as to draw attention to the fact that the corresponding situation has arisen<br /></dd>
<MarginText>6/5_1.3.5</MarginText>
<dt><br/><b>suppress a check</b></dt>
<dd>assert that the check cannot fail, and request that the compiler optimize by disabling the check<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>7/5_1.3.5</MarginText>
Note: The compiler is not required to honor this request. Suppressing checks that can fail can cause a program to behave in arbitrary ways.<br />

# 1. General

# 1. General

<MarginText>2.a/5</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>This Annotated Ada Reference Manual (AARM) contains the entire text of the fourth edition of the Ada Reference Manual (referred to here as the Ada 2022 RM), plus certain annotations. The annotations give a more in-depth analysis of the language. They describe the reason for each nonobvious rule, and point out interesting ramifications of the rules and interactions among the rules (interesting to language lawyers, that is). Differences between Ada 83, Ada 95, Ada 2005, Ada 2012, and Ada 2022 are listed. (The text you are reading now is an annotation.)<br />

<MarginText>2.b/3</MarginText>
The AARM stresses detailed correctness and uniformity over readability and understandability. We're not trying to make the language &ldquo;appear&rdquo; simple here; on the contrary, we're trying to expose hidden complexities, so we can more easily detect language bugs. The Ada 2022 RM, on the other hand, is intended to be a more readable document for programmers.<br />

<MarginText>2.c</MarginText>
The annotations in the AARM are as follows: <br />

<MarginText>2.d/3</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>Text that is logically redundant is shown [in square brackets, like this]. Technically, such text could be written as a Note in the Ada 2022 RM (and the Ada 95 and 2005 RMs before it), since it is really a theorem that can be proven from the nonredundant rules of the language. We use the square brackets instead when it seems to make the Ada 2022 RM more readable.<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.e</MarginText>
<li>The rules of the language (and some AARM-only text) are categorized, and placed under certain <i>sub-headings</i> that indicate the category. For example, the distinction between Name Resolution Rules and Legality Rules is particularly important, as explained in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>.<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.f</MarginText>
<li>Text under the following sub-headings appears in both documents: <br /></li>
</ul>

<MarginText>2.dd</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">

<MarginText>2.ee</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">

<MarginText>2.ff</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>An informal proof explaining how a given Note or [marked-as-redundant] piece of text follows from the other rules of the language. <br />

<MarginText>2.gg</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>A hint about how to implement a feature, or a particular potential pitfall that an implementer needs to be aware of.<br />

<MarginText>2.hh</MarginText>

<MarginText>2.ii</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Other annotations not covered by the above. <br />

<MarginText>2.jj</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>A rule that is considered logically necessary to the definition of the language, but which is so obscure or pedantic that only a language lawyer would care. These are the only annotations that could be considered part of the language definition. <br />

<MarginText>2.jj.1/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0443-1"]} />
<b>Term entry: </b>The text of a Term and Definition entry &mdash; this text will also appear in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-1/AA-1.3">1.3</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-1/AA-1.3">Terms and Definitions</a>&rdquo;. <br />

<MarginText>2.kk/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>In general, the Ada 2022 RM text appears in the normal font, whereas AARM-only text appears in a smaller font. Notes also appear in the smaller font, as recommended by ISO/IEC style guidelines. Ada examples are also usually printed in a smaller font.<br />

<MarginText>2.ll</MarginText>
If you have trouble finding things, be sure to use the index. Each defined term appears there, and also in <i>italics, like this</i>. Syntactic categories defined in BNF are also indexed.<br />

<MarginText>2.mm</MarginText>
A definition marked &ldquo;[distributed]&rdquo; is the main definition for a term whose complete definition is given in pieces distributed throughout the document. The pieces are marked &ldquo;[partial]&rdquo; or with a phrase explaining what cases the partial definition applies to. <br />

# 10.1. Separate Compilation

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1.mdx

sidebar_position:  86

# 10.1. Separate Compilation

<MarginText>1</MarginText>
<p>[ A <i>program unit</i> is either a package, a task unit, a protected unit, a protected entry, a generic unit, or an explicitly declared subprogram other than an enumeration literal. Certain kinds of program units can be separately compiled. Alternatively, they can appear physically nested within other program units. <br /></p>

<MarginText>1.a/5</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>program unit</b> &mdash; language construct that is a package, a task unit, a protected unit, a protected entry, a generic unit, or an explicitly declared subprogram other than an enumeration literal<br />Note: Certain kinds of program units can be separately compiled. Alternatively, they can appear physically nested within other program units.<br />

<MarginText>2</MarginText>
<p>The text of a program can be submitted to the compiler in one or more <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code>s. Each <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code> is a succession of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code>s. A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code> contains either the declaration, the body, or a renaming of a program unit.] The representation for a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code> is implementation-defined. <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-defined">
<b></b>The representation for a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code>.<br />

<MarginText>2.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Some implementations might choose to make a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code> be a source (text) file. Others might allow multiple source files to be automatically concatenated to form a single <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code>. Others still may represent the source in a nontextual form such as a parse tree. Note that the RM95 does not even define the concept of a source file.<br />

<MarginText>2.c</MarginText>
Note that a protected subprogram is a subprogram, and therefore a program unit. An instance of a generic unit is a program unit.<br />

<MarginText>2.d</MarginText>
A protected entry is a program unit, but protected entries cannot be separately compiled. <br />

<MarginText>2.e/5</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>compilation unit</b> &mdash; program unit that is separately compiled<br /><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code> contains either the declaration, the body, or a renaming of a program unit.<br />

<MarginText>3</MarginText>
<p>A library unit is a separately compiled program unit, and is a package, subprogram, or generic unit. Library units may have other (logically nested) library units as children, and may have other program units physically nested within them. A root library unit, together with its children and grandchildren and so on, form a <i>subsystem</i>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>3.a/5</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>library unit</b> &mdash; separately compiled program unit, which is a package, a subprogram, or a generic unit<br />Note: Library units can have other (logically nested) library units as children, and can have other program units physically nested within them. A root library unit, together with its children and grandchildren and so on, form a subsystem.<br />

#### Implementation Permissions

<MarginText>4</MarginText>
<p>An implementation may impose implementation-defined restrictions on <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code>s that contain multiple <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code>s. <br /></p>

<MarginText>4.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-defined">
<b></b>Any restrictions on <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code>s that contain multiple <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code>s.<br />

<MarginText>4.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>For example, an implementation might disallow a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code> that contains two versions of the same compilation unit, or that contains the declarations for library packages P1 and P2, where P1 precedes P2 in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code> but P1 has a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code> that mentions P2. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>4.c</MarginText>
The interactions between language issues and environmental issues are left open in Ada 95. The environment concept is new. In Ada 83, the concept of the program library, for example, appeared to be quite concrete, although the rules had no force, since implementations could get around them simply by defining various mappings from the concept of an Ada program library to whatever data structures were actually stored in support of separate compilation. Indeed, implementations were encouraged to do so.<br />

<MarginText>4.d</MarginText>
In RM83, it was unclear which was the official definition of &ldquo;program unit&rdquo;. Definitions appeared in RM83-5, 6, 7, and 9, but not 12. Placing it here seems logical, since a program unit is sort of a potential compilation unit. <br />

<a id="Subclause_10.1.1"></a>

## 10.1.1  Compilation Units - Library Units

<MarginText>1_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>[A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> is a compilation unit that is the declaration, body, or renaming of a library unit. Each library unit (except Standard) has a <i>parent unit</i>, which is a library package or generic library package.] A library unit is a <i>child</i> of its parent unit. The <i>root</i> library units are the children of the predefined library package Standard. <br /></p>

<MarginText>1.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Standard is a library unit. <br />

#### Syntax

<MarginText>2_10.1.1</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>compilation</code><a id="S0285"></a><code> ::= </code>{"{"}<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code>{"}"}<br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3_10.1.1</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>compilation{"_"}unit</code><a id="S0286"></a><code> ::= </code><br />    <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0292">context_clause</a></code> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code><br />  | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0292">context_clause</a></code> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0302">subunit</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>4_10.1.1</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>library{"_"}item</code><a id="S0287"></a><code> ::= </code>[<b>private</b>] <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0288">library_unit_declaration</a></code><br />  | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0290">library_unit_body</a></code><br />  | [<b>private</b>] <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0289">library_unit_renaming_declaration</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>5_10.1.1</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>library{"_"}unit{"_"}declaration</code><a id="S0288"></a><code> ::= </code><br />     <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0195">subprogram_declaration</a></code>	| <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0229">package_declaration</a></code><br />   | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code>	| <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>6_10.1.1</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>library{"_"}unit{"_"}renaming{"_"}declaration</code><a id="S0289"></a><code> ::= </code><br />   <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0241">package_renaming_declaration</a></code><br /> | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0243">generic_renaming_declaration</a></code><br /> | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0242">subprogram_renaming_declaration</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>7_10.1.1</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>library{"_"}unit{"_"}body</code><a id="S0290"></a><code> ::= </code><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.3#S0216">subprogram_body</a></code> | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.2#S0231">package_body</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>8_10.1.1</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>parent{"_"}unit{"_"}name</code><a id="S0291"></a><code> ::= </code><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>8.1/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00397-01"]} />
<p class="Indented2">An <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.3#S0234">overriding_indicator</a></code> is not allowed in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0195">subprogram_declaration</a></code>, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code>, or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0242">subprogram_renaming_declaration</a></code> that declares a library unit.<br /></p>

<MarginText>8.a.1/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>All of the listed items syntactically include <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.3#S0234">overriding_indicator</a></code>, but a library unit can never override anything. A majority of the ARG thought that allowing <b>not overriding</b> in that case would be confusing instead of helpful. <br />

<MarginText>9_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>A <i>library unit</i> is a program unit that is declared by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code>. When a program unit is a library unit, the prefix &ldquo;library&rdquo; is used to refer to it (or &ldquo;generic library&rdquo; if generic), as well as to its declaration and body, as in &ldquo;library procedure&rdquo;, &ldquo;library <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.2#S0231">package_body</a></code>&rdquo;, or &ldquo;generic library package&rdquo;. The term <i>compilation unit</i> is used to refer to a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code>. When the meaning is clear from context, the term is also used to refer to the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code> or to the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.11#S0090">proper_body</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0302">subunit</a></code> [(that is, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code> without the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0292">context_clause</a></code> and the <b>separate</b> (<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0291">parent_unit_name</a></code>))]. <br /></p>

<MarginText>9.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>In this example: <br />

<MarginText>9.b_10.1.1</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
with Ada.Text{"_"}IO;{"\n"}package P is{"\n"}    ...{"\n"}end P;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>9.c_10.1.1</MarginText>
the term &ldquo;compilation unit&rdquo; can refer to this text: &ldquo;<b>with</b> Ada.Text{"_"}IO; <b>package</b> P <b>is</b> ... <b>end</b> P;&rdquo; or to this text: &ldquo;<b>package</b> P <b>is</b> ... <b>end</b> P;&rdquo;. We use this shorthand because it corresponds to common usage.<br />

<MarginText>9.d_10.1.1</MarginText>
We like to use the word &ldquo;unit&rdquo; for declaration-plus-body things, and &ldquo;item&rdquo; for declaration or body separately (as in <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.11#S0087">declarative_item</a></code>). The terms &ldquo;<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code>&rdquo;, &ldquo;compilation unit&rdquo;, and &ldquo;<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0302">subunit</a></code>&rdquo; are exceptions to this rule. We considered changing &ldquo;<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code>&rdquo;, &ldquo;compilation unit&rdquo; to &ldquo;<code>compilation{"_"}item</code>&rdquo;, &ldquo;compilation item&rdquo;, respectively, but we decided not to. <br />

<MarginText>10_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>The <i>parent declaration</i> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> (and of the library unit) is the declaration denoted by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0291">parent{"_"}unit{"_"}name</a></code>, if any, of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0201">defining{"_"}program{"_"}unit{"_"}name</a></code> of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code>. If there is no <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0291">parent{"_"}unit{"_"}name</a></code>, the parent declaration is the declaration of Standard, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> is a <i>root</i> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code>, and the library unit (renaming) is a <i>root</i> library unit (renaming). The declaration and body of Standard itself have no parent declaration. The <i>parent unit</i> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> or library unit is the library unit declared by its parent declaration. <br /></p>

<MarginText>10.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The declaration and body of Standard are presumed to exist from the beginning of time, as it were. There is no way to actually write them, since there is no syntactic way to indicate lack of a parent. An attempt to compile a package Standard would result in Standard.Standard. <br />

<MarginText>10.b_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>Library units (other than Standard) have &ldquo;parent declarations&rdquo; and &ldquo;parent units&rdquo;. Subunits have &ldquo;parent bodies&rdquo;. We didn't bother to define the other possibilities: parent body of a library unit, parent declaration of a subunit, parent unit of a subunit. These are not needed, and might get in the way of a correct definition of &ldquo;child&rdquo;. <br />

<MarginText>11_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>[The children of a library unit occur immediately within the declarative region of the declaration of the library unit.] The <i>ancestors</i> of a library unit are itself, its parent, its parent's parent, and so on. [(Standard is an ancestor of every library unit.)] The <i>descendant</i> relation is the inverse of the ancestor relation. <br /></p>

<MarginText>11.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>These definitions are worded carefully to avoid defining subunits as children. Only library units can be children.<br />

<MarginText>11.b_10.1.1</MarginText>
We use the unadorned term &ldquo;ancestors&rdquo; here to concisely define both &ldquo;ancestor unit&rdquo; and &ldquo;ancestor declaration&rdquo;. <br />

<MarginText>12_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0288">library_unit_declaration</a></code> or a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0289">library{"_"}unit{"_"}renaming{"_"}declaration</a></code> is <i>private</i> if the declaration is immediately preceded by the reserved word <b>private</b>; it is otherwise <i>public</i>. A library unit is private or public according to its declaration. The <i>public descendants</i> of a library unit are the library unit itself, and the public descendants of its public children. Its other descendants are <i>private descendants</i>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>12.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The first concept defined here is that a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> is either public or private (not in relation to anything else &mdash; it's just a property of the library unit). The second concept is that a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> is a public descendant or private descendant <i>of a given ancestor</i>. A given <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> can be a public descendant of one of its ancestors, but a private descendant of some other ancestor.<br />

<MarginText>12.b_10.1.1</MarginText>
A subprogram declared by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.3#S0216">subprogram_body</a></code> (as opposed to a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0195">subprogram_declaration</a></code>) is always public, since the syntax rules disallow the reserved word <b>private</b> on a body.<br />

<MarginText>12.c_10.1.1</MarginText>
Note that a private library unit is a <i>public</i> descendant of itself, but a <i>private</i> descendant of its parent. This is because it is visible outside itself &mdash; its privateness means that it is not visible outside its parent.<br />

<MarginText>12.d_10.1.1</MarginText>
Private children of Standard are legal, and follow the normal rules. It is intended that implementations might have some method for taking an existing environment, and treating it as a package to be &ldquo;imported&rdquo; into another environment, treating children of Standard in the imported environment as children of the imported package. <br />

<MarginText>12.e_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Suppose we have a public library unit A, a private library unit A.B, and a public library unit A.B.C. A.B.C is a public descendant of itself and of A.B, but a private descendant of A; since A.B is private to A, we don't allow A.B.C to escape outside A either. This is similar to the situation that would occur with physical nesting, like this: <br />

<MarginText>12.f_10.1.1</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package A is{"\n"}private{"\n"}    package B is{"\n"}        package C is{"\n"}        end C;{"\n"}    private{"\n"}    end B;{"\n"}end A;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>12.g_10.1.1</MarginText>
Here, A.B.C is visible outside itself and outside A.B, but not outside A. (Note that this example is intended to illustrate the visibility of program units from the outside; the visibility within child units is not quite identical to that of physically nested units, since child units are nested after their parent's declaration.) <br />

<MarginText>12.1/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00217-06"]} />
<p>For each library <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0229">package_declaration</a></code> in the environment, there is an implicit declaration of a <i>limited view</i> of that library package. The limited view of a package contains:<br /></p>

<MarginText>12.2/3_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00217-06", "AI05-0129-1", "AI05-0262-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>For each <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0229">package_declaration</a></code> occurring immediately within the visible part, a declaration of the limited view of that package, with the same <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0201">defining_program_unit_name</a></code>.<br /></li>
<MarginText>12.3/3_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00217-06", "AI95-00326-01", "AI05-0108-1", "AI05-0129-1", "AI05-0262-1"]} />
<li>For each <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0023">type_declaration</a></code> occurring immediately within the visible part that is not an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0085">incomplete_type_declaration</a></code>, an incomplete view of the type with no <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0059">discriminant_part</a></code>; if the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0023">type_declaration</a></code> is tagged, then the view is a tagged incomplete view. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>12.g.1/3_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0108-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The incomplete view of a type does not have a discriminant{"_"}part even if the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0023">type_declaration</a></code> does have one. This is necessary because semantic analysis (and the associated dependence on <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code>s) would be necessary to determine the types of the discriminants.<br />

<MarginText>12.g.2/3_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0129-1"]} />
No incomplete views of incomplete types are included in the limited view. The rules of <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#Subclause_3.10.1">3.10.1</a> ensure that the completion of any visible incomplete type is declared in the same visible part, so such an incomplete view would simply be redundant. <br />

<MarginText>12.g.3/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00217-06"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The implementation model of a limited view is that it can be determined solely from the syntax of the source of the unit, without any semantic analysis. That allows it to be created without the semantic dependences of a full unit, which is necessary for it to break mutual dependences of units. <br />

<MarginText>12.g.4/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The limited view does not include package instances and their contents. Semantic analysis of a unit (and dependence on its <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code>s) would be needed to determine the contents of an instance. <br />

<MarginText>12.4/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>The limited view of a library <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0229">package_declaration</a></code> is private if that library <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0229">package_declaration</a></code> is immediately preceded by the reserved word <b>private</b>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>12.5/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>[There is no syntax for declaring limited views of packages, because they are always implicit.] The implicit declaration of a limited view of a library package [is not the declaration of a library unit (the library <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0229">package_declaration</a></code> is); nonetheless, it] is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code>. The implicit declaration of the limited view of a library package forms an (implicit) compilation unit whose <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0292">context_clause</a></code> is empty.<br /></p>

<MarginText>12.6/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>A library <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0229">package_declaration</a></code> is the completion of the declaration of its limited view.<br /></p>

<MarginText>12.h/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>This is notwithstanding the rule in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.11#Subclause_3.11.1">3.11.1</a> that says that implicit declarations don't have completions. <br />

<MarginText>12.i/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This rule explains where to find the completions of the incomplete views defined by the limited view. <br />

#### Legality Rules

<MarginText>13_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>The parent unit of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> shall be a [library] package or generic [library] package.<br /></p>

<MarginText>14_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>If a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0201">defining_program_unit_name</a></code> of a given declaration or body has a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0291">parent_unit_name</a></code>, then the given declaration or body shall be a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code>. The body of a program unit shall be a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> if and only if the declaration of the program unit is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code>. In a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0289">library{"_"}unit{"_"}renaming{"_"}declaration</a></code>, the [(old)] <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> shall denote a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>14.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>We could have allowed nested program units to be children of other program units; their semantics would make sense. We disallow them to keep things simpler and because they wouldn't be particularly useful. <br />

<MarginText>15/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00217-06"]} />
<p>A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0291">parent_unit_name</a></code> [(which can be used within a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0201">defining_program_unit_name</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> and in the <b>separate</b> clause of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0302">subunit</a></code>)], and each of its <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>es, shall not denote a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0238">renaming_declaration</a></code>. [On the other hand, a name that denotes a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0289">library{"_"}unit{"_"}renaming{"_"}declaration</a></code> is allowed in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0296">nonlimited_with_clause</a></code> and other places where the name of a library unit is allowed.]<br /></p>

<MarginText>16_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>If a library package is an instance of a generic package, then every child of the library package shall either be itself an instance or be a renaming of a library unit. <br /></p>

<MarginText>16.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>A child of an instance of a given generic unit will often be an instance of a (generic) child of the given generic unit. This is not required, however. <br />

<MarginText>16.b_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>Instances are forbidden from having noninstance children for two reasons: <br />

<MarginText>16.c_10.1.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/>1.</dt>
<dl>
<dd>We want all source code that can depend on information from the private part of a library unit to be inside the "subsystem" rooted at the library unit. If an instance of a generic unit were allowed to have a noninstance as a child, the source code of that child might depend on information from the private part of the generic unit, even though it is outside the subsystem rooted at the generic unit.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>16.d_10.1.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/>2.</dt>
<dd>Disallowing noninstance children simplifies the description of the semantics of children of generic packages. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>17/3_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0004-1"]} />
<p>A child of a generic library package shall either be itself a generic unit or be a renaming of some other child of the same generic unit.<br /></p>

<MarginText>18_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>A child of a parent generic package shall be instantiated or renamed only within the declarative region of the parent generic.<br /></p>

<MarginText>19/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00331-01"]} />
<p>For each child <i>C</i> of some parent generic package <i>P</i>, there is a corresponding declaration <i>C</i> nested immediately within each instance of <i>P</i>. For the purposes of this rule, if a child <i>C</i> itself has a child <i>D</i>, each corresponding declaration for <i>C</i> has a corresponding child <i>D</i>. [The corresponding declaration for a child within an instance is visible only within the scope of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code> that mentions the (original) child generic unit.]<br /></p>

<MarginText>19.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>Within the child, like anything nested in a generic unit, one can make up-level references to the current instance of its parent, and thereby gain access to the formal parameters of the parent, to the types declared in the parent, etc. This &ldquo;nesting&rdquo; model applies even within the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code> of the child, as it does for a generic child of a nongeneric unit. <br />

<MarginText>19.b_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Suppose P is a generic library package, and P.C is a generic child of P. P.C can be instantiated inside the declarative region of P. Outside P, P.C can be mentioned only in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code>. Conceptually, an instance I of P is a package that has a nested generic unit called I.C. Mentioning P.C in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code> allows I.C to be instantiated. I need not be a library unit, and the instantiation of I.C need not be a library unit. If I is a library unit, and an instance of I.C is a child of I, then this instance has to be called something other than C.<br />

<MarginText>20_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>A library subprogram shall not override a primitive subprogram. <br /></p>

<MarginText>20.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This prevents certain obscure anomalies. For example, if a library subprogram were to override a subprogram declared in its parent package, then in a compilation unit that depends <i>in</i>directly on the library subprogram, the library subprogram could hide the overridden operation from all visibility, but the library subprogram itself would not be visible.<br />

<MarginText>20.b_10.1.1</MarginText>
Note that even without this rule, such subprograms would be illegal for tagged types, because of the freezing rules. <br />

<MarginText>21_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>The defining name of a function that is a compilation unit shall not be an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0202">operator_symbol</a></code>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>21.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>Since overloading is not permitted among compilation units, it seems unlikely that it would be useful to define one as an operator. Note that a subunit could be renamed within its parent to be an operator. <br />

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>22_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0242">subprogram_renaming_declaration</a></code> that is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0289">library{"_"}unit{"_"}renaming{"_"}declaration</a></code> is a renaming-as-declaration, not a renaming-as-body.<br /></p>

<MarginText>23_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>[There are two kinds of dependences among compilation units:] <br /></p>

<MarginText>24/5_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0445-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>[The <i>semantic dependences</i> (see below) are the ones necessary to check the compile-time rules across compilation unit boundaries; a compilation unit depends semantically on the other compilation units necessary to determine its legality. The visibility rules are based on the semantic dependences.<br /></li>
<MarginText>25_10.1.1</MarginText>
<li>The <i>elaboration dependences</i> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.2">10.2</a>) determine the order of elaboration of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code>s.] <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>25.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Don't confuse these kinds of dependences with the run-time dependences among tasks and masters defined in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.3">9.3</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.3">Task Dependence - Termination of Tasks</a>&rdquo;. <br />

<MarginText>26/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00217-06"]} />
<p>A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> depends semantically upon its parent declaration. A subunit depends semantically upon its parent body. A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0290">library_unit_body</a></code> depends semantically upon the corresponding <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0288">library_unit_declaration</a></code>, if any. The declaration of the limited view of a library package depends semantically upon the declaration of the limited view of its parent. The declaration of a library package depends semantically upon the declaration of its limited view. A compilation unit depends semantically upon each <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code> mentioned in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code> of the compilation unit. In addition, if a given compilation unit contains an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0100">attribute_reference</a></code> of a type defined in another compilation unit, then the given compilation unit depends semantically upon the other compilation unit. The semantic dependence relationship is transitive.<br /></p>

<MarginText>26.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The &ldquo;if any&rdquo; in the third sentence is necessary because library subprograms are not required to have a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0195">subprogram_declaration</a></code>. <br />

<MarginText>26.b_10.1.1</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>If a given compilation unit contains a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.2#S0306">choice_parameter_specification</a></code>, then the given compilation unit depends semantically upon the declaration of Ada.Exceptions.<br />

<MarginText>26.c_10.1.1</MarginText>
If a given compilation unit contains a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.8#S0019">pragma</a></code> with an argument of a type defined in another compilation unit, then the given compilation unit depends semantically upon the other compilation unit. <br />

<MarginText>26.d_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>For example, a compilation unit containing X'Address depends semantically upon the declaration of package System.<br />

<MarginText>26.e_10.1.1</MarginText>
For the Address attribute, this fixes a hole in Ada 83. Note that in almost all cases, the dependence will need to exist due to <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code>s, even without this rule. Hence, the rule has very little effect on programmers.<br />

<MarginText>26.f_10.1.1</MarginText>
Note that the semantic dependence does not have the same effect as a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code>; in order to denote a declaration in one of those packages, a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code> will generally be needed.<br />

<MarginText>26.g_10.1.1</MarginText>
Note that no special rule is needed for an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code>, since an expression after <b>use</b> will require semantic dependence upon the compilation unit containing the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0023">type_declaration</a></code> of interest.<br />

<MarginText>26.h/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00217-06"]} />
Unlike a full view of a package, a limited view does not depend semantically on units mentioned in <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code>s of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0286">compilation_unit</a></code> that defines the package. Formally, this is achieved by saying that the limited view has an empty <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0292">context_clause</a></code>. This is necessary so that they can be useful for their intended purpose: allowing mutual dependences between packages. The lack of semantic dependence limits the contents of a limited view to the items that can be determined solely from the syntax of the source of the package, without any semantic analysis. That allows it to be created without the semantic dependences of a full package. <br />

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>26.1/2_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00217-06"]} />
<p>The elaboration of the declaration of the limited view of a package has no effect. <br /></p>

<MarginText>27/5_10.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0442-1"]} />
NOTE 1   A simple program can consist of a single compilation unit. A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code> can have no compilation units; for example, its text can consist of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.8#S0019">pragma</a></code>s. <br />

<MarginText>27.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Such <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.8#S0019">pragma</a></code>s cannot have any arguments that are <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>s, by a previous rule of this subclause. A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0285">compilation</a></code> can even be entirely empty, which is probably not useful.<br />

<MarginText>27.b_10.1.1</MarginText>
Some interesting properties of the three kinds of dependence: The elaboration dependences also include the semantic dependences, except that subunits are taken together with their parents. The semantic dependences partly determine the order in which the compilation units appear in the environment at compile time. At run time, the order is partly determined by the elaboration dependences.<br />

<MarginText>27.c_10.1.1</MarginText>
The model whereby a child is inside its parent's declarative region, after the parent's declaration, as explained in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.1">8.1</a>, has the following ramifications: <br />

<MarginText>27.d_10.1.1</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>The restrictions on &ldquo;early&rdquo; use of a private type (RM83-7.4.1(4)) or a deferred constant (RM83-7.4.3(2)) do not apply to uses in child units, because they follow the full declaration.<br /></li>
<MarginText>27.e_10.1.1</MarginText>
<li>A library subprogram is never primitive, even if its profile includes a type declared immediately within the parent's <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0230">package_specification</a></code>, because the child is not declared immediately within the same <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0230">package_specification</a></code> as the type (so it doesn't declare a new primitive subprogram), and because the child is forbidden from overriding an old primitive subprogram. It is immediately within the same declarative region, but not the same <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0230">package_specification</a></code>. Thus, for a tagged type, it is not possible to call a child subprogram in a dispatching manner. (This is also forbidden by the freezing rules.) Similarly, it is not possible for the user to declare primitive subprograms of the types declared in the declaration of Standard, such as Integer (even if the rules were changed to allow a library unit whose name is an operator symbol).<br /></li>
<MarginText>27.f_10.1.1</MarginText>
<li>When the parent unit is &ldquo;used&rdquo; the simple names of the with'd child units are directly visible (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.4">8.4</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.4">Use Clauses</a>&rdquo;).<br /></li>
<MarginText>27.g_10.1.1</MarginText>
<li>When a parent body with's its own child, the defining name of the child is directly visible, and the parent body is not allowed to include a declaration of a homograph of the child unit immediately within the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.11#S0086">declarative_part</a></code> of the body (RM83-8.3(17)). <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>27.h_10.1.1</MarginText>
Note that &ldquo;declaration of a library unit&rdquo; is different from &ldquo;<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0288">library_unit_declaration</a></code>&rdquo; &mdash; the former includes <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.3#S0216">subprogram_body</a></code>. Also, we sometimes really mean &ldquo;declaration of a view of a library unit&rdquo;, which includes <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0289">library{"_"}unit{"_"}renaming{"_"}declaration</a></code>s.<br />

<MarginText>27.i_10.1.1</MarginText>
The visibility rules generally imply that the renamed view of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0289">library{"_"}unit{"_"}renaming{"_"}declaration</a></code> has to be mentioned in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with{"_"}clause</a></code> of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0289">library{"_"}unit{"_"}renaming{"_"}declaration</a></code>. <br />

<MarginText>27.j_10.1.1</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>The real rule is that the renamed library unit has to be visible in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0289">library{"_"}unit{"_"}renaming{"_"}declaration</a></code>. <br />

<MarginText>27.k_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>In most cases, &ldquo;has to be visible&rdquo; means there has to be a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code>. However, it is possible in obscure cases to avoid the need for a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code>; in particular, a compilation unit such as &ldquo;<b>package</b> P.Q <b>renames</b> P;&rdquo; is legal with no <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code>s (though not particularly interesting). ASCII is physically nested in Standard, and so is not a library unit, and cannot be renamed as a library unit. <br />

<MarginText>28_10.1.1</MarginText>
NOTE 2   The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0199">designator</a></code> of a library function cannot be an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0202">operator_symbol</a></code>, but a nonlibrary <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0238">renaming_declaration</a></code> is allowed to rename a library function as an operator. Within a partition, two library subprograms are required to have distinct names and hence cannot overload each other. However, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0238">renaming_declaration</a></code>s are allowed to define overloaded names for such subprograms, and a locally declared subprogram is allowed to overload a library subprogram. The expanded name Standard.L can be used to denote a root library unit L (unless the declaration of Standard is hidden) since root library unit declarations occur immediately within the declarative region of package Standard. <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>29_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of library units:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>30_10.1.1</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package Rational{"_"}Numbers.IO is  -- public child of Rational{"_"}Numbers, see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1">7.1</a>{"\n"}   procedure Put(R : in  Rational);{"\n"}   procedure Get(R : out Rational);{"\n"}end Rational{"_"}Numbers.IO;{"\n"}
<MarginText>31_10.1.1</MarginText>
private procedure Rational{"_"}Numbers.Reduce(R : in out Rational);{"\n"}                                -- private child of Rational{"_"}Numbers{"\n"}
<MarginText>32_10.1.1</MarginText>
with Rational{"_"}Numbers.Reduce;   -- refer to a private child{"\n"}package body Rational{"_"}Numbers is{"\n"}   ...{"\n"}end Rational{"_"}Numbers;{"\n"}
<MarginText>33_10.1.1</MarginText>
with Rational{"_"}Numbers.IO; use Rational{"_"}Numbers;{"\n"}with Ada.Text{"_"}io;               -- see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-A/AA-A.10">A.10</a>{"\n"}procedure Main is               -- a root library procedure{"\n"}   R : Rational;{"\n"}begin{"\n"}   R := 5/3;                    -- construct a rational number, see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1">7.1</a>{"\n"}   Ada.Text{"_"}IO.Put("The answer is: ");{"\n"}   IO.Put(R);{"\n"}   Ada.Text{"_"}IO.New{"_"}Line;{"\n"}end Main;{"\n"}
<MarginText>34_10.1.1</MarginText>
with Rational{"_"}Numbers.IO;{"\n"}package Rational{"_"}IO renames Rational{"_"}Numbers.IO;{"\n"}                                -- a library unit renaming declaration{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>35_10.1.1</MarginText>
<p>Each of the above <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0287">library_item</a></code>s can be submitted to the compiler separately. <br /></p>

<MarginText>35.a_10.1.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b><i>Example of a generic package with children:</i><br />

<MarginText>35.b_10.1.1</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
generic{"\n"}   type Element is private;{"\n"}   with function Image(E : Element) return String;{"\n"}package Generic{"_"}Bags is{"\n"}   type Bag is limited private; -- A bag of Elements.{"\n"}   procedure Add(B : in out Bag; E : Element);{"\n"}   function Bag{"_"}Image(B : Bag) return String;{"\n"}private{"\n"}   type Bag is ...;{"\n"}end Generic{"_"}Bags;{"\n"}
<MarginText>35.c_10.1.1</MarginText>
