# 11.6. Exceptions and Optimization

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.6.mdx

sidebar_position:  94

# 11.6. Exceptions and Optimization

<MarginText>1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
<p>[ This subclause gives permission to the implementation to perform certain &ldquo;optimizations&rdquo; that do not necessarily preserve the canonical semantics.] <br /></p>

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>2/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
<p>The rest of this Reference Manual (outside this subclause) defines the <i>canonical semantics</i> of the language. [The canonical semantics of a given (legal) program determines a set of possible external effects that can result from the execution of the program with given inputs.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Note that the canonical semantics is a set of possible behaviors, since some reordering, parallelism, and nondeterminism is allowed by the canonical semantics. <br />

<MarginText>2.b/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The following parts of the canonical semantics are of particular interest to the reader of this subclause: <br />

<MarginText>2.c</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>Behavior in the presence of abnormal objects and objects with invalid representations (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.9#Subclause_13.9.1">13.9.1</a>).<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.d</MarginText>
<li>Various actions that are defined to occur in an arbitrary order.<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.e</MarginText>
<li>Behavior in the presence of a misuse of Unchecked{"_"}Deallocation, Unchecked{"_"}Access, or imported or exported entity (see Clause <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/">13</a>). <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>3/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
<p>[As explained in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-1/AA-1.1#Subclause_1.1.3">1.1.3</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-1/AA-1.1#Subclause_1.1.3">Conformity of an Implementation</a>&rdquo;, the external effect of a program is defined in terms of its interactions with its external environment. Hence, the implementation can perform any internal actions whatsoever, in any order or in parallel, so long as the external effect of the execution of the program is one that is allowed by the canonical semantics, or by the rules of this subclause.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>3.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Note that an optimization can change the external effect of the program, so long as the changed external effect is an external effect that is allowed by the semantics. Note that the canonical semantics of an erroneous execution allows any external effect whatsoever. Hence, if the implementation can prove that program execution will be erroneous in certain circumstances, there need not be any constraints on the machine code executed in those circumstances. <br />

#### Implementation Permissions

<MarginText>4</MarginText>
<p>The following additional permissions are granted to the implementation: <br /></p>

<MarginText>5/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0444-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>An implementation can omit raising an exception when a language-defined check fails. Instead, the operation that failed the check can simply yield an <i>undefined result</i>. The exception is required to be raised by the implementation only if, in the absence of raising it, the value of this undefined result would have some effect on the external interactions of the program. In determining this, the implementation shall not presume that an undefined result has a value that belongs to its subtype, nor even to the base range of its type, if scalar. [Having removed the raise of the exception, the canonical semantics will in general allow the implementation to omit the code for the check, and some or all of the operation itself.] <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>5.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Even without this permission, an implementation can always remove a check if it cannot possibly fail. <br />

<MarginText>5.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We express the permission in terms of removing the raise, rather than the operation or the check, as it minimizes the disturbance to the canonical semantics (thereby simplifying reasoning). By allowing the implementation to omit the raise, it thereby does not need to "look" at what happens in the exception handler to decide whether the optimization is allowed. <br />

<MarginText>5.c</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The implementation can also omit checks if they cannot possibly fail, or if they could only fail in erroneous executions. This follows from the canonical semantics. <br />

<MarginText>5.d</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>This permission is intended to allow normal "dead code removal" optimizations, even if some of the removed code might have failed some language-defined check. However, one may not eliminate the raise of an exception if subsequent code presumes in some way that the check succeeded. For example: <br />

<MarginText>5.e</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
  if X {"*"} Y {">"} Integer'Last then{"\n"}      Put{"_"}Line("X {"*"} Y overflowed");{"\n"}  end if;{"\n"}exception{"\n"}  when others ={">"}{"\n"}      Put{"_"}Line("X {"*"} Y overflowed");{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>5.e.1</MarginText>
If X{"*"}Y does overflow, you may not remove the raise of the exception if the code that does the comparison against Integer'Last presumes that it is comparing it with an in-range Integer value, and hence always yields False.<br />

<MarginText>5.f</MarginText>
As another example where a raise may not be eliminated: <br />

<MarginText>5.g</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
  subtype Str10 is String(1..10);{"\n"}  type P10 is access Str10;{"\n"}  X : P10 := null;{"\n"}begin{"\n"}  if X.all'Last = 10 then{"\n"}      Put{"_"}Line("Oops");{"\n"}  end if;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>5.g.1</MarginText>
In the above code, it would be wrong to eliminate the raise of Constraint{"_"}Error on the "X.all" (since X is null), if the code to evaluate 'Last always yields 10 by presuming that X.all belongs to the subtype Str10, without even "looking". <br />

<MarginText>6/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1", "AI12-0445-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>If an exception is raised due to the failure of a language-defined check, then upon reaching the corresponding <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.2#S0305">exception_handler</a></code> (or the termination of the task, if none), the external interactions that have occurred have to reflect only that the exception was raised somewhere within the execution of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.1#S0166">sequence_of_statements</a></code> with the handler (or the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.1#S0248">task_body</a></code>), possibly earlier (or later if the interactions are independent of the result of the checked operation) than that defined by the canonical semantics, but not within the execution of some abort-deferred operation or <i>independent</i> subprogram that does not dynamically enclose the execution of the construct whose check failed. An independent subprogram is one that is defined outside the library unit containing the construct whose check failed, and for which the Inline aspect is False. Any assignment that occurred outside of such abort-deferred operations or independent subprograms can be disrupted by the raising of the exception, causing the object or its parts to become abnormal, and certain subsequent uses of the object to be erroneous, as explained in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.9#Subclause_13.9.1">13.9.1</a>. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>6.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We allow such variables to become abnormal so that assignments (other than to atomic variables) can be disrupted due to &ldquo;imprecise&rdquo; exceptions or instruction scheduling, and so that assignments can be reordered so long as the correct results are produced in the end if no language-defined checks fail. <br />

<MarginText>6.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>If a check fails, no result dependent on the check may be incorporated in an external interaction. In other words, there is no permission to output meaningless results due to postponing a check. <br />

<MarginText>6.c</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>We believe it is important to state the extra permission to reorder actions in terms of what the programmer can expect at run time, rather than in terms of what the implementation can assume, or what transformations the implementation can perform. Otherwise, how can the programmer write reliable programs?<br />

<MarginText>6.d/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
This subclause has two conflicting goals: to allow as much optimization as possible, and to make program execution as predictable as possible (to ease the writing of reliable programs). The rules given above represent a compromise.<br />

<MarginText>6.e</MarginText>
Consider the two extremes:<br />

<MarginText>6.f/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
The extreme conservative rule would be to delete this subclause entirely. The semantics of Ada would be the canonical semantics. This achieves the best predictability. It sounds like a disaster from the efficiency point of view, but in practice, implementations would provide modes in which less predictability but more efficiency would be achieved. Such a mode could even be the out-of-the-box mode. In practice, implementers would provide a compromise based on their customer's needs. Therefore, we view this as one viable alternative.<br />

<MarginText>6.g</MarginText>
The extreme liberal rule would be &ldquo;the language does not specify the execution of a program once a language-defined check has failed; such execution can be unpredictable&rdquo;. This achieves the best efficiency. It sounds like a disaster from the predictability point of view, but in practice it might not be so bad. A user would have to assume that exception handlers for exceptions raised by language-defined checks are not portable. They would have to isolate such code (like all nonportable code), and would have to find out, for each implementation of interest, what behaviors can be expected. In practice, implementations would tend to avoid going so far as to punish their customers too much in terms of predictability.<br />

<MarginText>6.h/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
The most important thing about this subclause is that users understand what they can expect at run time, and implementers understand what optimizations are allowed. Any solution that makes this subclause contain rules that can interpreted in more than one way is unacceptable.<br />

<MarginText>6.i</MarginText>
We have chosen a compromise between the extreme conservative and extreme liberal rules. The current rule essentially allows arbitrary optimizations within a library unit and inlined subprograms reachable from it, but disallow semantics-disrupting optimizations across library units in the absence of inlined subprograms. This allows a library unit to be debugged, and then reused with some confidence that the abstraction it manages cannot be broken by bugs outside the library unit. <br />

<MarginText>7/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
NOTE   The permissions granted by this subclause can have an effect on the semantics of a program only if the program fails a language-defined check. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>7.a</MarginText>
RM83-11.6 was unclear. It has been completely rewritten here; we hope this version is clearer. Here's what happened to each paragraph of RM83-11.6: <br />

<MarginText>7.b</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>Paragraphs 1 and 2 contain no semantics; they are merely pointing out that anything goes if the canonical semantics is preserved. We have similar introductory paragraphs, but we have tried to clarify that these are not granting any &ldquo;extra&rdquo; permission beyond what the rest of the document allows.<br /></li>
<MarginText>7.c</MarginText>
<li>Paragraphs 3 and 4 are reflected in the &ldquo;extra permission to reorder actions&rdquo;. Note that this permission now allows the reordering of assignments in many cases.<br /></li>
<MarginText>7.d</MarginText>
<li>Paragraph 5 is moved to <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5">4.5</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5">Operators and Expression Evaluation</a>&rdquo;, where operator association is discussed. Hence, this is no longer an &ldquo;extra permission&rdquo; but is part of the canonical semantics.<br /></li>
<MarginText>7.e</MarginText>
<li>Paragraph 6 now follows from the general permission to store out-of-range values for unconstrained subtypes. Note that the parameters and results of all the predefined operators of a type are of the unconstrained subtype of the type.<br /></li>
<MarginText>7.f</MarginText>
<li>Paragraph 7 is reflected in the &ldquo;extra permission to avoid raising exceptions&rdquo;. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>7.g/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1", "AI12-0005-1"]} />
We moved subclause <a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.5">11.5</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.5">Suppressing Checks</a>&rdquo; (which was numbered 11.7) from after 11.6 to before 11.6, in order to preserve the famous number &ldquo;11.6&rdquo; (given the changes to earlier subclauses in Clause <a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/">11</a>). <br />

# 11. Exceptions

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.mdx

sidebar_position:  88

# 11. Exceptions

<MarginText>1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
<p>[This clause defines the facilities for dealing with errors or other exceptional situations that arise during program execution.] An <i>exception</i> represents a kind of exceptional situation; an occurrence of such a situation (at run time) is called an <i>exception occurrence</i>. [ To <i>raise</i> an exception is to abandon normal program execution so as to draw attention to the fact that the corresponding situation has arisen. Performing some actions in response to the arising of an exception is called <i>handling</i> the exception. ]<br /></p>

<MarginText>1.a</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>...or handling the exception occurrence. <br />

<MarginText>1.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>For example, an exception End{"_"}Error might represent error situations in which an attempt is made to read beyond end-of-file. During the execution of a partition, there might be numerous occurrences of this exception. <br />

<MarginText>1.c/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0426-1"]} />
<b>To be honest: </b>When the meaning is clear from the context, we sometimes use &ldquo;<i>occurrence</i>&rdquo; as a shorthand for &ldquo;exception occurrence&rdquo;. <br />

<MarginText>1.d/5</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>exception</b> &mdash; kind of exceptional situation<br />

<MarginText>1.e/5</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>exception occurrence</b> &mdash; run-time occurrence of an exceptional situation<br />

<MarginText>2/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0043-1", "AI05-0258-1"]} />
<p>[An <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.1#S0303">exception_declaration</a></code> declares a name for an exception. An exception can be raised explicitly (for example, by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.3#S0308">raise_statement</a></code>) or implicitly (for example, by the failure of a language-defined check). When an exception arises, control can be transferred to a user-provided <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.2#S0305">exception_handler</a></code> at the end of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.2#S0304">handled{"_"}sequence{"_"}of{"_"}statements</a></code>, or it can be propagated to a dynamically enclosing execution.] <br /></p>

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>2.a</MarginText>
We are more explicit about the difference between an exception and an occurrence of an exception. This is necessary because we now have a type (Exception{"_"}Occurrence) that represents exception occurrences, so the program can manipulate them. Furthermore, we say that when an exception is propagated, it is the same occurrence that is being propagated (as opposed to a new occurrence of the same exception). The same issue applies to a re-raise statement. In order to understand these semantics, we have to make this distinction. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>2.b/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0043-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Generalized the introductory description of how an exception can be raised so that it does not appear to cover all of the cases. <br />

# 12.1. Generic Declarations

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1.mdx

# 12.1. Generic Declarations

<MarginText>1</MarginText>
<p>[A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code> declares a generic unit, which is either a generic subprogram or a generic package. A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code> includes a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code> declaring any generic formal parameters. A generic formal parameter can be an object; alternatively (unlike a parameter of a subprogram), it can be a type, a subprogram, or a package.] <br /></p>

#### Syntax

<MarginText>2</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>generic{"_"}declaration</code><a id="S0310"></a><code> ::= </code><br />    <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0311">generic_subprogram_declaration</a></code> | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0312">generic_package_declaration</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0183-1"]} />

<CodeBlock>
<code>generic{"_"}subprogram{"_"}declaration</code><a id="S0311"></a><code> ::= </code><br />    <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0196">subprogram_specification</a></code><br />       [<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code>];<br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>4</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>generic{"_"}package{"_"}declaration</code><a id="S0312"></a><code> ::= </code><br />    <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code>  <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0230">package_specification</a></code>;<br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>4.a/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0183-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>No syntax change is needed here to allow an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code>; a generic package can have an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code> because a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0230">package_specification</a></code> allows an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code>. <br />

<MarginText>5</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>generic{"_"}formal{"_"}part</code><a id="S0313"></a><code> ::= </code><br />    <b>generic</b> {"{"}<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code> | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.4#S0235">use_clause</a></code>{"}"}<br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>6</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>generic{"_"}formal{"_"}parameter{"_"}declaration</code><a id="S0314"></a><code> ::= </code><br />    <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.4#S0319">formal_object_declaration</a></code><br />  | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.5#S0320">formal_type_declaration</a></code><br />  | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6#S0335">formal_subprogram_declaration</a></code><br />  | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.7#S0340">formal_package_declaration</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>7</MarginText>
<p class="Indented2">The only form of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> allowed within a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code> is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code> [(that is, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> shall not include an explicit <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0029">constraint</a></code>)]. The defining name of a generic subprogram shall be an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.3#S0002">identifier</a></code> [(not an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0202">operator_symbol</a></code>)]. <br /></p>

<MarginText>7.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The reason for forbidding <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0029">constraint</a></code>s in <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code>s is that it simplifies the elaboration of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code>s (since there is nothing to evaluate), and that it simplifies the matching rules, and makes them more checkable at compile time. <br />

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>8/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00434-01"]} />
<p>A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code> declares a generic unit &mdash; a generic package, generic procedure, or generic function, as appropriate.<br /></p>

<MarginText>9</MarginText>
<p>An entity is a <i>generic formal</i> entity if it is declared by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code>. &ldquo;Generic formal&rdquo;, or simply &ldquo;formal&rdquo;, is used as a prefix in referring to objects, subtypes (and types), functions, procedures and packages, that are generic formal entities, as well as to their respective declarations. [Examples: &ldquo;generic formal procedure&rdquo; or a &ldquo;formal integer type declaration&rdquo;.]<br /></p>

<MarginText>9.1/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0371-1"]} />
<p>The list of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code>s of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code> form a <i>declaration list</i> of the generic unit.<br /></p>

<MarginText>9.a/5</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Aspect specifications (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#Subclause_13.1.1">13.1.1</a>) given in a generic formal part can only use declarations given in the formal part, and not those in the visible part of the generic unit. <br />

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>10</MarginText>
<p>The elaboration of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code> has no effect. <br /></p>

<MarginText>11</MarginText>
NOTE 1   Outside a generic unit a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> that denotes the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code> denotes the generic unit. In contrast, within the declarative region of the generic unit, a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> that denotes the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code> denotes the current instance. <br />

<MarginText>11.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>This is stated officially as part of the &ldquo;current instance&rdquo; rule in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">The Context of Overload Resolution</a>&rdquo;. See also <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3">12.3</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3">Generic Instantiation</a>&rdquo;. <br />

<MarginText>12</MarginText>
NOTE 2   Within a generic <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.3#S0216">subprogram_body</a></code>, the name of this program unit acts as the name of a subprogram. Hence this name can be overloaded, and it can appear in a recursive call of the current instance. For the same reason, this name cannot appear after the reserved word <b>new</b> in a (recursive) <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code>.<br />

<MarginText>13/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0447-1"]} />
NOTE 3   A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0063">default_expression</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6#S0339">default_name</a></code> appearing in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code> is not evaluated during elaboration of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code>; instead, it is evaluated when used. However, the usual visibility rules apply to any <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> used in a default, with name resolution performed based on the location of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> within the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code>. <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>14</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of generic formal parts:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>15</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
generic     --  parameterless {"\n"}
<MarginText>16</MarginText>
generic{"\n"}   Size : Natural;  --  formal object {"\n"}
<MarginText>17</MarginText>
generic{"\n"}   Length : Integer := 200;          -- formal object with a default expression{"\n"}
<MarginText>18</MarginText>
   Area   : Integer := Length{"*"}Length; -- formal object with a default expression{"\n"}
<MarginText>19</MarginText>
generic{"\n"}   type Item  is private;                       -- formal type{"\n"}   type Index is ({"<"}{">"});                          -- formal type{"\n"}   type Row   is array(Index range {"<"}{">"}) of Item; -- formal type{"\n"}   with function "{"<"}"(X, Y : Item) return Boolean;    -- formal subprogram {"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>20</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of generic declarations declaring generic subprograms Exchange and Squaring:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>21</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
generic{"\n"}   type Elem is private;{"\n"}procedure Exchange(U, V : in out Elem);{"\n"}
<MarginText>22/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0178-1"]} />
generic{"\n"}   type Item ({"<"}{">"}) is private;{"\n"}   with function "{"*"}"(U, V : Item) return Item is {"<"}{">"};{"\n"}function Squaring(X : Item) return Item;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>23</MarginText>
<p><i>Example of a generic declaration declaring a generic package:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>24</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
generic{"\n"}   type Item   is private;{"\n"}   type Vector is array (Positive range {"<"}{">"}) of Item;{"\n"}   with function Sum(X, Y : Item) return Item;{"\n"}package On{"_"}Vectors is{"\n"}   function Sum  (A, B : Vector) return Vector;{"\n"}   function Sigma(A    : Vector) return Item;{"\n"}   Length{"_"}Error : exception;{"\n"}end On{"_"}Vectors;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>24.a</MarginText>
The syntax rule for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code> is modified to allow the reserved words <b>tagged</b> and <b>abstract</b>, to allow formal derived types, and to allow formal packages.<br />

<MarginText>24.b</MarginText>
<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.4#S0235">Use_clause</a></code>s are allowed in <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code>s. This is necessary in order to allow a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.4#S0235">use_clause</a></code> within a formal part to provide direct visibility of declarations within a generic formal package. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>24.c/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
The syntax for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code> and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.5#S0323">formal_type_definition</a></code> is split up into more named categories. The rules for these categories are moved to the appropriate subclauses. The names of the categories are changed to be more intuitive and uniform. For example, we changed <code>generic{"_"}parameter{"_"}declaration</code> to <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code>, because the thing it declares is a generic formal, not a generic. In the others, we abbreviate &ldquo;generic{"_"}formal&rdquo; to just &ldquo;formal&rdquo;. We can't do that for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code>, because of confusion with normal formal parameters of subprograms. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 2005

<MarginText>24.d/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0183-1"]} />
An optional <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code> can be used in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0311">generic_subprogram_declaration</a></code> (as well as a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0312">generic_package_declaration</a></code>). This is described in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#Subclause_13.1.1">13.1.1</a>. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2012

<MarginText>24.e/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0371-1"]} />
Defined a formal part as a declaration list, so that the visibility of entities in aspect specifications is properly defined. <br />

---

# 12.2. Generic Bodies

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.2.mdx

sidebar_position:  97

# 12.2. Generic Bodies

<MarginText>1</MarginText>
<p>The body of a generic unit (a <i>generic body</i>) [is a template for the instance bodies. The syntax of a generic body is identical to that of a nongeneric body]. <br /></p>

<MarginText>1.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>We also use terms like &ldquo;generic function body&rdquo; and &ldquo;nongeneric package body&rdquo;. <br />

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>2</MarginText>
<p>The elaboration of a generic body has no other effect than to establish that the generic unit can from then on be instantiated without failing the Elaboration{"_"}Check. If the generic body is a child of a generic package, then its elaboration establishes that each corresponding declaration nested in an instance of the parent (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#Subclause_10.1.1">10.1.1</a>) can from then on be instantiated without failing the Elaboration{"_"}Check. <br /></p>

<MarginText>3</MarginText>
NOTE   The syntax of generic subprograms implies that a generic subprogram body is always the completion of a declaration. <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>4</MarginText>
<p><i>Example of a generic procedure body:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>5</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
procedure Exchange(U, V : in out Elem) is  -- see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1">12.1</a>{"\n"}   T : Elem;  --  the generic formal type{"\n"}begin{"\n"}   T := U;{"\n"}   U := V;{"\n"}   V := T;{"\n"}end Exchange;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>6</MarginText>
<p><i>Example of a generic function body:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>7</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
function Squaring(X : Item) return Item is  --  see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1">12.1</a>{"\n"}begin{"\n"}   return X{"*"}X;  --  the formal operator "{"*"}"{"\n"}end Squaring;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>8</MarginText>
<p><i>Example of a generic package body:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>9</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package body On{"_"}Vectors is  --  see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1">12.1</a>{"\n"}
<MarginText>10</MarginText>
   function Sum(A, B : Vector) return Vector is{"\n"}      Result : Vector(A'Range); --  the formal type Vector{"\n"}      Bias   : constant Integer := B'First - A'First;{"\n"}   begin{"\n"}      if A'Length /= B'Length then{"\n"}         raise Length{"_"}Error;{"\n"}      end if;{"\n"}
<MarginText>11</MarginText>
      for N in A'Range loop{"\n"}         Result(N) := Sum(A(N), B(N + Bias)); -- the formal function Sum{"\n"}      end loop;{"\n"}      return Result;{"\n"}   end Sum;{"\n"}
<MarginText>12</MarginText>
   function Sigma(A : Vector) return Item is{"\n"}      Total : Item := A(A'First); --  the formal type Item{"\n"}   begin{"\n"}      for N in A'First + 1 .. A'Last loop{"\n"}         Total := Sum(Total, A(N)); --  the formal function Sum{"\n"}      end loop;{"\n"}      return Total;{"\n"}   end Sigma;{"\n"}end On{"_"}Vectors;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

# 12.3. Generic Instantiation

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3.mdx

sidebar_position:  98

# 12.3. Generic Instantiation

<MarginText>1</MarginText>
<p>[ An instance of a generic unit is declared by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code>.] <br /></p>

#### Language Design Principles

<MarginText>1.a/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0300-1"]} />
The legality of an instance should be determinable without looking at the generic body. Likewise, the legality of a generic body should be determinable without looking at any instances. Thus, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code> forms a contract between the body and the instances; if each obeys the rules with respect to the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code>, then no legality problems will arise. This is really a special case of the &ldquo;legality determinable via semantic dependences&rdquo; Language Design Principle (see Clause <a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/">10</a>), given that a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code> does not depend semantically upon the generic body, nor vice versa.<br />

<MarginText>1.b</MarginText>
Run-time issues are another story. For example, whether parameter passing is by copy or by reference is determined in part by the properties of the generic actuals, and thus cannot be determined at compile time of the generic body. Similarly, the contract model does not apply to Post-Compilation Rules. <br />

#### Syntax

<MarginText>2/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00218-03", "AI05-0183-1"]} />

<CodeBlock>
<code>generic{"_"}instantiation</code><a id="S0315"></a><code> ::= </code><br />     <b>package</b> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0201">defining_program_unit_name</a></code> <b>is</b><br />         <b>new</b> <i>generic{"_"}package{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> [<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0316">generic_actual_part</a></code>]<br />            [<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code>];<br />   | [<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.3#S0234">overriding_indicator</a></code>]<br />     <b>procedure</b> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0201">defining_program_unit_name</a></code> <b>is</b><br />         <b>new</b> <i>generic{"_"}procedure{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> [<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0316">generic_actual_part</a></code>]<br />            [<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code>];<br />   | [<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.3#S0234">overriding_indicator</a></code>]<br />     <b>function</b> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0200">defining_designator</a></code> <b>is</b><br />         <b>new</b> <i>generic{"_"}function{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> [<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0316">generic_actual_part</a></code>]<br />            [<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code>];<br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>generic{"_"}actual{"_"}part</code><a id="S0316"></a><code> ::= </code><br />   (<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0317">generic_association</a></code> {"{"}, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0317">generic_association</a></code>{"}"})<br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>4</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>generic{"_"}association</code><a id="S0317"></a><code> ::= </code><br />   [<i>generic{"_"}formal{"_"}parameter{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0099">selector_name</a></code> ={">"}] <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0318">explicit_generic_actual_parameter</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>5</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>explicit{"_"}generic{"_"}actual{"_"}parameter</code><a id="S0318"></a><code> ::= </code><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> | <i>variable{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code><br />   | <i>subprogram{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> | <i>entry{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code><br />   | <i>package{"_"}instance{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>6</MarginText>
<p class="Indented2">A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0317">generic_association</a></code> is <i>named</i> or <i>positional</i> according to whether or not the <i>generic{"_"}formal{"_"}parameter{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0099">selector{"_"}name</a></code> is specified. Any positional associations shall precede any named associations. <br /></p>

<MarginText>7/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0004-1", "AI12-0205-1"]} />
<p>The <i>generic actual parameter</i> is either the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0318">explicit_generic_actual_parameter</a></code> given in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0317">generic{"_"}association</a></code> for each formal, or the corresponding <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0063">default{"_"}expression</a></code>, <i>default{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code>, or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6#S0339">default{"_"}name</a></code> if no <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0317">generic{"_"}association</a></code> is given for the formal. When the meaning is clear from context, the term &ldquo;generic actual&rdquo;, or simply &ldquo;actual&rdquo;, is used as a synonym for &ldquo;generic actual parameter&rdquo; and also for the view denoted by one, or the value of one.<br /></p>

<MarginText>7.a/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0205-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Any matching or other Legality Rules that apply to a generic actual are applied to any <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0063">default_expression</a></code>, <i>default{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code>, or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6#S0339">default_name</a></code> that are used as an actual. <br />

#### Legality Rules

<MarginText>8</MarginText>
<p>In a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code> for a particular kind of program unit [(package, procedure, or function)], the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> shall denote a generic unit of the corresponding kind [(generic package, generic procedure, or generic function, respectively)].<br /></p>

<MarginText>9/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0118-1"]} />
<p>The <i>generic{"_"}formal{"_"}parameter{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0099">selector_name</a></code> of a named <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0317">generic_association</a></code> shall denote a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code> of the generic unit being instantiated. If two or more formal subprograms have the same defining name, then named associations are not allowed for the corresponding actuals.<br /></p>

<MarginText>9.1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0118-1"]} />
<p>The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code> for a positional <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0317">generic_association</a></code> is the parameter with the corresponding position in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code> of the generic unit being instantiated.<br /></p>

<MarginText>10/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0205-1"]} />
<p>A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code> shall contain at most one <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0317">generic_association</a></code> for each formal. Each formal without an association shall have a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0063">default_expression</a></code>, <i>default{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code>, or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6#S0338">subprogram_default</a></code>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>11/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0418-1"]} />
<p>In a generic unit, Legality Rules are enforced at compile time of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code> and generic body, given the properties of the formals. In the visible part and formal part of an instance, Legality Rules are enforced at compile time of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code>, given the properties of the actuals. In other parts of an instance, Legality Rules are not enforced; this rule does not apply when a given rule explicitly specifies otherwise. <br /></p>

<MarginText>11.a/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>Since rules are checked using the properties of the formals, and since these properties do not always carry over to the actuals, we need to check the rules again in the visible part of the instance. For example, only if a tagged type is limited may an extension of it have limited components in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0075">record_extension_part</a></code>. A formal tagged limited type is limited, but the actual might be nonlimited. Hence any rule that requires a tagged type to be limited runs into this problem. Such rules are rare; in most cases, the rules for matching of formals and actuals guarantee that if the rule is obeyed in the generic unit, then it has to be obeyed in the instance.<br />

<MarginText>11.a.1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1"]} />
Ada 2012 addendum: Such Legality Rules are not as rare as the authors of Ada 95 hoped; there are more than 30 of them known at this point. They are indexed under &ldquo;generic contract issue&rdquo; and are associated with the boilerplate &ldquo;In addition to the places where Legality Rules normally apply...&rdquo;. Indeed, there is only one known rule where rechecking in the specification is needed and where rechecking in the private part is <i>not</i> wanted (it is in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4">3.4</a>, but even it needs rechecking when tagged types are involved). <br />

<MarginText>11.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The &ldquo;properties&rdquo; of the formals are determined without knowing anything about the actuals: <br />

<MarginText>11.c/1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00034-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>{"{"}<i>8652/0095</i>{"}"} A formal derived subtype is constrained if and only if the ancestor subtype is constrained. A formal array type is constrained if and only if the declarations say so. A formal private type is constrained if it does not have a discriminant part. Other formal subtypes are unconstrained, even though they might be constrained in an instance.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.d</MarginText>
<li>A formal subtype can be indefinite, even though the copy might be definite in an instance.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.e</MarginText>
<li>A formal object of mode <b>in</b> is not a static constant; in an instance, the copy is static if the actual is.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.f</MarginText>
<li>A formal subtype is not static, even though the actual might be.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.g</MarginText>
<li>Formal types are specific, even though the actual can be class-wide.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.h</MarginText>
<li>The subtype of a formal object of mode <b>in out</b> is not static. (This covers the case of AI83-00878.)<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.i</MarginText>
<li>The subtype of a formal parameter of a formal subprogram does not provide an applicable index constraint.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.j/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0239-1"]} />
<li>The profile of a formal subprogram is not subtype conformant with any other profile. <br /></li>
<MarginText>11.k</MarginText>
<li>A generic formal function is not static. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>11.l</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The exceptions to the above rule about when legality rules are enforced fall into these categories: <br />

<MarginText>11.m</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>Some rules are checked in the generic declaration, and then again in both the visible and private parts of the instance: <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>11.n</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>The parent type of a record extension has to be specific (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.1">3.9.1</a>). This rule is not checked in the instance body.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.o</MarginText>
<li>The parent type of a private extension has to be specific (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3">7.3</a>). This rule is not checked in the instance body.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.p/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00402-01", "AI05-0093-1"]} />
<li>A type with an access discriminant with a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0063">default_expression</a></code> has to be immutably limited. In the generic body, the definition of immutably limited is adjusted in an assume-the-worst manner (thus the rule is checked that way).<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.q</MarginText>
<li>In the declaration of a record extension, if the parent type is nonlimited, then each of the components of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0075">record_extension_part</a></code> have to be nonlimited (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.1">3.9.1</a>). In the generic body, this rule is checked in an assume-the-worst manner.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.r</MarginText>
<li>A preelaborated library unit has to be preelaborable (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.2#Subclause_10.2.1">10.2.1</a>). In the generic body, this rule is checked in an assume-the-worst manner. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>11.r.1/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00402-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>The corrections made by the Corrigendum added a number of such rules, and the Amendment added many more. There doesn't seem to be much value in repeating all of these rules here (as of this writing, there are roughly 33 such rules). As noted below, all such rules are indexed in the AARM.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.s</MarginText>
<li>For the accessibility rules, the formals have nothing to say about the property in question. Like the above rules, these rules are checked in the generic declaration, and then again in both the visible and private parts of the instance. In the generic body, we have explicit rules that essentially assume the worst (in the cases of type extensions and access-to-subprogram types), and we have runtime checks (in the case of access-to-object types). See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.1">3.9.1</a>, <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#Subclause_3.10.2">3.10.2</a>, and <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6">4.6</a>.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.t</MarginText>
<li>We considered runtime checks for access-to-subprogram types as well. However, this would present difficulties for implementations that share generic bodies.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.u</MarginText>
<li>The rules requiring &ldquo;reasonable&rdquo; values for static expressions are ignored when the expected type for the expression is a descendant of a generic formal type other than a generic formal derived type, and do not apply in an instance.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.v</MarginText>
<li>The rule forbidding two explicit homographs in the same declarative region does not apply in an instance of a generic unit, except that it <i>does</i> apply in the declaration of a record extension that appears in the visible part of an instance.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.w</MarginText>
<li>Some rules do not apply at all in an instance, not even in the visible part: <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>11.x</MarginText>
<ul>
<li><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0297">Body_stub</a></code>s are not normally allowed to be multiply nested, but they can be in instances. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>11.y</MarginText>
Each rule that is an exception is marked with &ldquo;generic contract issue;&rdquo; look that up in the index to find them all. <br />

<MarginText>11.z</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The Legality Rules are the ones labeled Legality Rules. We are talking about all Legality Rules in the entire language here. Note that, with some exceptions, the legality of a generic unit is checked even if there are no instantiations of the generic unit. <br />

<MarginText>11.aa/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1", "AI12-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The Legality Rules are described here, and the overloading rules were described earlier in this subclause. Presumably, every Static Semantic Item is included indirectly by one of those. Thus, we have covered all the compile-time rules of the language. There is no need to say anything special about the Post-Compilation Rules or the Dynamic Semantic Items. <br />

<MarginText>11.bb</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Here is an example illustrating how this rule is checked: &ldquo;In the declaration of a record extension, if the parent type is nonlimited, then each of the components of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0075">record_extension_part</a></code> shall be nonlimited.&rdquo; <br />

<MarginText>11.cc</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
generic{"\n"}    type Parent is tagged private;{"\n"}    type Comp is limited private;{"\n"}package G1 is{"\n"}    type Extension is new Parent with{"\n"}        record{"\n"}            C : Comp; -- Illegal!{"\n"}        end record;{"\n"}end G1;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>11.dd/1</MarginText>
The parent type is nonlimited, and the component type is limited, which is illegal. It doesn't matter that one could imagine writing an instantiation with the actual for Comp being nonlimited &mdash; we never get to the instance, because the generic itself is illegal.<br />

<MarginText>11.ee</MarginText>
On the other hand: <br />

<MarginText>11.ff</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
generic{"\n"}    type Parent is tagged limited private; -- Parent is limited.{"\n"}    type Comp is limited private;{"\n"}package G2 is{"\n"}    type Extension is new Parent with{"\n"}        record{"\n"}            C : Comp; -- OK.{"\n"}        end record;{"\n"}end G2;{"\n"}
<MarginText>11.gg</MarginText>
type Limited{"_"}Tagged is tagged limited null record;{"\n"}type Non{"_"}Limited{"_"}Tagged is tagged null record;{"\n"}
<MarginText>11.hh</MarginText>
type Limited{"_"}Untagged is limited null record;{"\n"}type Non{"_"}Limited{"_"}Untagged is null record;{"\n"}
<MarginText>11.ii</MarginText>
package Good{"_"}1 is new G2(Parent ={">"} Limited{"_"}Tagged,{"\n"}                         Comp ={">"} Limited{"_"}Untagged);{"\n"}package Good{"_"}2 is new G2(Parent ={">"} Non{"_"}Limited{"_"}Tagged,{"\n"}                         Comp ={">"} Non{"_"}Limited{"_"}Untagged);{"\n"}package Bad  is new G2(Parent ={">"} Non{"_"}Limited{"_"}Tagged,{"\n"}                         Comp ={">"} Limited{"_"}Untagged); -- Illegal!{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>11.jj</MarginText>
The first instantiation is legal, because in the instance the parent is limited, so the rule is not violated. Likewise, in the second instantiation, the rule is not violated in the instance. However, in the Bad instance, the parent type is nonlimited, and the component type is limited, so this instantiation is illegal. <br />

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>12</MarginText>
<p>A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code> declares an instance; it is equivalent to the instance declaration (a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0229">package{"_"}declaration</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0195">subprogram{"_"}declaration</a></code>) immediately followed by the instance body, both at the place of the instantiation. <br /></p>

<MarginText>12.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The declaration and the body of the instance are not &ldquo;implicit&rdquo; in the technical sense, even though you can't see them in the program text. Nor are declarations within an instance &ldquo;implicit&rdquo; (unless they are implicit by other rules). This is necessary because implicit declarations have special semantics that should not be attached to instances. For a generic subprogram, the profile of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code> is that of the instance declaration, by the stated equivalence. <br />

<MarginText>12.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The visible and private parts of a package instance are defined in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1">7.1</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1">Package Specifications and Declarations</a>&rdquo; and <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.7">12.7</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.7">Formal Packages</a>&rdquo;. The visible and private parts of a subprogram instance are defined in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.2">8.2</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.2">Scope of Declarations</a>&rdquo;. <br />

<MarginText>13</MarginText>
<p>The instance is a copy of the text of the template. [Each use of a formal parameter becomes (in the copy) a use of the actual, as explained below.] An instance of a generic package is a package, that of a generic procedure is a procedure, and that of a generic function is a function. <br /></p>

<MarginText>13.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>An instance is a package or subprogram (because we say so), even though it contains a copy of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code>, and therefore doesn't look like one. This is strange, but it's OK, since the syntax rules are overloading rules, and therefore do not apply in an instance. <br />

<MarginText>13.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>We use a macro-expansion model, with some explicitly-stated exceptions (see below). The main exception is that the interpretation of each construct in a generic unit (especially including the denotation of each name) is determined when the declaration and body of the generic unit (as opposed to the instance) are compiled, and in each instance this interpretation is (a copy of) the template interpretation. In other words, if a construct is interpreted as a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> denoting a declaration D, then in an instance, the copy of the construct will still be a name, and will still denote D (or a copy of D). From an implementation point of view, overload resolution is performed on the template, and not on each copy.<br />

<MarginText>13.c</MarginText>
We describe the substitution of generic actual parameters by saying (in most cases) that the copy of each generic formal parameter declares a view of the actual. Suppose a name in a generic unit denotes a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code>. The copy of that name in an instance will denote the copy of that <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code> in the instance. Since the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code> in the instance declares a view of the actual, the name will denote a view of the actual.<br />

<MarginText>13.d/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00442-01"]} />
Other properties of the copy (for example, staticness, categories to which types belong) are recalculated for each instance; this is implied by the fact that it's a copy.<br />

<MarginText>13.e/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00317-01"]} />
Although the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code> is included in an instance, the declarations in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code> are only visible outside the instance in the case of a generic formal package whose <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.7#S0341">formal_package_actual_part</a></code> includes one or more {"<"}{">"} indicators &mdash; see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.7">12.7</a>. <br />

<MarginText>14</MarginText>
<p>The interpretation of each construct within a generic declaration or body is determined using the overloading rules when that generic declaration or body is compiled. In an instance, the interpretation of each (copied) construct is the same, except in the case of a name that denotes the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0310">generic_declaration</a></code> or some declaration within the generic unit; the corresponding name in the instance then denotes the corresponding copy of the denoted declaration. The overloading rules do not apply in the instance. <br /></p>

<MarginText>14.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">The Context of Overload Resolution</a>&rdquo; for definitions of &ldquo;interpretation&rdquo; and &ldquo;overloading rule&rdquo;.<br />

<MarginText>14.b</MarginText>
Even the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code>s have corresponding declarations in the instance, which declare views of the actuals.<br />

<MarginText>14.c</MarginText>
Although the declarations in the instance are copies of those in the generic unit, they often have quite different properties, as explained below. For example a constant declaration in the generic unit might declare a nonstatic constant, whereas the copy of that declaration might declare a static constant. This can happen when the staticness depends on some generic formal.<br />

<MarginText>14.d</MarginText>
This rule is partly a ramification of the &ldquo;current instance&rdquo; rule in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">The Context of Overload Resolution</a>&rdquo;. Note that that rule doesn't cover the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0313">generic_formal_part</a></code>.<br />

<MarginText>14.e/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0347-1"]} />
Although the overloading rules are not observed in the instance, they are, of course, observed in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code> in order to determine the interpretation of the constituents of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code>.<br />

<MarginText>14.f</MarginText>
Since children are considered to occur within their parent's declarative region, the above rule applies to a name that denotes a child of a generic unit, or a declaration inside such a child.<br />

<MarginText>14.g</MarginText>
Since the Syntax Rules are overloading rules, it is possible (legal) to violate them in an instance. For example, it is possible for an instance body to occur in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0230">package_specification</a></code>, even though the Syntax Rules forbid bodies in <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0230">package_specification</a></code>s. <br />

<MarginText>15/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0407-1"]} />
<p>In an instance, a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code> declares a view whose properties are identical to those of the actual, except when specified otherwise (in particular, see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#Subclause_6.1.1">6.1.1</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#Subclause_6.1.1">Preconditions and Postconditions</a>&rdquo;, <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.4">12.4</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.4">Formal Objects</a>&rdquo;, and <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6">12.6</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6">Formal Subprograms</a>&rdquo;). Similarly, for a declaration within a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1#S0314">generic_formal_parameter_declaration</a></code>, the corresponding declaration in an instance declares a view whose properties are identical to the corresponding declaration within the declaration of the actual. <br /></p>

<MarginText>15.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>In an instance, there are no &ldquo;properties&rdquo; of types and subtypes that come from the formal. The primitive operations of the type come from the formal, but these are declarations in their own right, and are therefore handled separately.<br />

<MarginText>15.b</MarginText>
Note that certain properties that come from the actuals are irrelevant in the instance. For example, if an actual type is of a class deeper in the derived-type hierarchy than the formal, it is impossible to call the additional operations of the deeper class in the instance, because any such call would have to be a copy of some corresponding call in the generic unit, which would have been illegal. However, it is sometimes possible to reach into the specification of the instance from outside, and notice such properties. For example, one could pass an object declared in the instance specification to one of the additional operations of the deeper type.<br />

<MarginText>15.c/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01"]} />
A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.5#S0320">formal_type_declaration</a></code> can contain <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0062">discriminant_specification</a></code>s, a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6#S0335">formal_subprogram_declaration</a></code> can contain <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0207">parameter_specification</a></code>s, and a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.7#S0340">formal_package_declaration</a></code> can contain many kinds of declarations. These are all inside the generic unit, and have corresponding declarations in the instance.<br />

<MarginText>15.d</MarginText>
This rule implies, for example, that if a subtype in a generic unit is a subtype of a generic formal subtype, then the corresponding subtype in the instance is a subtype of the corresponding actual subtype.<br />

<MarginText>15.e</MarginText>
For a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code>, if a generic actual is a static [(scalar or string)] subtype, then each use of the corresponding formal parameter within the specification of the instance is considered to be static. (See AI83-00409.)<br />

<MarginText>15.f</MarginText>
Similarly, if a generic actual is a static expression and the corresponding formal parameter has a static [(scalar or string)] subtype, then each use of the formal parameter in the specification of the instance is considered to be static. (See AI83-00505.)<br />

<MarginText>15.g</MarginText>
If a primitive subprogram of a type derived from a generic formal derived tagged type is not overriding (that is, it is a new subprogram), it is possible for the copy of that subprogram in an instance to override a subprogram inherited from the actual. For example: <br />

<MarginText>15.h</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type T1 is tagged record ... end record;{"\n"}
<MarginText>15.i/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0005-1"]} />
generic{"\n"}    type Formal is new T1 with private;{"\n"}package G is{"\n"}    type Derived{"_"}From{"_"}Formal is new Formal with record ... end record;{"\n"}    procedure Foo(X : in Derived{"_"}From{"_"}Formal); -- Does not override anything.{"\n"}end G;{"\n"}
<MarginText>15.j</MarginText>
type T2 is new T1 with record ... end record;{"\n"}procedure Foo(X : in T2);{"\n"}
<MarginText>15.k</MarginText>
package Inst is new G(Formal ={">"} T2);{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>15.l</MarginText>
In the instance Inst, the declaration of Foo for Derived{"_"}From{"_"}Formal overrides the Foo inherited from T2. <br />

<MarginText>15.m/1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00137-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>{"{"}<i>8652/0009</i>{"}"} For formal types, an implementation that shares the code among multiple instances of the same generic unit needs to beware that things like parameter passing mechanisms (by-copy vs. by-reference) and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0343">aspect_clause</a></code>s are determined by the actual. <br />

<MarginText>15.n/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0407-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>In particular, we allow differences for aspects that can be specified on generic formal parameters. For instance, Pre (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#Subclause_6.1.1">6.1.1</a>) can be specified on generic formal subprograms to be added to the Pre of the actual. <br />

<MarginText>16</MarginText>
<p>[Implicit declarations are also copied, and a name that denotes an implicit declaration in the generic denotes the corresponding copy in the instance. However, for a type declared within the visible part of the generic, a whole new set of primitive subprograms is implicitly declared for use outside the instance, and may differ from the copied set if the properties of the type in some way depend on the properties of some actual type specified in the instantiation. For example, if the type in the generic is derived from a formal private type, then in the instance the type will inherit subprograms from the corresponding actual type.<br /></p>

<MarginText>17</MarginText>
<p>These new implicit declarations occur immediately after the type declaration in the instance, and override the copied ones. The copied ones can be called only from within the instance; the new ones can be called only from outside the instance, although for tagged types, the body of a new one can be executed by a call to an old one.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>17.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>This rule is stated officially in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.3">8.3</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.3">Visibility</a>&rdquo;. <br />

<MarginText>17.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The new ones follow from the class(es) of the formal types. For example, for a type T derived from a generic formal private type, if the actual is Integer, then the copy of T in the instance has a "+" primitive operator, which can be called from outside the instance (assuming T is declared in the visible part of the instance).<br />

<MarginText>17.c</MarginText>
AI83-00398.<br />

<MarginText>17.d/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00442-01"]} />
Since an actual type is always in the category determined for the formal, the new subprograms hide all of the copied ones, except for a declaration of "/=" that corresponds to an explicit declaration of "=". Such "/=" operators are special, because unlike other implicit declarations of primitive subprograms, they do not appear by virtue of the class, but because of an explicit declaration of "=". If the declaration of "=" is implicit (and therefore overridden in the instance), then a corresponding implicitly declared "/=" is also overridden. But if the declaration of "=" is explicit (and therefore not overridden in the instance), then a corresponding implicitly declared "/=" is not overridden either, even though it's implicit.<br />

<MarginText>17.e</MarginText>
Note that the copied ones can be called from inside the instance, even though they are hidden from all visibility, because the names are resolved in the generic unit &mdash; visibility is irrelevant for calls in the instance. <br />

<MarginText>18</MarginText>
<p>[In the visible part of an instance, an explicit declaration overrides an implicit declaration if they are homographs, as described in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.3">8.3</a>.] On the other hand, an explicit declaration in the private part of an instance overrides an implicit declaration in the instance, only if the corresponding explicit declaration in the generic overrides a corresponding implicit declaration in the generic. Corresponding rules apply to the other kinds of overriding described in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.3">8.3</a>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>18.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>For example: <br />

<MarginText>18.b</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type Ancestor is tagged null record;{"\n"}
<MarginText>18.c</MarginText>
generic{"\n"}    type Formal is new Ancestor with private;{"\n"}package G is{"\n"}    type T is new Formal with null record;{"\n"}    procedure P(X : in T); -- (1){"\n"}private{"\n"}    procedure Q(X : in T); -- (2){"\n"}end G;{"\n"}
<MarginText>18.d</MarginText>
type Actual is new Ancestor with null record;{"\n"}procedure P(X : in Actual);{"\n"}procedure Q(X : in Actual);{"\n"}
<MarginText>18.e</MarginText>
package Instance is new G(Formal ={">"} Actual);{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>18.f</MarginText>
In the instance, the copy of P at (1) overrides Actual's P, whereas the copy of Q at (2) does not override anything; in implementation terms, it occupies a separate slot in the type descriptor. <br />

<MarginText>18.g/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0347-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The reason for this rule is so a programmer writing a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code> need not look at the private part of the generic in order to determine which subprograms will be overridden. <br />

#### Post-Compilation Rules

<MarginText>19</MarginText>
<p>Recursive generic instantiation is not allowed in the following sense: if a given generic unit includes an instantiation of a second generic unit, then the instance generated by this instantiation shall not include an instance of the first generic unit [(whether this instance is generated directly, or indirectly by intermediate instantiations)]. <br /></p>

<MarginText>19.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Note that this rule is not a violation of the generic contract model, because it is not a Legality Rule. Some implementations may be able to check this rule at compile time, but that requires access to all the bodies, so we allow implementations to check the rule at link time. <br />

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>20</MarginText>
<p>For the elaboration of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0315">generic_instantiation</a></code>, each <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0317">generic_association</a></code> is first evaluated. If a default is used, an implicit <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0317">generic_association</a></code> is assumed for this rule. These evaluations are done in an arbitrary order, except that the evaluation for a default actual takes place after the evaluation for another actual if the default includes a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> that denotes the other one. Finally, the instance declaration and body are elaborated. <br /></p>

<MarginText>20.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Note that if the evaluation of a default depends on some side effect of some other evaluation, the order is still arbitrary. <br />

<MarginText>21</MarginText>
<p>For the evaluation of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0317">generic_association</a></code> the generic actual parameter is evaluated. Additional actions are performed in the case of a formal object of mode <b>in</b> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.4">12.4</a>). <br /></p>

<MarginText>21.a</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>Actually, the actual is evaluated only if evaluation is defined for that kind of construct &mdash; we don't actually &ldquo;evaluate&rdquo; <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code>s. <br />

<MarginText>22</MarginText>
NOTE   If a formal type is not tagged, then the type is treated as an untagged type within the generic body. Deriving from such a type in a generic body is permitted; the new type does not get a new tag value, even if the actual is tagged. Overriding operations for such a derived type cannot be dispatched to from outside the instance. <br />

<MarginText>22.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>If two overloaded subprograms declared in a generic package specification differ only by the (formal) type of their parameters and results, then there exist legal instantiations for which all calls of these subprograms from outside the instance are ambiguous. For example: <br />

<MarginText>22.b</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
generic{"\n"}   type A is ({"<"}{">"});{"\n"}   type B is private;{"\n"}package G is{"\n"}   function Next(X : A) return A;{"\n"}   function Next(X : B) return B;{"\n"}end G;{"\n"}
<MarginText>22.c</MarginText>
package P is new G(A ={">"} Boolean, B ={">"} Boolean);{"\n"}-- All calls of P.Next are ambiguous.{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>22.d</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The following example illustrates some of the subtleties of the substitution of formals and actuals: <br />

<MarginText>22.e/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0005-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
generic{"\n"}    type T1 is private;{"\n"}    -- A predefined "=" operator is implicitly declared here:{"\n"}    -- function "="(Left, Right : T1) return Boolean;{"\n"}    -- Call this "="1.{"\n"}    ...{"\n"}package G is{"\n"}    subtype S1 is T1; -- So we can get our hands on the type from{"\n"}                      -- outside an instance.{"\n"}    type T2 is new T1;{"\n"}    -- An inherited "=" operator is implicitly declared here:{"\n"}    -- function "="(Left, Right : T2) return Boolean;{"\n"}    -- Call this "="2.{"\n"}
<MarginText>22.f</MarginText>
    T1{"_"}Obj : T1 := ...;{"\n"}    Bool{"_"}1 : Boolean := T1{"_"}Obj = T1{"_"}Obj;{"\n"}
<MarginText>22.g</MarginText>
    T2{"_"}Obj : T2 := ...;{"\n"}    Bool{"_"}2 : Boolean := T2{"_"}Obj = T2{"_"}Obj;{"\n"}end G;{"\n"}...{"\n"}
<MarginText>22.h/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0005-1"]} />
package P is{"\n"}    type My{"_"}Int is new Integer;{"\n"}    -- A predefined "=" operator is implicitly declared here:{"\n"}    -- function "="(Left, Right : My{"_"}Int) return Boolean;{"\n"}    -- Call this "="3.{"\n"}    function "="(X, Y : My{"_"}Int) return Boolean;{"\n"}    -- Call this "="4.{"\n"}    -- "="3 is hidden from all visibility by "="4.{"\n"}    -- Nonetheless, "="3 can &ldquo;reemerge&rdquo; in certain circumstances.{"\n"}end P;{"\n"}use P;{"\n"}...{"\n"}package I is new G(T1 ={">"} My{"_"}Int, ...); -- "="5 is declared in I (see below).{"\n"}use I;{"\n"}
<MarginText>22.i</MarginText>
Another{"_"}T1{"_"}Obj : S1 := 13; -- Can't denote T1, but S1 will do.{"\n"}Bool{"_"}3 : Boolean := Another{"_"}T1{"_"}Obj = Another{"_"}T1{"_"}Obj;{"\n"}
<MarginText>22.j</MarginText>
Another{"_"}T2{"_"}Obj : T2 := 45;{"\n"}Bool{"_"}4 : Boolean := Another{"_"}T2{"_"}Obj = Another{"_"}T2{"_"}Obj;{"\n"}
<MarginText>22.k</MarginText>
Double : T2 := T2{"_"}Obj + Another{"_"}T2{"_"}Obj;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>22.l</MarginText>
In the instance I, there is a copy of "="1 (call it "="1i) and "="2 (call it "="2i). The "="1i and "="2i declare views of the predefined "=" of My{"_"}Int (that is, "="3). In the initialization of Bool{"_"}1 and Bool{"_"}2 in the generic unit G, the names "=" denote "="1 and "="2, respectively. Therefore, the copies of these names in the instances denote "="1i and "="2i, respectively. Thus, the initialization of I.Bool{"_"}1 and I.Bool{"_"}2 call the predefined equality operator of My{"_"}Int; they will not call "="4.<br />

<MarginText>22.m</MarginText>
The declarations "="1i and "="2i are hidden from all visibility. This prevents them from being called from outside the instance.<br />

<MarginText>22.n</MarginText>
The declaration of Bool{"_"}3 calls "="4.<br />

<MarginText>22.o</MarginText>
The instance I also contains implicit declarations of the primitive operators of T2, such as "=" (call it "="5) and "+". These operations cannot be called from within the instance, but the declaration of Bool{"_"}4 calls "="5. <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>23</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of generic instantiations (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.1">12.1</a>):</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>24/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0178-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
procedure Swap is new Exchange(Elem ={">"} Integer);{"\n"}procedure Swap is new Exchange(Character);  	--  Swap is overloaded {"\n"}function Square is new Squaring(Integer); 	--  "{"*"}" of Integer used by default{"\n"}function Square1 is new Squaring(Item ={">"} Matrix, "{"*"}" ={">"} Matrix{"_"}Product);{"\n"}function Square2 is new Squaring(Matrix, Matrix{"_"}Product); -- same as previous{"\n"}
<MarginText>25</MarginText>
package Int{"_"}Vectors is new On{"_"}Vectors(Integer, Table, "+");{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>26</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of uses of instantiated units:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>27</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
Swap(A, B);{"\n"}A := Square(A);{"\n"}
<MarginText>28</MarginText>
T : Table(1 .. 5) := (10, 20, 30, 40, 50);{"\n"}N : Integer := Int{"_"}Vectors.Sigma(T);  --  150{"\n"}                                      -- (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.2">12.2</a> for the body of Sigma){"\n"}
<MarginText>29</MarginText>
use Int{"_"}Vectors;{"\n"}M : Integer := Sigma(T);  --  150{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

#### Inconsistencies With Ada 83

<MarginText>29.a</MarginText>
In Ada 83, all explicit actuals are evaluated before all defaults, and the defaults are evaluated in the order of the formal declarations. This ordering requirement is relaxed in Ada 95. <br />

#### Incompatibilities With Ada 83

<MarginText>29.b</MarginText>
We have attempted to remove every violation of the contract model. Any remaining contract model violations should be considered bugs in the RM95. The unfortunate property of reverting to the predefined operators of the actual types is retained for upward compatibility. (Note that fixing this would require subtype conformance rules.) However, tagged types do not revert in this sense. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>29.c</MarginText>
The syntax rule for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3#S0318">explicit_generic_actual_parameter</a></code> is modified to allow a <i>package{"_"}instance{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>29.d</MarginText>
