# 13.3. Operational and Representation Attributes

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3.mdx

sidebar_position:  107

# 13.3. Operational and Representation Attributes

<MarginText>1/1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00137-01"]} />
<p>{"{"}<i>8652/0009</i>{"}"} [ The values of certain implementation-dependent characteristics can be obtained by interrogating appropriate operational or representation attributes. Some of these attributes are specifiable via an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code>.] <br /></p>

#### Language Design Principles

<MarginText>1.a</MarginText>
In general, the meaning of a given attribute should not depend on whether the attribute was specified via an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code>, or chosen by default by the implementation. <br />

#### Syntax

<MarginText>2</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>attribute{"_"}definition{"_"}clause</code><a id="S0349"></a><code> ::= </code><br />      <b>for</b> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0345">local_name</a></code>'<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0101">attribute_designator</a></code> <b>use</b> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code>;<br />    | <b>for</b> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0345">local_name</a></code>'<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0101">attribute_designator</a></code> <b>use</b> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>;<br />

</CodeBlock>

#### Name Resolution Rules

<MarginText>3</MarginText>
<p>For an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code> that specifies an attribute that denotes a value, the form with an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> shall be used. Otherwise, the form with a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> shall be used.<br /></p>

<MarginText>4</MarginText>
<p>For an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code> that specifies an attribute that denotes a value or an object, the expected type for the expression or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> is that of the attribute. For an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code> that specifies an attribute that denotes a subprogram, the expected profile for the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> is the profile required for the attribute. For an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code> that specifies an attribute that denotes some other kind of entity, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> shall resolve to denote an entity of the appropriate kind. <br /></p>

<MarginText>4.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>For example, the Size attribute is of type <i>universal{"_"}integer</i>. Therefore, the expected type for Y in &ldquo;<b>for</b> X'Size <b>use</b> Y;&rdquo; is <i>universal{"_"}integer</i>, which means that Y can be of any integer type. <br />

<MarginText>4.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>For attributes that denote subprograms, the required profile is indicated separately for the individual attributes. <br />

<MarginText>4.c</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>For an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code> with a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> need not statically denote the entity it denotes. For example, the following kinds of things are allowed: <br />

<MarginText>4.d</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
for Some{"_"}Access{"_"}Type'Storage{"_"}Pool use Storage{"_"}Pool{"_"}Array(I);{"\n"}for Some{"_"}Type'Read use Subprogram{"_"}Pointer.all;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

#### Legality Rules

<MarginText>5/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00137-01", "AI05-0183-1"]} />
<p>{"{"}<i>8652/0009</i>{"}"} An <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0101">attribute_designator</a></code> is allowed in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code> only if this Reference Manual explicitly allows it, or for an implementation-defined attribute if the implementation allows it. Each specifiable attribute constitutes an operational aspect or aspect of representation; the name of the aspect is that of the attribute. <br /></p>

<MarginText>5.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>For each specifiable attribute, we generally say something like, &ldquo;The ... attribute may be specified for ... via an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code>.&rdquo;<br />

<MarginText>5.b</MarginText>
The above wording allows for T'Class'Alignment, T'Class'Size, T'Class'Input, and T'Class'Output to be specifiable.<br />

<MarginText>5.c</MarginText>
A specifiable attribute is not necessarily specifiable for all entities for which it is defined. For example, one is allowed to ask T'Component{"_"}Size for an array subtype T, but &ldquo;<b>for</b> T'Component{"_"}Size <b>use</b> ...&rdquo; is only allowed if T is a first subtype, because Component{"_"}Size is a type-related aspect. <br />

<MarginText>6/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0427-1"]} />
<p><i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br /></p>

<MarginText>6.a/5</MarginText>
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>6.b/5</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
This paragraph was deleted.{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>6.c/5</MarginText>
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>7/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00270-01"]} />
<p>A <i>Size clause</i> is an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code> whose <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0101">attribute_designator</a></code> is Size. Similar definitions apply to the other specifiable attributes. <br /></p>

<MarginText>7.a</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>An <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code> is type-related or subtype-specific if the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0101">attribute_designator</a></code> denotes a type-related or subtype-specific attribute, respectively. <br />

<MarginText>8</MarginText>
<p>A <i>storage element</i> is an addressable element of storage in the machine. A <i>word</i> is the largest amount of storage that can be conveniently and efficiently manipulated by the hardware, given the implementation's run-time model. A word consists of an integral number of storage elements. <br /></p>

<MarginText>8.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>A storage element is not intended to be a single bit, unless the machine can efficiently address individual bits. <br />

<MarginText>8.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>For example, on a machine with 8-bit storage elements, if there exist 32-bit integer registers, with a full set of arithmetic and logical instructions to manipulate those registers, a word ought to be 4 storage elements &mdash; that is, 32 bits. <br />

<MarginText>8.c</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The &ldquo;given the implementation's run-time model&rdquo; part is intended to imply that, for example, on an 80386 running MS-DOS, the word might be 16 bits, even though the hardware can support 32 bits.<br />

<MarginText>8.d</MarginText>
A word is what ACID refers to as a &ldquo;natural hardware boundary&rdquo;.<br />

<MarginText>8.e</MarginText>
Storage elements may, but need not be, independently addressable (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.10">9.10</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.10">Shared Variables</a>&rdquo;). Words are expected to be independently addressable. <br />

<MarginText>8.1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00133-01", "AI05-0092-1"]} />
<p>A <i>machine scalar</i> is an amount of storage that can be conveniently and efficiently loaded, stored, or operated upon by the hardware. Machine scalars consist of an integral number of storage elements. The set of machine scalars is implementation defined, but includes at least the storage element and the word. Machine scalars are used to interpret <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.5#S0353">component_clause</a></code>s when the nondefault bit ordering applies. <br /></p>

<MarginText>8.e.1/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-defined">
<b></b>The set of machine scalars.<br />

<MarginText>8.f/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0092-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>A single storage element is a machine scalar in all Ada implementations. Similarly, a word is a machine scalar in all implementations (although it might be the same as a storage element). An implementation may define other machine scalars that make sense on the target (a half-word, for instance). <br />

<MarginText>9/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00137-01", "AI05-0191-1", "AI12-0059-1"]} />
<p>{"{"}<i>8652/0009</i>{"}"} The following representation attributes are defined: Address, Alignment, Size, Object{"_"}Size, Storage{"_"}Size, Component{"_"}Size, Has{"_"}Same{"_"}Storage, and Overlaps{"_"}Storage.<br /></p>

<MarginText>10/1</MarginText>
<p>For a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> X that denotes an object, program unit, or label: <br /></p>

<MarginText>11</MarginText>
<dt><br/>X'Address</dt>
<dl>
<dd>Denotes the address of the first of the storage elements allocated to X. For a program unit or label, this value refers to the machine code associated with the corresponding body or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.1#S0167">statement</a></code>. The value of this attribute is of type System.Address.<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>11.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Here, the &ldquo;first of the storage elements&rdquo; is intended to mean the one with the lowest address; the endianness of the machine doesn't matter. <br />

<MarginText>11.1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0095-1"]} />
<dl>
<dd>The prefix of X'Address shall not statically denote a subprogram that has convention Intrinsic. X'Address raises Program{"_"}Error if X denotes a subprogram that has convention Intrinsic.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>12</MarginText>
<dd>Address may be specified for stand-alone objects and for program units via an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code>. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>12.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Address is not allowed for enumeration literals, predefined operators, derived task types, or derived protected types, since they are not program units.<br />

<MarginText>12.b/3</MarginText>
Address is not allowed for intrinsic subprograms, either. That can be checked statically unless the prefix is a generic formal subprogram and the attribute reference is in the body of a generic unit. We define that case to raise Program{"_"}Error, in order that the compiler does not have to build a wrapper for intrinsic subprograms.<br />

<MarginText>12.c</MarginText>
The validity of a given address depends on the run-time model; thus, in order to use Address clauses correctly, one needs intimate knowledge of the run-time model.<br />

<MarginText>12.d/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
If the Address of an object is specified, any explicit or implicit initialization takes place as usual, unless the Import aspect is also specified for the object (in which case any necessary initialization is presumably done in the foreign language).<br />

<MarginText>12.e</MarginText>
Any compilation unit containing an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0100">attribute_reference</a></code> of a given type depends semantically on the declaration of the package in which the type is declared, even if not mentioned in an applicable <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code> &mdash; see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#Subclause_10.1.1">10.1.1</a>. In this case, it means that if a compilation unit contains X'Address, then it depends on the declaration of System. Otherwise, the fact that the value of Address is of a type in System wouldn't make sense; it would violate the &ldquo;legality determinable via semantic dependences&rdquo; Language Design Principle.<br />

<MarginText>12.f</MarginText>
AI83-00305 &mdash; If X is a task type, then within the body of X, X denotes the current task object; thus, X'Address denotes the object's address.<br />

<MarginText>12.g</MarginText>
Interrupt entries and their addresses are described in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-J/AA-J.7#Subclause_J.7.1">J.7.1</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-J/AA-J.7#Subclause_J.7.1">Interrupt Entries</a>&rdquo;.<br />

<MarginText>12.h</MarginText>
If X is not allocated on a storage element boundary, X'Address points at the first of the storage elements that contains any part of X. This is important for the definition of the Position attribute to be sensible. <br />

<MarginText>12.i/3</MarginText>
<b>Aspect Description for </b><b>Address: </b>Machine address of an entity.<br />

#### Erroneous Execution

<MarginText>13/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0009-1"]} />
<p>If an Address is specified, it is the programmer's responsibility to ensure that the address is valid and appropriate for the entity and its use; otherwise, program execution is erroneous.<br /></p>

<MarginText>13.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>&ldquo;Appropriate for the entity and its use&rdquo; covers cases such as misaligned addresses, read-only code addresses for variable data objects (and nonexecutable data addresses for code units), and addresses which would force objects that are supposed to be independently addressable to not be. Such addresses may be &ldquo;valid&rdquo; as they designate locations that are accessible to the program, but the program execution is still erroneous (meaning that implementations do not have to worry about these cases). <br />

#### Implementation Advice

<MarginText>14</MarginText>
<p>For an array X, X'Address should point at the first component of the array, and not at the array bounds. <br /></p>

<MarginText>14.a.1/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-advice">
<b></b>For an array X, X'Address should point at the first component of the array rather than the array bounds.<br />

<MarginText>14.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>On the other hand, we have no advice to offer about discriminants and tag fields; whether or not the address points at them is not specified by the language. If discriminants are stored separately, then the Position of a discriminant might be negative, or might raise an exception. <br />

<MarginText>15</MarginText>
<p>The recommended level of support for the Address attribute is: <br /></p>

<MarginText>16</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>X'Address should produce a useful result if X is an object that is aliased or of a by-reference type, or is an entity whose Address has been specified. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>16.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>Aliased objects are the ones for which the Unchecked{"_"}Access attribute is allowed; hence, these have to be allocated on an addressable boundary anyway. Similar considerations apply to objects of a by-reference type.<br />

<MarginText>16.b</MarginText>
An implementation need not go to any trouble to make Address work in other cases. For example, if an object X is not aliased and not of a by-reference type, and the implementation chooses to store it in a register, X'Address might return System.Null{"_"}Address (assuming registers are not addressable). For a subprogram whose calling convention is Intrinsic, or for a package, the implementation need not generate an out-of-line piece of code for it. <br />

<MarginText>17</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>An implementation should support Address clauses for imported subprograms.<br /></li>
<MarginText>18/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02"]} />
<li><i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>18.a/2</MarginText>
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>19</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>If the Address of an object is specified, or it is imported or exported, then the implementation should not perform optimizations based on assumptions of no aliases. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>19.a/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-advice">
<b></b>The recommended level of support for the Address attribute should be followed.<br />

<MarginText>20</MarginText>
NOTE 1   The specification of a link name with the Link{"_"}Name aspect (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-B/AA-B.1">B.1</a>) for a subprogram or object is an alternative to explicit specification of its link-time address, allowing a link-time directive to place the subprogram or object within memory.<br />

<MarginText>21</MarginText>
NOTE 2   The rules for the Size attribute imply, for an aliased object X, that if X'Size = Storage{"_"}Unit, then X'Address points at a storage element containing all of the bits of X, and only the bits of X. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>21.a</MarginText>
The intended meaning of the various attributes, and their <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code>s, is more explicit.<br />

<MarginText>21.b</MarginText>
The <code>address{"_"}clause</code> has been renamed to <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-J/AA-J.7#S0368">at_clause</a></code> and moved to <a href="/docs/arm/AA-J/">Annex J</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-J/">Obsolescent Features</a>&rdquo;. One can use an Address clause (&ldquo;for T'Address <b>use</b> ...;&rdquo;) instead.<br />

<MarginText>21.c</MarginText>
The attributes defined in RM83-13.7.3 are moved to <a href="/docs/arm/AA-G/">Annex G</a>, <a href="/docs/arm/AA-A/AA-A.5#Subclause_A.5.3">A.5.3</a>, and <a href="/docs/arm/AA-A/AA-A.5#Subclause_A.5.4">A.5.4</a>. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>21.c.1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0183-1"]} />
Defined that the names of aspects are the same as the name of the attribute; that gives a name to use in <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code>s (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#Subclause_13.1.1">13.1.1</a>). <br />

#### Language Design Principles

<MarginText>21.d</MarginText>
By default, the Alignment of a subtype should reflect the &ldquo;natural&rdquo; alignment for objects of the subtype on the machine. The Alignment, whether specified or default, should be known at compile time, even though Addresses are generally not known at compile time. (The generated code should never need to check at run time the number of zero bits at the end of an address to determine an alignment).<br />

<MarginText>21.e</MarginText>
There are two symmetric purposes of Alignment clauses, depending on whether or not the implementation has control over object allocation. If the implementation allocates an object, the implementation should ensure that the Address and Alignment are consistent with each other. If something outside the implementation allocates an object, the implementation should be allowed to assume that the Address and Alignment are consistent, but should not assume stricter alignments than that. <br />

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>22/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02"]} />
<p>For a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> X that denotes an object: <br /></p>

<MarginText>23/2</MarginText>
<dt><br/>X'Alignment</dt>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02"]} />
<dl>
<dd>The value of this attribute is of type <i>universal{"_"}integer</i>, and nonnegative; zero means that the object is not necessarily aligned on a storage element boundary. If X'Alignment is not zero, then X is aligned on a storage unit boundary and X'Address is an integral multiple of X'Alignment (that is, the Address modulo the Alignment is zero).<br /></dd>
<MarginText>24/2</MarginText>
<dt><br/></dt>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02"]} />
<dd><i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>24.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The Alignment is passed by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> to the Allocate operation; the implementation has to choose a value such that if the address returned by Allocate is aligned as requested, the generated code can correctly access the object.<br />

<MarginText>24.b</MarginText>
The above mention of &ldquo;modulo&rdquo; is referring to the "<b>mod</b>" operator declared in System.Storage{"_"}Elements; if X <b>mod</b> N = 0, then X is by definition aligned on an N-storage-element boundary. <br />

<MarginText>25/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02"]} />
<dl>
<dd>Alignment may be specified for [stand-alone] objects via an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute{"_"}definition{"_"}clause</a></code>; the expression of such a clause shall be static, and its value nonnegative.<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>25.a/3</MarginText>
<b>Aspect Description for </b><b>Alignment (object): </b>Alignment of an object.<br />

<MarginText>26/2</MarginText>
<dt><br/></dt>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00247-01"]} />
<dl>
<dd><i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>26.1/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02"]} />
<p>For every subtype S: <br /></p>

<MarginText>26.2/2</MarginText>
<dt><br/>S'Alignment</dt>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02"]} />
<dl>
<dd>The value of this attribute is of type <i>universal{"_"}integer</i>, and nonnegative.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>26.3/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00051-02", "AI95-00291-02"]} />
<dd>For an object X of subtype S, if S'Alignment is not zero, then X'Alignment is a nonzero integral multiple of S'Alignment unless specified otherwise by a representation item.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>26.4/2</MarginText>

#### Erroneous Execution

<MarginText>27</MarginText>
<p>Program execution is erroneous if an Address clause is given that conflicts with the Alignment. <br /></p>

<MarginText>27.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The user has to either give an Alignment clause also, or else know what Alignment the implementation will choose by default. <br />

<MarginText>28/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00051-02", "AI95-00291-02"]} />
<p>For an object that is not allocated under control of the implementation, execution is erroneous if the object is not aligned according to its Alignment.<br /></p>

#### Implementation Advice

<MarginText>28.1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0116-1"]} />
<p>For any tagged specific subtype <i>S</i>, <i>S</i>'Class'Alignment should equal <i>S</i>'Alignment.<br /></p>

<MarginText>28.a/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>A tagged object should never be less aligned than the alignment of the type of its view, so for a class-wide type T'Class, the alignment should be no greater than that of any type covered by T'Class. If the implementation only supports alignments that are required by the recommended level of support (and this is most likely), then the alignment of any covered type has to be the same or greater than that of T &mdash; which leaves the only reasonable value of T'Class'Alignment being T'Alignment. Thus we recommend this, but don't require it so that in the unlikely case that the implementation does support smaller alignments for covered types, it can select a smaller value for T'Class'Alignment. <br />

<MarginText>28.a.1/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-advice">
<b></b>For any tagged specific subtype <i>S</i>, <i>S</i>'Class'Alignment should equal <i>S</i>'Alignment.<br />

<MarginText>29</MarginText>
<p>The recommended level of support for the Alignment attribute for subtypes is: <br /></p>

<MarginText>30/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00051-02"]} />
<ul>
<li>An implementation should support an Alignment clause for a discrete type, fixed point type, record type, or array type, specifying an Alignment value that is zero or a power of two, subject to the following:<br /></li>
<MarginText>31/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00051-02", "AI12-0444-1"]} />
<li>An implementation is not required to support an Alignment clause for a signed integer type specifying an Alignment greater than the largest Alignment value that is ever chosen by default by the implementation for any signed integer type. A corresponding limitation may be imposed for modular integer types, fixed point types, enumeration types, record types, and array types.<br /></li>
<MarginText>32/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00051-02", "AI12-0444-1"]} />
<li>An implementation is not required to support a nonconfirming Alignment clause that can cause the creation of an object of an elementary type that cannot be easily loaded and stored by available machine instructions.<br /></li>
<MarginText>32.1/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02", "AI12-0444-1"]} />
<li>An implementation is not required to support an Alignment specified for a derived tagged type that is not a multiple of the Alignment of the parent type. An implementation is not required to support a nonconfirming Alignment specified for a derived untagged by-reference type. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>32.a/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>There is no recommendation to support any nonconfirming Alignment clauses for types not mentioned above. Remember that <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1">13.1</a> requires support for confirming Alignment clauses for all types. <br />

<MarginText>32.b/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0116-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>An implementation that tries to support other alignments for derived tagged types will need to allow inherited subprograms to be passed objects that are less aligned than expected by the parent subprogram and type. This is unlikely to work if alignment has any effect on code selection. Similar issues arise for untagged derived types whose parameters are passed by reference. <br />

<MarginText>33</MarginText>
<p>The recommended level of support for the Alignment attribute for objects is: <br /></p>

<MarginText>34/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02"]} />
<ul>
<li><i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br /></li>
<MarginText>35</MarginText>
<li>For stand-alone library-level objects of statically constrained subtypes, the implementation should support all Alignments supported by the target linker. For example, page alignment is likely to be supported for such objects, but not for subtypes.<br /></li>
<MarginText>35.1/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02"]} />
<li>For other objects, an implementation should at least support the alignments supported for their subtype, subject to the following:<br /></li>
<MarginText>35.2/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00291-02", "AI12-0444-1"]} />
<li>An implementation is not required to support Alignments specified for objects of a by-reference type or for objects of types containing aliased subcomponents if the specified Alignment is not a multiple of the Alignment of the subtype of the object. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>35.a/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-advice">
<b></b>The recommended level of support for the Alignment attribute should be followed.<br />

<MarginText>36</MarginText>
NOTE 3   Alignment is a subtype-specific attribute.<br />

<MarginText>37/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00247-01"]} />
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>37.a/2</MarginText>
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>38/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1", "AI05-0269-1"]} />
NOTE 4   A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.5#S0353">component_clause</a></code>, Component{"_"}Size clause, or specifying the Pack aspect as True can override a specified Alignment. <br />

<MarginText>38.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Most objects are allocated by the implementation; for these, the implementation obeys the Alignment. The implementation is of course allowed to make an object <i>more</i> aligned than its Alignment requires &mdash; an object whose Alignment is 4 might just happen to land at an address that's a multiple of 4096. For formal parameters, the implementation might want to force an Alignment stricter than the parameter's subtype. For example, on some systems, it is customary to always align parameters to 4 storage elements.<br />

<MarginText>38.b</MarginText>
Hence, one might initially assume that the implementation could evilly make all Alignments 1 by default, even though integers, say, are normally aligned on a 4-storage-element boundary. However, the implementation cannot get away with that &mdash; if the Alignment is 1, the generated code cannot assume an Alignment of 4, at least not for objects allocated outside the control of the implementation.<br />

<MarginText>38.c</MarginText>
Of course implementations can assume anything they can prove, but typically an implementation will be unable to prove much about the alignment of, say, an imported object. Furthermore, the information about where an address &ldquo;came from&rdquo; can be lost to the compiler due to separate compilation.<br />

<MarginText>38.d/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01", "AI05-0229-1"]} />
The Alignment of an object that is a component of a packed composite object will usually be 0, to indicate that the component is not necessarily aligned on a storage element boundary. For a subtype, an Alignment of 0 means that objects of the subtype are not normally aligned on a storage element boundary at all. For example, an implementation might choose to make Component{"_"}Size be 1 for an array of Booleans, even when the Pack aspect has not been specified for the array. In this case, Boolean'Alignment would be 0. (In the presence of tasking, this would in general be feasible only on a machine that had atomic test-bit and set-bit instructions.)<br />

<MarginText>38.e</MarginText>
If the machine has no particular natural alignments, then all subtype Alignments will probably be 1 by default.<br />

<MarginText>38.f</MarginText>
Specifying an Alignment of 0 in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute_definition_clause</a></code> does not require the implementation to do anything (except return 0 when the Alignment is queried). However, it might be taken as advice on some implementations.<br />

<MarginText>38.g</MarginText>
It is an error for an Address clause to disobey the object's Alignment. The error cannot be detected at compile time, in general, because the Address is not necessarily known at compile time (and is almost certainly not static). We do not require a runtime check, since efficiency seems paramount here, and Address clauses are treading on thin ice anyway. Hence, this misuse of Address clauses is just like any other misuse of Address clauses &mdash; it's erroneous.<br />

<MarginText>38.h</MarginText>
A type extension can have a stricter Alignment than its parent. This can happen, for example, if the Alignment of the parent is 4, but the extension contains a component with Alignment 8. The Alignment of a class-wide type or object will have to be the maximum possible Alignment of any extension.<br />

<MarginText>38.i</MarginText>
The recommended level of support for the Alignment attribute is intended to reflect a minimum useful set of capabilities. An implementation can assume that all Alignments are multiples of each other &mdash; 1, 2, 4, and 8 might be the only supported Alignments for subtypes. An Alignment of 3 or 6 is unlikely to be useful. For objects that can be allocated statically, we recommend that the implementation support larger alignments, such as 4096. We do not recommend such large alignments for subtypes, because the maximum subtype alignment will also have to be used as the alignment of stack frames, heap objects, and class-wide objects. Similarly, we do not recommend such large alignments for stack-allocated objects.<br />

<MarginText>38.j</MarginText>
If the maximum default Alignment is 8 (say, Long{"_"}Float'Alignment = 8), then the implementation can refuse to accept stricter alignments for subtypes. This simplifies the generated code, since the compiler can align the stack and class-wide types to this maximum without a substantial waste of space (or time).<br />

<MarginText>38.k</MarginText>
Note that the recommended level of support takes into account interactions between Size and Alignment. For example, on a 32-bit machine with 8-bit storage elements, where load and store instructions have to be aligned according to the size of the thing being loaded or stored, the implementation might accept an Alignment of 1 if the Size is 8, but might reject an Alignment of 1 if the Size is 32. On a machine where unaligned loads and stores are merely inefficient (as opposed to causing hardware traps), we would expect an Alignment of 1 to be supported for any Size. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>38.l/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0005-1"]} />
The nonnegative part is missing from RM83 (for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-J/AA-J.8#S0369">mod_clause</a></code>s, known in Ada 83 as <code>alignment{"_"}clause</code>s, which are an obsolete version of Alignment clauses). <br />

#### Implementation Advice

<MarginText>41.1/2</MarginText>

<p>The size of an array object should not include its bounds. <br /></p>

<MarginText>41.a.1/2</MarginText>
