# 13.7. The Package System

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.7.mdx

sidebar_position:  111

# 13.7. The Package System

<MarginText>1</MarginText>
<p>[For each implementation there is a library package called System which includes the definitions of certain configuration-dependent characteristics.] <br /></p>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>2</MarginText>
<p>The following language-defined library package exists: <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.a/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-defined">
<b></b>The contents of the visible part of package System.<br />

<MarginText>3/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00362-01", "AI12-0414-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package System{"\n"}   with Pure is{"\n"}
<MarginText>4</MarginText>
   type Name is implementation-defined-enumeration-type;{"\n"}   System{"_"}Name : constant Name := implementation-defined;{"\n"}
<MarginText>5</MarginText>
   -- System-Dependent Named Numbers:{"\n"}
<MarginText>6</MarginText>
   Min{"_"}Int               : constant := root{"_"}integer'First;{"\n"}   Max{"_"}Int               : constant := root{"_"}integer'Last;{"\n"}
<MarginText>7</MarginText>
   Max{"_"}Binary{"_"}Modulus    : constant := implementation-defined;{"\n"}   Max{"_"}Nonbinary{"_"}Modulus : constant := implementation-defined;{"\n"}
<MarginText>8</MarginText>
   Max{"_"}Base{"_"}Digits       : constant := root{"_"}real'Digits;{"\n"}   Max{"_"}Digits            : constant := implementation-defined;{"\n"}
<MarginText>9</MarginText>
   Max{"_"}Mantissa          : constant := implementation-defined;{"\n"}   Fine{"_"}Delta            : constant := implementation-defined;{"\n"}
<MarginText>10</MarginText>
   Tick                  : constant := implementation-defined;{"\n"}
<MarginText>11</MarginText>
   -- Storage-related Declarations:{"\n"}
<MarginText>12</MarginText>
   type Address is implementation-defined;{"\n"}   Null{"_"}Address : constant Address;{"\n"}
<MarginText>13</MarginText>
   Storage{"_"}Unit : constant := implementation-defined;{"\n"}   Word{"_"}Size    : constant := implementation-defined {"*"} Storage{"_"}Unit;{"\n"}   Memory{"_"}Size  : constant := implementation-defined;{"\n"}
<MarginText>14/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
   -- Address Comparison:{"\n"}   function "{"<"}" (Left, Right : Address) return Boolean{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}   function "{"<"}="(Left, Right : Address) return Boolean{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}   function "{">"}" (Left, Right : Address) return Boolean{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}   function "{">"}="(Left, Right : Address) return Boolean{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}   function "=" (Left, Right : Address) return Boolean{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}-- function "/=" (Left, Right : Address) return Boolean;{"\n"}   -- "/=" is implicitly defined{"\n"}
<MarginText>15/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00221-01"]} />
   -- Other System-Dependent Declarations:{"\n"}   type Bit{"_"}Order is (High{"_"}Order{"_"}First, Low{"_"}Order{"_"}First);{"\n"}   Default{"_"}Bit{"_"}Order : constant Bit{"_"}Order := implementation-defined;{"\n"}
<MarginText>16</MarginText>
   -- Priority-related declarations (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-D/AA-D.1">D.1</a>):{"\n"}   subtype Any{"_"}Priority is Integer range implementation-defined;{"\n"}   subtype Priority is Any{"_"}Priority range Any{"_"}Priority'First ..{"\n"}             implementation-defined;{"\n"}   subtype Interrupt{"_"}Priority is Any{"_"}Priority range Priority'Last+1 ..{"\n"}             Any{"_"}Priority'Last;{"\n"}
<MarginText>17</MarginText>
   Default{"_"}Priority : constant Priority :={"\n"}             (Priority'First + Priority'Last)/2;{"\n"}
<MarginText>18</MarginText>
private{"\n"}   ... -- not specified by the language{"\n"}end System;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>19</MarginText>
<p>Name is an enumeration subtype. Values of type Name are the names of alternative machine configurations handled by the implementation. System{"_"}Name represents the current machine configuration.<br /></p>

<MarginText>20</MarginText>
<p>The named numbers Fine{"_"}Delta and Tick are of the type <i>universal{"_"}real</i>; the others are of the type <i>universal{"_"}integer</i>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>21</MarginText>
<p>The meanings of the named numbers are: <br /></p>

<MarginText>22</MarginText>
<dt><br/>[ Min{"_"}Int </dt>
<dl>
<dd>The smallest (most negative) value allowed for the expressions of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0042">signed{"_"}integer{"_"}type{"_"}definition</a></code>.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>23</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Max{"_"}Int </dt>
<dd>The largest (most positive) value allowed for the expressions of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0042">signed{"_"}integer{"_"}type{"_"}definition</a></code>.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>24</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Max{"_"}Binary{"_"}Modulus </dt>
<dd>A power of two such that it, and all lesser positive powers of two, are allowed as the modulus of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0043">modular_type_definition</a></code>.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>25</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Max{"_"}Nonbinary{"_"}Modulus </dt>
<dd>A value such that it, and all lesser positive integers, are allowed as the modulus of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0043">modular_type_definition</a></code>. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>25.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>There is no requirement that Max{"_"}Nonbinary{"_"}Modulus be less than or equal to Max{"_"}Binary{"_"}Modulus, although that's what makes most sense. On a typical 32-bit machine, for example, Max{"_"}Binary{"_"}Modulus will be 2{"*"}{"*"}32 and Max{"_"}Nonbinary{"_"}Modulus will be 2{"*"}{"*"}31, because supporting nonbinary moduli in above 2{"*"}{"*"}31 causes implementation difficulties. <br />

<MarginText>26</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Max{"_"}Base{"_"}Digits </dt>
<dl>
<dd>The largest value allowed for the requested decimal precision in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0045">floating{"_"}point{"_"}definition</a></code>.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>27</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Max{"_"}Digits </dt>
<dd>The largest value allowed for the requested decimal precision in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0045">floating{"_"}point{"_"}definition</a></code> that has no <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0046">real{"_"}range{"_"}specification</a></code>. Max{"_"}Digits is less than or equal to Max{"_"}Base{"_"}Digits.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>28</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Max{"_"}Mantissa </dt>
<dd>The largest possible number of binary digits in the mantissa of machine numbers of a user-defined ordinary fixed point type. (The mantissa is defined in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-G/">Annex G</a>.)<br /></dd>
<MarginText>29</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Fine{"_"}Delta </dt>
<dd>The smallest delta allowed in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0048">ordinary_fixed_point_definition</a></code> that has the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0046">real{"_"}range{"_"}specification</a></code> <b>range</b> &ndash;1.0 .. 1.0. ]<br /></dd>
<MarginText>30</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Tick </dt>
<dd>A period in seconds approximating the real time interval during which the value of Calendar.Clock remains constant. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>30.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>There is no required relationship between System.Tick and Duration'Small, other than the one described here.<br />

<MarginText>30.b</MarginText>
The inaccuracy of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.6#S0266">delay_statement</a></code> has no relation to Tick. In particular, it is possible that the clock used for the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.6#S0266">delay_statement</a></code> is less accurate than Calendar.Clock.<br />

<MarginText>30.c</MarginText>
We considered making Tick a run-time-determined quantity, to allow for easier configurability. However, this would not be upward compatible, and the desired configurability can be achieved using functionality defined in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-D/">Annex D</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-D/">Real-Time Systems</a>&rdquo;. <br />

<MarginText>31</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Storage{"_"}Unit </dt>
<dl>
<dd>The number of bits per storage element.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>32</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Word{"_"}Size </dt>
<dd>The number of bits per word.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>33</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Memory{"_"}Size </dt>
<dd>An implementation-defined value [that is intended to reflect the memory size of the configuration in storage elements.] <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>33.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>It is unspecified whether this refers to the size of the address space, the amount of physical memory on the machine, or perhaps some other interpretation of &ldquo;memory size&rdquo;. In any case, the value has to be given by a static expression, even though the amount of memory on many modern machines is a dynamic quantity in several ways. Thus, Memory{"_"}Size is not very useful. <br />

<MarginText>34/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00161-01"]} />
<p>Address is a definite, nonlimited type with preelaborable initialization (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.2#Subclause_10.2.1">10.2.1</a>). Address represents machine addresses capable of addressing individual storage elements. Null{"_"}Address is an address that is distinct from the address of any object or program unit. <br /></p>

<MarginText>34.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The implementation has to ensure that there is at least one address that nothing will be allocated to; Null{"_"}Address will be one such address. <br />

<MarginText>34.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Address is the type of the result of the attribute Address. <br />

<MarginText>34.c</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>Address is required to be nonlimited and definite because it is important to be able to assign addresses, and to declare uninitialized address variables. <br />

<MarginText>34.d/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00161-01", "AI12-0417-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>If System.Address is defined as a private type (as suggested below), it might be necessary to add the Preelaborable{"_"}Initialization aspect to the declaration of Address in order that it have preelaborable initialization as required. <br />

<MarginText>35/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00221-01"]} />
<p>Default{"_"}Bit{"_"}Order shall be a static constant. See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.5#Subclause_13.5.3">13.5.3</a> for an explanation of Bit{"_"}Order and Default{"_"}Bit{"_"}Order. <br /></p>

#### Implementation Permissions

<MarginText>36/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00362-01"]} />
<p>An implementation may add additional implementation-defined declarations to package System and its children. [However, it is usually better for the implementation to provide additional functionality via implementation-defined children of System.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>36.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The declarations in package System and its children can be implicit. For example, since Address is not limited, the predefined "=" and "/=" operations are probably sufficient. However, the implementation is not <i>required</i> to use the predefined "=". <br />

#### Implementation Advice

<MarginText>37</MarginText>
<p>Address should be a private type. <br /></p>

<MarginText>37.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This promotes uniformity by avoiding having implementation-defined predefined operations for the type. We don't require it, because implementations may want to stick with what they have. <br />

<MarginText>37.a.1/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-advice">
<b></b>Type System.Address should be a private type.<br />

<MarginText>37.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>It is not necessary for Address to be able to point at individual bits within a storage element. Nor is it necessary for it to be able to point at machine registers. It is intended as a memory address that matches the hardware's notion of an address.<br />

<MarginText>37.c</MarginText>
The representation of the <b>null</b> value of a general access type should be the same as that of Null{"_"}Address; instantiations of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion should work accordingly. If the implementation supports interfaces to other languages, the representation of the <b>null</b> value of a general access type should be the same as in those other languages, if appropriate.<br />

<MarginText>37.d</MarginText>
Note that the children of the Interfaces package will generally provide foreign-language-specific null values where appropriate. See UI-0065 regarding Null{"_"}Address. <br />

<MarginText>38</MarginText>
NOTE   There are also some language-defined child packages of System defined elsewhere. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>38.a.1/1</MarginText>
The declarations Max{"_"}Binary{"_"}Modulus, Max{"_"}Nonbinary{"_"}Modulus, Max{"_"}Base{"_"}Digits, Null{"_"}Address, Word{"_"}Size, Bit{"_"}Order, Default{"_"}Bit{"_"}Order, Any{"_"}Priority, Interrupt{"_"}Priority, and Default{"_"}Priority are added to System in Ada 95. The presence of ordering operators for type Address is also guaranteed (the existence of these depends on the definition of Address in an Ada 83 implementation). We do not list these as incompatibilities, as the contents of System can vary between implementations anyway; thus a program that depends on the contents of System (by using <b>use</b> System; for example) is already at risk of being incompatible when moved between Ada implementations. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>38.a</MarginText>
Much of the content of System is standardized, to provide more uniformity across implementations. Implementations can still add their own declarations to System, but are encouraged to do so via children of System.<br />

<MarginText>38.b</MarginText>
Some of the named numbers are defined more explicitly in terms of the standard numeric types.<br />

<MarginText>38.c</MarginText>
The pragmas System{"_"}Name, Storage{"_"}Unit, and Memory{"_"}Size are no longer defined by the language. However, the corresponding declarations in package System still exist. Existing implementations may continue to support the three pragmas as implementation-defined pragmas, if they so desire.<br />

<MarginText>38.d</MarginText>
Priority semantics, including subtype Priority, have been moved to the Real Time Annex. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 95

<MarginText>38.e/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00161-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-advice">
<b>Amendment </b> Type Address is defined to have preelaborable initialization, so that it can be used without restriction in preelaborated units. (If Address is defined to be a private type, as suggested by the , in Ada 95 it cannot be used in some contexts in a preelaborated units. This is an unnecessary portability issue.)<br />

<MarginText>38.f/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00221-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b>Amendment </b> Default{"_"}Bit{"_"}Order is now a static constant.<br />

<MarginText>38.g/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00362-01"]} />
Package System is now Pure, so it can be portably used in more places. (Ada 95 allowed it to be Pure, but did not require that.) <br />

<a id="Subclause_13.7.1"></a>

## 13.7.1  The Package System.Storage_Elements

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>1_13.7.1</MarginText>
<p>The following language-defined library package exists: <br /></p>

<MarginText>2/5_13.7.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00362-01", "AI12-0399-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package System.Storage{"_"}Elements{"\n"}   with Pure is{"\n"}
<MarginText>3_13.7.1</MarginText>
   type Storage{"_"}Offset is range implementation-defined;{"\n"}
<MarginText>4_13.7.1</MarginText>
   subtype Storage{"_"}Count is Storage{"_"}Offset range 0..Storage{"_"}Offset'Last;{"\n"}
<MarginText>5_13.7.1</MarginText>
   type Storage{"_"}Element is mod implementation-defined;{"\n"}   for Storage{"_"}Element'Size use Storage{"_"}Unit;{"\n"}   type Storage{"_"}Array is array{"\n"}     (Storage{"_"}Offset range {"<"}{">"}) of aliased Storage{"_"}Element;{"\n"}   for Storage{"_"}Array'Component{"_"}Size use Storage{"_"}Unit;{"\n"}
<MarginText>6_13.7.1</MarginText>
   -- Address Arithmetic:{"\n"}
<MarginText>7/3_13.7.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
   function "+"(Left : Address; Right : Storage{"_"}Offset) return Address{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}   function "+"(Left : Storage{"_"}Offset; Right : Address) return Address{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}   function "-"(Left : Address; Right : Storage{"_"}Offset) return Address{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}   function "-"(Left, Right : Address) return Storage{"_"}Offset{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}
<MarginText>8/3_13.7.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
   function "mod"(Left : Address; Right : Storage{"_"}Offset){"\n"}      return Storage{"_"}Offset{"\n"}         with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}
<MarginText>9_13.7.1</MarginText>
   -- Conversion to/from integers:{"\n"}
<MarginText>10/3_13.7.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
   type Integer{"_"}Address is implementation-defined;{"\n"}   function To{"_"}Address(Value : Integer{"_"}Address) return Address{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}   function To{"_"}Integer(Value : Address) return Integer{"_"}Address{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}
<MarginText>11/3_13.7.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
end System.Storage{"_"}Elements;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>11.a/3_13.7.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The Convention aspects imply that the attribute Access is not allowed for those operations.<br />

<MarginText>11.b_13.7.1</MarginText>
The <b>mod</b> function is needed so that the definition of Alignment makes sense. <br />

<MarginText>11.c/2_13.7.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-defined">
<b></b>The range of Storage{"_"}Elements.Storage{"_"}Offset, the modulus of Storage{"_"}Elements.Storage{"_"}Element, and the declaration of Storage{"_"}Elements.Integer{"_"}Address.<br />

<MarginText>12_13.7.1</MarginText>
<p>Storage{"_"}Element represents a storage element. Storage{"_"}Offset represents an offset in storage elements. Storage{"_"}Count represents a number of storage elements. Storage{"_"}Array represents a contiguous sequence of storage elements. <br /></p>

<MarginText>12.a_13.7.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The index subtype of Storage{"_"}Array is Storage{"_"}Offset because we wish to allow maximum flexibility. Most Storage{"_"}Arrays will probably have a lower bound of 0 or 1, but other lower bounds, including negative ones, make sense in some situations.<br />

<MarginText>12.b/2_13.7.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01"]} />
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>13_13.7.1</MarginText>
<p>Integer{"_"}Address is a [(signed or modular)] integer subtype. To{"_"}Address and To{"_"}Integer convert back and forth between this type and Address. <br /></p>

#### Implementation Requirements

<MarginText>14_13.7.1</MarginText>
<p>Storage{"_"}Offset'Last shall be greater than or equal to Integer'Last or the largest possible storage offset, whichever is smaller. Storage{"_"}Offset'First shall be {"<"}= (&ndash;Storage{"_"}Offset'Last). <br /></p>

<p><i>Paragraph 15 was deleted.</i> <br /></p>

#### Implementation Advice

<MarginText>16_13.7.1</MarginText>
<p>Operations in System and its children should reflect the target environment semantics as closely as is reasonable. For example, on most machines, it makes sense for address arithmetic to &ldquo;wrap around&rdquo;. Operations that do not make sense should raise Program{"_"}Error. <br /></p>

<MarginText>16.a.1/2_13.7.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-advice">
<b></b>Operations in System and its children should reflect the target environment; operations that do not make sense should raise Program{"_"}Error.<br />

<MarginText>16.a_13.7.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>For example, on a segmented architecture, X {"<"} Y might raise Program{"_"}Error if X and Y do not point at the same segment (assuming segments are unordered). Similarly, on a segmented architecture, the conversions between Integer{"_"}Address and Address might not make sense for some values, and so might raise Program{"_"}Error. <br />

<MarginText>16.b_13.7.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We considered making Storage{"_"}Element a private type. However, it is better to declare it as a modular type in the visible part, since code that uses it is already low level, and might as well have access to the underlying representation. We also considered allowing Storage{"_"}Element to be any integer type, signed integer or modular, but it is better to have uniformity across implementations in this regard, and viewing storage elements as unsigned seemed to make the most sense. <br />

<MarginText>16.c_13.7.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>To{"_"}Address is intended for use in Address clauses. Implementations should overload To{"_"}Address if appropriate. For example, on a segmented architecture, it might make sense to have a record type representing a segment/offset pair, and have a To{"_"}Address conversion that converts from that record type to type Address. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 95

<MarginText>16.d/2_13.7.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00362-01"]} />
Package System.Storage{"_"}Elements is now Pure, so it can be portably used in more places. (Ada 95 allowed it to be Pure, but did not require that.) <br />

<a id="Subclause_13.7.2"></a>

## 13.7.2  The Package System.Address_To_Access_Conversions

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>1_13.7.2</MarginText>
<p>The following language-defined generic library package exists: <br /></p>

<MarginText>2/5_13.7.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0241-1", "AI12-0302-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
generic{"\n"}   type Object({"<"}{">"}) is limited private;{"\n"}package System.Address{"_"}To{"_"}Access{"_"}Conversions {"\n"}   with Preelaborate, Nonblocking, Global ={">"} in out synchronized is{"\n"}
<MarginText>3/3_13.7.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
   type Object{"_"}Pointer is access all Object;{"\n"}   function To{"_"}Pointer(Value : Address) return Object{"_"}Pointer{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}   function To{"_"}Address(Value : Object{"_"}Pointer) return Address{"\n"}      with Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}
<MarginText>4/3_13.7.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
end System.Address{"_"}To{"_"}Access{"_"}Conversions;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>5/2_13.7.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00230-01"]} />
<p>The To{"_"}Pointer and To{"_"}Address subprograms convert back and forth between values of types Object{"_"}Pointer and Address. To{"_"}Pointer(X'Address) is equal to X'Unchecked{"_"}Access for any X that allows Unchecked{"_"}Access. To{"_"}Pointer(Null{"_"}Address) returns <b>null</b>. For other addresses, the behavior is unspecified. To{"_"}Address(<b>null</b>) returns Null{"_"}Address. To{"_"}Address(Y), where Y /= <b>null</b>, returns Y.<b>all</b>'Address. <br /></p>

<MarginText>5.a/3_13.7.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01", "AI05-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The programmer should ensure that the address passed to To{"_"}Pointer is either Null{"_"}Address, or the address of an object of type Object. (If Object is not a by-reference type, the object ought to be aliased; recall that the Address attribute is not required to provide a useful result for other objects.) Otherwise, the behavior of the program is unspecified; it might raise an exception or crash, for example. <br />

<MarginText>5.b_13.7.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>Unspecified is almost the same thing as erroneous; they both allow arbitrarily bad behavior. We don't say erroneous here, because the implementation might allow the address passed to To{"_"}Pointer to point at some memory that just happens to &ldquo;look like&rdquo; an object of type Object. That's not necessarily an error; it's just not portable. However, if the actual type passed to Object is (for example) an array type, the programmer would need to be aware of any dope that the implementation expects to exist, when passing an address that did not come from the Address attribute of an object of type Object.<br />

<MarginText>5.c_13.7.2</MarginText>
One might wonder why To{"_"}Pointer and To{"_"}Address are any better than unchecked conversions. The answer is that Address does not necessarily have the same representation as an access type. For example, an access value might point at the bounds of an array when an address would point at the first element. Or an access value might be an offset in words from someplace, whereas an address might be an offset in bytes from the beginning of memory. <br />

#### Implementation Permissions

<MarginText>6_13.7.2</MarginText>
<p>An implementation may place restrictions on instantiations of Address{"_"}To{"_"}Access{"_"}Conversions. <br /></p>

<MarginText>6.a_13.7.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>For example, if the hardware requires aligned loads and stores, then dereferencing an access value that is not properly aligned might raise an exception.<br />

<MarginText>6.b_13.7.2</MarginText>
For another example, if the implementation has chosen to use negative component offsets (from an access value), it might not be possible to preserve the semantics, since negative offsets from the Address are not allowed. (The Address attribute always points at &ldquo;the first of the storage elements...&rdquo;.) Note that while the implementation knows how to convert an access value into an address, it might not be able to do the reverse. To avoid generic contract model violations, the restriction might have to be detected at run time in some cases. <br />

---

# 13.8. Machine Code Insertions

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.8.mdx

sidebar_position:  112

# 13.8. Machine Code Insertions

<MarginText>1</MarginText>
<p>[ A machine code insertion can be achieved by a call to a subprogram whose <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.1#S0166">sequence_of_statements</a></code> contains <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.8#S0357">code_statement</a></code>s.] <br /></p>

#### Syntax

<MarginText>2</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>code{"_"}statement</code><a id="S0357"></a><code> ::= </code><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code>;<br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3</MarginText>
<p class="Indented2">A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.8#S0357">code_statement</a></code> is only allowed in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.2#S0304">handled{"_"}sequence{"_"}of{"_"}statements</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.3#S0216">subprogram{"_"}body</a></code>. If a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.3#S0216">subprogram{"_"}body</a></code> contains any <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.8#S0357">code{"_"}statement</a></code>s, then within this <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.3#S0216">subprogram{"_"}body</a></code> the only allowed form of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.1#S0167">statement</a></code> is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.8#S0357">code{"_"}statement</a></code> (labeled or not), the only allowed <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.11#S0087">declarative{"_"}item</a></code>s are <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.4#S0235">use{"_"}clause</a></code>s, and no <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.2#S0305">exception{"_"}handler</a></code> is allowed (<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.7#S0018">comment</a></code>s and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.8#S0019">pragma</a></code>s are allowed as usual). <br /></p>

#### Name Resolution Rules

<MarginText>4</MarginText>
<p>The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code> is expected to be of any type. <br /></p>

#### Legality Rules

<MarginText>5</MarginText>
<p>The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code> shall be of a type declared in package System.Machine{"_"}Code. <br /></p>

<MarginText>5.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>This includes types declared in children of System.Machine{"_"}Code. <br />

<MarginText>6</MarginText>
<p>A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.8#S0357">code_statement</a></code> shall appear only within the scope of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0294">with_clause</a></code> that mentions package System.Machine{"_"}Code. <br /></p>

<MarginText>6.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Note that this is not a note; without this rule, it would be possible to write machine code in compilation units which depend on System.Machine{"_"}Code only indirectly. <br />

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>7</MarginText>
<p>The contents of the library package System.Machine{"_"}Code (if provided) are implementation defined. The meaning of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.8#S0357">code_statement</a></code>s is implementation defined. [Typically, each <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code> represents a machine instruction or assembly directive.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>7.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>For example, an instruction might be a record with an Op{"_"}Code component and other components for the operands. <br />

<MarginText>7.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-defined">
<b></b>The contents of the visible part of package System.Machine{"_"}Code, and the meaning of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.8#S0357">code_statement</a></code>s.<br />

#### Implementation Permissions

<MarginText>8</MarginText>
<p>An implementation may place restrictions on <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.8#S0357">code_statement</a></code>s. An implementation is not required to provide package System.Machine{"_"}Code. <br /></p>

<MarginText>9/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0440-1"]} />
NOTE 1   An implementation can provide implementation-defined pragmas specifying register conventions and calling conventions.<br />

<MarginText>10/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00318-02"]} />
NOTE 2   Machine code functions are exempt from the rule that a return statement is required. In fact, return statements are forbidden, since only <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.8#S0357">code_statement</a></code>s are allowed. <br />

<MarginText>10.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The idea is that the author of a machine code subprogram knows the calling conventions, and refers to parameters and results accordingly. The implementation should document where to put the result of a machine code function, for example, &ldquo;Scalar results are returned in register 0&rdquo;. <br />

<MarginText>11</MarginText>
NOTE 3   Intrinsic subprograms (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.3#Subclause_6.3.1">6.3.1</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.3#Subclause_6.3.1">Conformance Rules</a>&rdquo;) can also be used to achieve machine code insertions. Interface to assembly language can be achieved using the features in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-B/">Annex B</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-B/">Interface to Other Languages</a>&rdquo;. <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>12</MarginText>
<p><i>Example of a code statement:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>13/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
M : Mask;{"\n"}procedure Set{"_"}Mask{"\n"}  with Inline;{"\n"}
<MarginText>14</MarginText>
procedure Set{"_"}Mask is{"\n"}  use System.Machine{"_"}Code; -- assume &ldquo;with System.Machine{"_"}Code;&rdquo; appears somewhere above{"\n"}begin{"\n"}  SI{"_"}Format'(Code ={">"} SSM, B ={">"} M'Base{"_"}Reg, D ={">"} M'Disp);{"\n"}  --  Base{"_"}Reg and Disp are implementation-defined attributes{"\n"}end Set{"_"}Mask;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>14.a</MarginText>
Machine code functions are allowed in Ada 95; in Ada 83, only procedures were allowed. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>14.b</MarginText>
The syntax for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.8#S0357">code_statement</a></code> is changed to say &ldquo;<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code>&rdquo; instead of &ldquo;<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code>'<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0107">record_aggregate</a></code>&rdquo;. Requiring the type of each instruction to be a record type is overspecification. <br />

---

# 13.9. Unchecked Type Conversions

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.9.mdx

sidebar_position:  113

# 13.9. Unchecked Type Conversions

<MarginText>1</MarginText>
<p>[ An unchecked type conversion can be achieved by a call to an instance of the generic function Unchecked{"_"}Conversion.] <br /></p>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>2</MarginText>
<p>The following language-defined generic library function exists: <br /></p>

<MarginText>3/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1", "AI12-0241-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
generic{"\n"}   type Source({"<"}{">"}) is limited private;{"\n"}   type Target({"<"}{">"}) is limited private;{"\n"}function Ada.Unchecked{"_"}Conversion(S : Source) return Target{"\n"}   with Pure, Nonblocking, Convention ={">"} Intrinsic;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3.a/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The aspect Convention implies that the attribute Access is not allowed for instances of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion. <br />

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>4</MarginText>
<p>The size of the formal parameter S in an instance of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion is that of its subtype. [This is the actual subtype passed to Source, except when the actual is an unconstrained composite subtype, in which case the subtype is constrained by the bounds or discriminants of the value of the actual expression passed to S.]<br /></p>

<MarginText>5</MarginText>
<p>If all of the following are true, the effect of an unchecked conversion is to return the value of an object of the target subtype whose representation is the same as that of the source object S: <br /></p>

<MarginText>6</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>S'Size = Target'Size. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>6.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Note that there is no requirement that the Sizes be known at compile time. <br />

<MarginText>7/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0078-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>S'Alignment is a multiple of Target'Alignment or Target'Alignment is zero.<br /></li>
<MarginText>8</MarginText>
<li>The target subtype is not an unconstrained composite subtype.<br /></li>
<MarginText>9</MarginText>
<li>S and the target subtype both have a contiguous representation.<br /></li>
<MarginText>10</MarginText>
<li>The representation of S is a representation of an object of the target subtype. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>11/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01"]} />
<p>Otherwise, if the result type is scalar, the result of the function is implementation defined, and can have an invalid representation (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.9#Subclause_13.9.1">13.9.1</a>). If the result type is nonscalar, the effect is implementation defined; in particular, the result can be abnormal (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.9#Subclause_13.9.1">13.9.1</a>).<br /></p>

<MarginText>11.a.1/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-defined">
<b></b>The result of unchecked conversion for instances with scalar result types whose result is not defined by the language.<br />

<MarginText>11.a/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-defined">
<b></b>The effect of unchecked conversion for instances with nonscalar result types whose effect is not defined by the language.<br />

<MarginText>11.a.1/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>Note the difference between these sentences; the first only says that the bits returned are implementation defined, while the latter allows any effect. The difference is because scalar objects should never be abnormal unless their assignment was disrupted or if they are a subcomponent of an abnormal composite object. Neither exception applies to instances of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion. <br />

<MarginText>11.a.2/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Whenever unchecked conversions are used, it is the programmer's responsibility to ensure that these conversions maintain the properties that are guaranteed by the language for objects of the target type. For nonscalar types, this requires the user to understand the underlying run-time model of  the implementation. The execution of a program that violates these properties by means of unchecked conversions returning a nonscalar type is erroneous. Properties of scalar types can be checked by using the Valid attribute (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.9#Subclause_13.9.2">13.9.2</a>); programs can avoid violating properties of the type (and erroneous execution) by careful use of this attribute.<br />

<MarginText>11.b</MarginText>
An instance of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion can be applied to an object of a private type, assuming the implementation allows it. <br />

#### Implementation Permissions

<MarginText>12</MarginText>
<p>An implementation may return the result of an unchecked conversion by reference, if the Source type is not a by-copy type. [In this case, the result of the unchecked conversion represents simply a different (read-only) view of the operand of the conversion.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>12.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>In other words, the result object of a call on an instance of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion can occupy the same storage as the formal parameter S. <br />

<MarginText>13</MarginText>
<p>An implementation may place restrictions on Unchecked{"_"}Conversion. <br /></p>

<MarginText>13.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>For example, an instantiation of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion for types for which unchecked conversion doesn't make sense may be disallowed. <br />

#### Implementation Advice

<MarginText>14/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00051-02"]} />
<p>Since the Size of an array object generally does not include its bounds, the bounds should not be part of the converted data. <br /></p>

<MarginText>14.a.1/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-advice">
<b></b>Since the Size of an array object generally does not include its bounds, the bounds should not be part of the converted data in an instance of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion.<br />

<MarginText>14.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>On the other hand, we have no advice to offer about discriminants and tag fields. <br />

<MarginText>15</MarginText>
<p>The implementation should not generate unnecessary runtime checks to ensure that the representation of S is a representation of the target type. It should take advantage of the permission to return by reference when possible. Restrictions on unchecked conversions should be avoided unless required by the target environment. <br /></p>

<MarginText>15.a.1/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-advice">
<b></b>There should not be unnecessary runtime checks on the result of an Unchecked{"_"}Conversion; the result should be returned by reference when possible. Restrictions on Unchecked{"_"}Conversions should be avoided.<br />

<MarginText>15.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>As an example of an unnecessary runtime check, consider a record type with gaps between components. The compiler might assume that such gaps are always zero bits. If a value is produced that does not obey that assumption, then the program might misbehave. The implementation should not generate extra code to check for zero bits (except, perhaps, in a special error-checking mode). <br />

<MarginText>16</MarginText>
<p>The recommended level of support for unchecked conversions is: <br /></p>

<MarginText>17/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>Unchecked conversions should be supported and should be reversible in the cases where this subclause defines the result. To enable meaningful use of unchecked conversion, a contiguous representation should be used for elementary subtypes, for statically constrained array subtypes whose component subtype is one of the subtypes described in this paragraph, and for record subtypes without discriminants whose component subtypes are described in this paragraph. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>17.a/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-advice">
<b></b>The recommended level of support for Unchecked{"_"}Conversion should be followed.<br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>17.b/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00051-02"]} />
The implementation advice about the size of array objects was moved to 13.3 so that all of the advice about Size is in one place.<br />

<MarginText>17.c/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01"]} />
Clarified that the result of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion for scalar types can be invalid, but not abnormal. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>17.d/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0078-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Relaxed the alignment requirement slightly, giving a defined result in more cases. <br />

<a id="Subclause_13.9.1"></a>

## 13.9.1  Data Validity

<MarginText>1_13.9.1</MarginText>
<p>Certain actions that can potentially lead to erroneous execution are not directly erroneous, but instead can cause objects to become <i>abnormal</i>. Subsequent uses of abnormal objects can be erroneous.<br /></p>

<MarginText>2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<p>A scalar object can have an <i>invalid representation</i>, which means that the object's representation does not represent any value of the object's subtype. The primary cause of invalid representations is uninitialized variables.<br /></p>

<MarginText>3_13.9.1</MarginText>
<p>Abnormal objects and invalid representations are explained in this subclause. <br /></p>

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>4_13.9.1</MarginText>
<p>When an object is first created, and any explicit or default initializations have been performed, the object and all of its parts are in the <i>normal</i> state. Subsequent operations generally leave them normal. However, an object or part of an object can become <i>abnormal</i> in the following ways: <br /></p>

<MarginText>5_13.9.1</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>An assignment to the object is disrupted due to an abort (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.8">9.8</a>) or due to the failure of a language-defined check (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.6">11.6</a>).<br /></li>
<MarginText>6/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01"]} />
<li>The object is not scalar, and is passed to an <b>in out</b> or <b>out</b> parameter of an imported procedure, the Read procedure of an instance of Sequential{"_"}IO, Direct{"_"}IO, or Storage{"_"}IO, or the stream attribute T'Read, if after return from the procedure the representation of the parameter does not represent a value of the parameter's subtype.<br /></li>
<MarginText>6.1/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01"]} />
<li>The object is the return object of a function call of a nonscalar type, and the function is an imported function, an instance of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion, or the stream attribute T'Input, if after return from the function the representation of the return object does not represent a value of the function's subtype.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>6.a/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>We explicitly list the routines involved in order to avoid future arguments. All possibilities are listed.<br />

<MarginText>6.b/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
We did not include Stream{"_"}IO.Read in the list above. A Stream{"_"}Element should include all possible bit patterns, and thus it cannot be invalid. Therefore, the parameter will always represent a value of its subtype. By omitting this routine, we make it possible to write arbitrary I/O operations without any possibility of abnormal objects. <br />

<MarginText>6.2/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01"]} />
<p>[For an imported object, it is the programmer's responsibility to ensure that the object remains in a normal state.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>6.c/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>This follows (and echos) the standard rule of interfacing; the programmer must ensure that Ada semantics are followed (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-B/AA-B.1">B.1</a>). <br />

<MarginText>7_13.9.1</MarginText>
<p>Whether or not an object actually becomes abnormal in these cases is not specified. An abnormal object becomes normal again upon successful completion of an assignment to the object as a whole. <br /></p>

#### Erroneous Execution

<MarginText>8_13.9.1</MarginText>
<p>It is erroneous to evaluate a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0141">primary</a></code> that is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> denoting an abnormal object, or to evaluate a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> that denotes an abnormal object. <br /></p>

<MarginText>8.a/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01"]} />
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>8.b_13.9.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The <b>in out</b> or <b>out</b> parameter case does not apply to scalars; bad scalars are merely invalid representations, rather than abnormal, in this case. <br />

<MarginText>8.c/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The reason we allow access objects, and objects containing subcomponents of an access type, to become abnormal is because the correctness of an access value cannot necessarily be determined merely by looking at the bits of the object. The reason we allow scalar objects to become abnormal is that we wish to allow the compiler to optimize assuming that the value of a scalar object belongs to the object's subtype, if the compiler can prove that the object is initialized with a value that belongs to the subtype. The reason we allow composite objects to become abnormal is that such object might be represented with implicit levels of indirection; if those are corrupted, then even assigning into a component of the object, or simply asking for its Address, might have an unpredictable effect. The same is true if the discriminants have been destroyed. <br />

#### Bounded (Run-Time) Errors

<MarginText>9_13.9.1</MarginText>
<p>If the representation of a scalar object does not represent a value of the object's subtype (perhaps because the object was not initialized), the object is said to have an <i>invalid representation</i>. It is a bounded error to evaluate the value of such an object. If the error is detected, either Constraint{"_"}Error or Program{"_"}Error is raised. Otherwise, execution continues using the invalid representation. The rules of the language outside this subclause assume that all objects have valid representations. The semantics of operations on invalid representations are as follows:<br /></p>

<MarginText>9.a_13.9.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The AARM is more explicit about what happens when the value of the case expression is an invalid representation.<br />

<MarginText>9.b/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>This includes the result object of functions, including the result of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion, T'Input, and imported functions. <br />

<MarginText>10_13.9.1</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>If the representation of the object represents a value of the object's type, the value of the type is used.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11_13.9.1</MarginText>
<li>If the representation of the object does not represent a value of the object's type, the semantics of operations on such representations is implementation-defined, but does not by itself lead to erroneous or unpredictable execution, or to other objects becoming abnormal. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>11.a/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>This means that the implementation must take care not to use an invalid representation in a way that might cause erroneous execution. For instance, the exception mandated for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.4#S0176">case_statement</a></code>s must be raised. Array indexing must not cause memory outside of the array to be written (and usually, not read either). These cases and similar cases may require explicit checks by the implementation. <br />

#### Erroneous Execution

<MarginText>12/3_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00167-01", "AI05-0279-1"]} />
<p>A call to an imported function or an instance of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion is erroneous if the result is scalar, the result object has an invalid representation, and the result is used other than as the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code> or an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#S0032">object_declaration</a></code>, as the <i>object{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0239">object_renaming_declaration</a></code>, or as the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> of a Valid attribute. If such a result object is used as the source of an assignment, and the assigned value is an invalid representation for the target of the assignment, then any use of the target object prior to a further assignment to the target object, other than as the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> of a Valid attribute reference, is erroneous. <br /></p>

<MarginText>12.a/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00167-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>In a typical implementation, every bit pattern that fits in an object of a signed integer subtype will represent a value of the type, if not of the subtype. However, for an enumeration or floating point type, as well as some modular types, there are typically bit patterns that do not represent any value of the type. In such cases, the implementation ought to define the semantics of operations on the invalid representations in the obvious manner (assuming the bounded error is not detected): a given representation should be equal to itself, a representation that is in between the internal codes of two enumeration literals should behave accordingly when passed to comparison operators and membership tests, etc. We considered <i>requiring</i> such sensible behavior, but it resulted in too much arcane verbiage, and since implementations have little incentive to behave irrationally, such verbiage is not important to have.<br />

<MarginText>12.b/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00167-01"]} />
If a stand-alone scalar object is initialized to a an in-range value, then the implementation can take advantage of the fact that the use of any out-of-range value has to be erroneous. Such an out-of-range value can be produced only by things like unchecked conversion, imported functions, and abnormal values caused by disruption of an assignment due to abort or to failure of a language-defined check. This depends on out-of-range values being checked before assignment (that is, checks are not optimized away unless they are proven redundant).<br />

<MarginText>12.c_13.9.1</MarginText>
Consider the following example: <br />

<MarginText>12.d/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00167-01"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type My{"_"}Int is range 0..99;{"\n"}function Safe{"_"}Convert is new Unchecked{"_"}Conversion(My{"_"}Int, Integer);{"\n"}function Unsafe{"_"}Convert is new Unchecked{"_"}Conversion(My{"_"}Int, Positive);{"\n"}X : Positive := Safe{"_"}Convert(0); -- Raises Constraint{"_"}Error.{"\n"}Y : Positive := Unsafe{"_"}Convert(0); -- Bounded Error, may be invalid.{"\n"}B : Boolean  := Y'Valid; -- OK, B = False.{"\n"}Z : Positive := Y+1; -- Erroneous to use Y.{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>12.e/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00167-01", "AI95-00426-01"]} />
The call to Unsafe{"_"}Convert  is a bounded error, which might raise Constraint{"_"}Error, Program{"_"}Error, or return an invalid value. Moreover, if an exception is not raised, most uses of that invalid value (including the use of Y) cause erroneous execution. The call to Safe{"_"}Convert is not erroneous. The result object is an object of subtype Integer containing the value 0. The assignment to X is required to do a constraint check; the fact that the conversion is unchecked does not obviate the need for subsequent checks required by the language rules.<br />

<MarginText>12.e.1/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00167-01", "AI95-00426-01"]} />
The reason for delaying erroneous execution until the object is used is so that the invalid representation can be tested for validity using the Valid attribute (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.9#Subclause_13.9.2">13.9.2</a>) without causing execution to become erroneous. Note that this delay does not imply an exception will not be raised; an implementation could treat both conversions in the example in the same way and raise Constraint{"_"}Error.<br />

<MarginText>12.e.2/3_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0279-1"]} />
The rules are defined in terms of the result object, and thus the name used to reference that object is irrelevant. That is why we don't need any special rules to describe what happens when the function result is renamed.<br />

<MarginText>12.f_13.9.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>If an implementation wants to have a &ldquo;friendly&rdquo; mode, it might always assign an uninitialized scalar a default initial value that is outside the object's subtype (if there is one), and check for this value on some or all reads of the object, so as to help detect references to uninitialized scalars. Alternatively, an implementation might want to provide an &ldquo;unsafe&rdquo; mode where it presumed even uninitialized scalars were always within their subtype. <br />

<MarginText>12.g_13.9.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The above rules imply that it is a bounded error to apply a predefined operator to an object with a scalar subcomponent having an invalid representation, since this implies reading the value of each subcomponent. Either Program{"_"}Error or Constraint{"_"}Error is raised, or some result is produced, which if composite, might have a corresponding scalar subcomponent still with an invalid representation.<br />

<MarginText>12.h_13.9.1</MarginText>
Note that it is not an error to assign, convert, or pass as a parameter a composite object with an uninitialized scalar subcomponent. In the other hand, it is a (bounded) error to apply a predefined operator such as =, {"<"}, and <b>xor</b> to a composite operand with an invalid scalar subcomponent. <br />

<MarginText>13/3_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0054-2"]} />
<p>The dereference of an access value is erroneous if it does not designate an object of an appropriate type or a subprogram with an appropriate profile, if it designates a nonexistent object, or if it is an access-to-variable value that designates a constant object and it did not originate from an attribute{"_"}reference applied to an aliased variable view of a controlled or immutably limited object. [An access value whose dereference is erroneous can exist, for example, because of Unchecked{"_"}Deallocation, Unchecked{"_"}Access, or Unchecked{"_"}Conversion.]<br /></p>

<MarginText>13.a_13.9.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The above mentioned Unchecked{"_"}... features are not the only causes of such access values. For example, interfacing to other languages can also cause the problem.<br />

<MarginText>13.b/3_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0054-2"]} />
We permit the use of access-to-variable values that designate constant objects so long as they originate from an aliased variable view of a controlled or immutably limited constant, such as during the initialization of a constant (both via the &ldquo;current instance&rdquo; and during a call to Initialize) or during an assignment (during a call to Adjust). <br />

<MarginText>14_13.9.1</MarginText>
NOTE   Objects can become abnormal due to other kinds of actions that directly update the object's representation; such actions are generally considered directly erroneous, however. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>14.a_13.9.1</MarginText>
In order to reduce the amount of erroneousness, we separate the concept of an undefined value into objects with invalid representation (scalars only) and abnormal objects.<br />

<MarginText>14.b_13.9.1</MarginText>
Reading an object with an invalid representation is a bounded error rather than erroneous; reading an abnormal object is still erroneous. In fact, the only safe thing to do to an abnormal object is to assign to the object as a whole. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>14.c/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00167-01"]} />
The description of erroneous execution for Unchecked{"_"}Conversion and imported objects was tightened up so that using the Valid attribute to test such a value is not erroneous.<br />

<MarginText>14.d/2_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01"]} />
Clarified the definition of objects that can become abnormal; made sure that all of the possibilities are included. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>14.e/3_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0054-2"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Common programming techniques such as squirreling away an access to a controlled object during initialization and using a self-referencing discriminant (the so-called &ldquo;Rosen trick&rdquo;) no longer are immediately erroneous if the object is declared constant, so these techniques can be used portably and safely. Practically, these techniques already worked as compilers did not take much advantage of this rule, so the impact of this change will be slight. <br />

<MarginText>14.f/3_13.9.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0279-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> The description of erroneous execution for Unchecked{"_"}Conversion and imported objects was adjusted to clarify that renaming such an object is not, by itself, erroneous. <br />

<a id="Subclause_13.9.2"></a>

## 13.9.2  The Valid Attribute

<MarginText>1_13.9.2</MarginText>
<p>The Valid attribute can be used to check the validity of data produced by unchecked conversion, input, interface to foreign languages, and the like. <br /></p>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>2_13.9.2</MarginText>
<p>For a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> X that denotes a scalar object [(after any implicit dereference)], the following attribute is defined: <br /></p>

<MarginText>3/4_13.9.2</MarginText>
<dt><br/>X'Valid</dt>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0153-3", "AI12-0071-1"]} />
<dl>
<dd>Yields True if and only if the object denoted by X is normal, has a valid representation, and then, if the preceding conditions hold, the value of X also satisfies the predicates of the nominal subtype of X. The value of this attribute is of the predefined type Boolean. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>3.a_13.9.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Having checked that X'Valid is True, it is safe to read the value of X without fear of erroneous execution caused by abnormality, or a bounded error caused by an invalid representation. Such a read will produce a value in the subtype of X. <br />

<MarginText>4_13.9.2</MarginText>
NOTE 1   Invalid data can be created in the following cases (not counting erroneous or unpredictable execution): <br />

<MarginText>5_13.9.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>an uninitialized scalar object,<br /></li>
<MarginText>6_13.9.2</MarginText>
<li>the result of an unchecked conversion,<br /></li>
<MarginText>7_13.9.2</MarginText>
<li>input,<br /></li>
<MarginText>8_13.9.2</MarginText>
<li>interface to another language (including machine code),<br /></li>
<MarginText>9_13.9.2</MarginText>
<li>aborting an assignment,<br /></li>
<MarginText>10_13.9.2</MarginText>
<li>disrupting an assignment due to the failure of a language-defined check (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.6">11.6</a>), and<br /></li>
<MarginText>11_13.9.2</MarginText>
<li>use of an object whose Address has been specified. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>12/5_13.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0071-1", "AI12-0440-1"]} />
NOTE 2   Determining whether X is normal and has a valid representation as part of the evaluation of X'Valid is not considered to include an evaluation of X; hence, it is not an error to check the validity of an object that is invalid or abnormal. Determining whether X satisfies the predicates of its nominal subtype can include an evaluation of X, but only after it has been determined that X has a valid representation.<br />

<MarginText>13/4_13.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0071-1"]} />
If X is volatile, the evaluation of X'Valid is considered a read of X.<br />

<MarginText>13.a/4_13.9.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>Since an implementation is not allowed to add, remove, or reorder accesses to volatile objects, we have to define X'Valid as a read so that it is implementable for most subtypes as the value of the object is required. <br />

<MarginText>14/5_13.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01", "AI12-0442-1"]} />
NOTE 3   The Valid attribute can be used to check the result of calling an instance of Unchecked{"_"}Conversion (or any other operation that can return invalid values). However, an exception handler is still useful because implementations are permitted to raise Constraint{"_"}Error or Program{"_"}Error if they detect the use of an invalid representation (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.9#Subclause_13.9.1">13.9.1</a>).<br />

<MarginText>14.a_13.9.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>If X is of an enumeration type with a representation clause, then X'Valid checks that the value of X when viewed as an integer is one of the specified internal codes. <br />

<MarginText>14.b_13.9.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>Valid is defined only for scalar objects because the implementation and description burden would be too high for other types. For example, given a typical run-time model, it is impossible to check the validity of an access value. The same applies to composite types implemented with internal pointers. One can check the validity of a composite object by checking the validity of each of its scalar subcomponents. The user should ensure that any composite types that need to be checked for validity are represented in a way that does not involve implementation-defined components, or gaps between components. Furthermore, such types should not contain access subcomponents.<br />

<MarginText>14.c/2_13.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01"]} />
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>14.d_13.9.2</MarginText>
X'Valid is new in Ada 95. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>14.e/2_13.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00426-01"]} />
Added a note explaining that handlers for Constraint{"_"}Error and Program{"_"}Error are needed in the general case of testing for validity. (An implementation could document cases where these are not necessary, but there is no language requirement.) <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>14.f/3_13.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0153-3"]} />
The validity check now also includes a check of the predicate aspects (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#Subclause_3.2.4">3.2.4</a>), if any, of the subtype of the object. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2012

<MarginText>14.g/4_13.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0071-1"]} />
<b>Corrigendum:</b> Updated wording of the attributes X'Valid to use the new term "satisfies the predicates" (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#Subclause_3.2.4">3.2.4</a>). Also updated the notes to make sense when evaluating predicates and testing validity of volatile objects. <br />

# 13. Representation Issues

<MarginText>1/3</MarginText>

# 2.1. Character Set

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.1.mdx

# 2.1. Character Set

<MarginText>1/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI95-00395-01", "AI05-0266-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0450-1", "AI12-0454-1"]} />
<p>The character repertoire for the text of an Ada program consists of the entire coding space described by the ISO/IEC 10646:2020 Universal Coded Character Set. This coding space is organized in <i>planes</i>, each plane comprising 65536 characters. <br /></p>

<MarginText>1.a/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01"]} />
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>1.b/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01"]} />
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>1.c/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI05-0266-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0450-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>It is our intent to follow the terminology of ISO/IEC 10646:2020 where appropriate, and to remain compatible with the character classifications defined in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-A/AA-A.3">A.3</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-A/AA-A.3">Character Handling</a>&rdquo;. <br />

#### Syntax

<p class="Indented2"><i>Paragraphs 2 and 3 were deleted.</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>3.1/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI95-00395-01", "AI05-0266-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0450-1"]} />
<p class="Indented2">A <code>character</code> is defined by this Reference Manual for each cell in the coding space described by ISO/IEC 10646:2020, regardless of whether or not ISO/IEC 10646:2020 allocates a character to that cell. <br /></p>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>4/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI95-00395-01", "AI05-0079-1", "AI05-0262-1", "AI05-0266-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0444-1", "AI12-0450-1"]} />
<p>The coded representation for characters is implementation defined [(it can be a representation that is not defined within ISO/IEC 10646:2020)]. A character whose relative code point in its plane is 16{"#"}FFFE{"#"} or 16{"#"}FFFF{"#"} is not allowed anywhere in the text of a program. The only characters allowed outside of comments are those in categories <code>other{"_"}format</code>, <code>format{"_"}effector</code>, and <code>graphic{"_"}character</code>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>4.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-defined">
<b></b>The coded representation for the text of an Ada program.<br />

<MarginText>4.b/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Note that this rule doesn't really have much force, since the implementation can represent characters in the source in any way it sees fit. For example, an implementation could simply define that what seems to be an <code>other{"_"}private{"_"}use</code> character is actually a representation of the space character. <br />

<MarginText>4.1/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI05-0266-1", "AI05-0299-1", "AI12-0004-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0450-1"]} />
<p>The semantics of an Ada program whose text is not in Normalization Form C (as defined by Clause 22 of ISO/IEC 10646:2020) is implementation defined. <br /></p>

<MarginText>4.c/5</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-defined">
<b></b>The semantics of an Ada program whose text is not in Normalization Form C.<br />

<MarginText>4.d/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0004-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>In particular, an implementation can reject such program source. It is easy during lexical analysis to reject source that contains any code point not present in Normalization Form C. Portable programs should always be encoded in Normalization Form C. <br />

<MarginText>4.e/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0004-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>Normalization Form C ensures that all source is in a unique format; it eliminates ambiguities and security issues potentially caused by source using unusual sequences of characters. Note that WC3 (the Internet standards group) recommends that all Internet content be in Normalization Form C. We don't require this as there is a potentially significant cost to checking this (just rejecting unallowed code points is not enough), and some implementations may need to be interoperable with tools that produce unnormalized text. <br />

<MarginText>5/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI05-0266-1", "AI05-0299-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0450-1"]} />
<p>The description of the language definition in this document uses the character properties General Category, Simple Uppercase Mapping, Uppercase Mapping, and Special Case Condition of the documents referenced by Clause 2 of ISO/IEC 10646:2020. The actual set of graphic symbols used by an implementation for the visual representation of the text of an Ada program is not specified. <br /></p>

<MarginText>5.a/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0263-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The &ldquo;documents referenced&rdquo; means Unicode, Chapter 4. See the Discussion after the the character categorization definition for a source for machine-readable definitions of these properties. <br />

<MarginText>6/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI05-0266-1"]} />
<p>Characters are categorized as follows: <br /></p>

<MarginText>6.a/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1", "AI05-0262-1", "AI05-0266-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0450-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Our character classification considers that the cells not allocated in ISO/IEC 10646:2020 are graphic characters, except for those whose relative code point in their plane is 16{"#"}FFFE{"#"} or 16{"#"}FFFF{"#"}. This seems to provide the best compatibility with future versions of ISO/IEC 10646, as future characters can already be used in Ada character and string literals. <br />

<MarginText>14.a/2</MarginText>
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>14.b/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>We considered basing the definition of lexical elements on Annex A of ISO/IEC TR 10176 (4th edition), which lists the characters which should be supported in identifiers for all programming languages, but we finally decided against this option. Note that it is not our intent to diverge from ISO/IEC TR 10176, except to the extent that ISO/IEC TR 10176 itself diverges from ISO/IEC 10646:2003 (which is the case at the time of this writing [January 2005]).<br />

<MarginText>14.c/2</MarginText>
More precisely, we intend to align strictly with ISO/IEC 10646:2003. It must be noted that ISO/IEC TR 10176 is a Technical Report while ISO/IEC 10646:2003 is a Standard. If one has to make a choice, one should conform with the Standard rather than with the Technical Report. And, it turns out that one <i>must</i> make a choice because there are important differences between the two:<br />

<MarginText>14.d/2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>ISO/IEC TR 10176 is still based on ISO/IEC 10646:2000 while ISO/IEC 10646:2003 has already been published for a year. We cannot afford to delay the adoption of our amendment until ISO/IEC TR 10176 has been revised.<br /></li>
<MarginText>14.e/2</MarginText>
<li>There are considerable differences between the two editions of ISO/IEC 10646, notably in supporting characters beyond the BMP (this might be significant for some languages, e.g. Korean).<br /></li>
<MarginText>14.f/2</MarginText>
<li>ISO/IEC TR 10176 does not define case conversion tables, which are essential for a case-insensitive language like Ada. To get case conversion tables, we would have to reference either ISO/IEC 10646:2003 or Unicode, or we would have to invent our own. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>14.g/2</MarginText>
For the purpose of defining the lexical elements of the language, we need character properties like categorization, as well as case conversion tables. These are mentioned in ISO/IEC 10646:2003 as useful for implementations, with a reference to Unicode. Machine-readable tables are available on the web at URLs: <br />

<MarginText>14.h/2</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
<a href="http://www.unicode.org/Public/UCD/latest/ucd/UnicodeData.txt">http://www.unicode.org/Public/UCD/latest/ucd/UnicodeData.txt</a>{"\n"}<a href="http://www.unicode.org/Public/UCD/latest/ucd/CaseFolding.txt">http://www.unicode.org/Public/UCD/latest/ucd/CaseFolding.txt</a>{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>14.i/2</MarginText>
with an explanatory document found at URL: <br />

<MarginText>14.j/2</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
<a href="http://www.unicode.org/reports/tr44/tr44-20.html">http://www.unicode.org/reports/tr44/tr44-20.html</a>{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>14.k/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0263-1"]} />
The actual text of the standard only makes specific references to the corresponding clauses of ISO/IEC 10646, not to Unicode.<br />

<MarginText>15/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI05-0266-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0450-1"]} />
<p>The following names are used when referring to certain characters (the first name is that given in ISO/IEC 10646:2020): <br /></p>
