As subprogram profiles now may include any kind of incomplete type, we also disallow passing objects of untagged incomplete types in subprogram calls (as the parameter passing method is not known as it is for tagged types) and disallow returning any sort of incomplete objects (since we don't know how big they are). <br />

<MarginText>10.1/5_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0155-1"]} />
<p>The controlling operand or controlling result of a dispatching call shall not be of an incomplete view if the operand or result is dynamically tagged.<br /></p>

<MarginText>10.e/5_3.10.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This rule is needed to prevent the following case:<br />

<MarginText>10.f/5_3.10.1</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package Pack is{"\n"}   type T is tagged;{"\n"}   function F return access T'Class;{"\n"}   function G (X : access T) return Integer;{"\n"}   I : Integer := G (F);                 -- Illegal by above rule.{"\n"}   type T is tagged null record;{"\n"}end Pack;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>10.g/5_3.10.1</MarginText>
If this was not illegal, the compiler would have to generate a dispatching call on G without necessarily knowing where the tag of type T is stored (the completion of T might not be until the body of Pack). The fact that any such call will raise Program{"_"}Error does not absolve us of detecting the problem; see the Language Design Principles in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.14">13.14</a>. <br />

<p><i>Paragraph 11 was deleted.</i> <br /></p>

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>12_3.10.1</MarginText>
<p>The elaboration of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0085">incomplete_type_declaration</a></code> has no effect. <br /></p>

<MarginText>12.a_3.10.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>An incomplete type has no real existence, so it doesn't need to be "created" in the usual sense we do for other types. It is roughly equivalent to a "forward;" declaration in Pascal. Private types are different, because they have a different set of characteristics from their full type. <br />

<MarginText>13/5_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0447-1"]} />
NOTE 1   Within a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.11#S0086">declarative_part</a></code>, an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0085">incomplete_type_declaration</a></code> and a corresponding <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0024">full_type_declaration</a></code> cannot be separated by an intervening body. This is because, by the rules given in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.14">13.14</a>, a type is illegal if it is not completely defined before it is frozen, and a body freezes all types declared prior to it in the same <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.11#S0086">declarative_part</a></code>.<br />

<MarginText>13.1/3_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0151-1", "AI05-0269-1"]} />
NOTE 2   A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> that denotes an object of an incomplete view is defined to be of a limited type. Hence, the target of an assignment statement cannot be of an incomplete view.<br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>14_3.10.1</MarginText>
<p><i>Example of a recursive type:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>15_3.10.1</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type Cell;  --  incomplete type declaration{"\n"}type Link is access Cell;{"\n"}
<MarginText>16_3.10.1</MarginText>
type Cell is{"\n"}   record{"\n"}      Value  : Integer;{"\n"}      Succ   : Link;{"\n"}      Pred   : Link;{"\n"}   end record;{"\n"}
<MarginText>17_3.10.1</MarginText>
Head   : Link  := new Cell'(0, null, null);{"\n"}Next   : Link  := Head.Succ;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>18_3.10.1</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of mutually dependent access types:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>19/2_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00433-01"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type Person({"<"}{">"});    -- incomplete type declaration{"\n"}type Car is tagged; -- incomplete type declaration{"\n"}
<MarginText>20/2_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00433-01"]} />
type Person{"_"}Name is access Person;{"\n"}type Car{"_"}Name    is access all Car'Class;{"\n"}
<MarginText>21/2_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00433-01"]} />
type Car is tagged{"\n"}   record{"\n"}      Number  : Integer;{"\n"}      Owner   : Person{"_"}Name;{"\n"}   end record;{"\n"}
<MarginText>22_3.10.1</MarginText>
type Person(Sex : Gender) is{"\n"}   record{"\n"}      Name     : String(1 .. 20);{"\n"}      Birth    : Date;{"\n"}      Age      : Integer range 0 .. 130;{"\n"}      Vehicle  : Car{"_"}Name;{"\n"}      case Sex is{"\n"}         when M ={">"} Wife           : Person{"_"}Name(Sex ={">"} F);{"\n"}         when F ={">"} Husband        : Person{"_"}Name(Sex ={">"} M);{"\n"}      end case;{"\n"}   end record;{"\n"}
<MarginText>23/5_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0312-1"]} />
My{"_"}Car, Your{"_"}Car, Next{"_"}Car : Car{"_"}Name := new Car;  -- see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8">4.8</a>{"\n"}Casey : Person{"_"}Name := new Person(M);{"\n"}   ...{"\n"}Casey.Vehicle := Your{"_"}Car;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>23.a_3.10.1</MarginText>
The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0024">full_type_declaration</a></code> that completes an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0085">incomplete_type_declaration</a></code> may have a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0061">known_discriminant_part</a></code> even if the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0085">incomplete_type_declaration</a></code> does not.<br />

<MarginText>23.b/1_3.10.1</MarginText>
A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0064">discriminant_constraint</a></code> may be applied to an incomplete type, even if its completion is deferred to the package body, because there is no &ldquo;dependent compatibility check&rdquo; required any more. Of course, the constraint can be specified only if a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0061">known_discriminant_part</a></code> was given in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0085">incomplete_type_declaration</a></code>. As mentioned in the previous paragraph, that is no longer required even when the full type has discriminants. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>23.c_3.10.1</MarginText>
Dereferences producing incomplete types were not explicitly disallowed in RM83, though AI83-00039 indicated that it was not strictly necessary since troublesome cases would result in Constraint{"_"}Error at run time, since the access value would necessarily be null. However, this introduces an undesirable implementation burden, as illustrated by Example 4 of AI83-00039: <br />

<MarginText>23.d_3.10.1</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package Pack is{"\n"}    type Pri is private;{"\n"}private{"\n"}    type Sep;{"\n"}    type Pri is access Sep;{"\n"}    X : Pri;{"\n"}end Pack;{"\n"}
<MarginText>23.e_3.10.1</MarginText>
package body Pack is -- Could be separately compiled!{"\n"}    type Sep is ...;{"\n"}    X := new Sep;{"\n"}end Pack;{"\n"}
<MarginText>23.f_3.10.1</MarginText>
pragma Elaborate(Pack);{"\n"}private package Pack.Child is{"\n"}    I : Integer := X.all'Size; -- Legal, by AI-00039.{"\n"}end Pack.Child;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>23.g_3.10.1</MarginText>
Generating code for the above example could be a serious implementation burden, since it would require all aliased objects to store size dope, and for that dope to be in the same format for all kinds of types (or some other equivalently inefficient implementation). On the contrary, most implementations allocate dope differently (or not at all) for different designated subtypes. <br />

#### Incompatibilities With Ada 95

<MarginText>23.h/2_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00326-01"]} />
It is now illegal to use an incomplete view (type) as the parameter or result of an access-to-subprogram type unless the incomplete view is completed in the same declaration list as the use. This was allowed in Ada 95 for incomplete types where the completion was deferred to the body. By disallowing this rare use of incomplete views, we can allow the use of incomplete views in many more places, which is especially valuable for limited views.<br />

<MarginText>23.i/2_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00326-01"]} />
It is now illegal to use an incomplete view (type) in a primitive subprogram of the type unless the incomplete view is completed in the package specification. This was allowed in Ada 95 for incomplete types where the completion was deferred to the body (the use would have to be in an access parameter). This incompatibility was caused by the fix for the hole noted in Legality Rules above. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 95

<MarginText>23.j/2_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00326-01"]} />
Tagged incomplete types are new. They are allowed in parameter declarations as well as the usual places, as tagged types are always by-reference types (and thus there can be no code generation issue).<br />

<MarginText>23.k/2_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00412-01"]} />
A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0026">subtype_declaration</a></code> can be used to give a new name to an incomplete view of a type. This is valuable to give shorter names to entities imported with a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0295">limited_with_clause</a></code>. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>23.l/2_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00326-01"]} />
The description of incomplete types as <i>incomplete views</i> is new. Ada 95 defined these as separate types, but neglected to give any rules for matching them with other types. Luckily, implementers did the right thing anyway. This change also makes it easier to describe the meaning of a limited view. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 2005

<MarginText>23.m/3_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0098-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Fixed the definition so that an anonymous access-to-subprogram type can use an incomplete view in the same way that a named access-to-subprogram type can.<br />

<MarginText>23.n/3_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0151-1"]} />
Incomplete types now can be used in subprogram declarations. The type has to be complete before any calls or the body is declared. This reduces the places where access types are required for types imported from limited views of packages.<br />

<MarginText>23.o/3_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0162-1"]} />
Incomplete types now can be completed by private types and private extensions. Since this can already happen for limited views, there is no remaining reason to disallow it for explicitly declared incomplete types. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>23.p/3_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0208-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Changed the rules of uses of dereferences of incomplete views such that it does not introduce an unintentional incompatibility with Ada 83 and Ada 95.<br />

<MarginText>23.q/3_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0213-1"]} />
Incomplete types now can be used as actuals to formal incomplete types (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.5#Subclause_12.5.1">12.5.1</a>). <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2012

<MarginText>23.r/5_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0005-1", "AI12-0137-1"]} />
<b>Corrigendum:</b> Changed the wording to clarify that the class-wide type associated with a specific tagged type that has an incomplete view is also an incomplete view. While this was previously undefined, an interpretation where it is not an incomplete view leads to semantic nonsense, and thus we don't consider this a potential incompatibility, as compilers most likely are doing the right thing.<br />

<MarginText>23.s/5_3.10.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0155-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Added a rule preventing a dispatching call on an incomplete type before the completion. This is not an incompatibility as previously this was prevented by the freezing rules. However, that violated the intended design of the freezing rules, so we've now changed to an explicit Legality Rule here, and eliminated the associated freezing rules. <br />

<a id="Subclause_3.10.2"></a>

## 3.10.2  Operations of Access Types

<MarginText>1_3.10.2</MarginText>
<p>[The attribute Access is used to create access values designating aliased objects and nonintrinsic subprograms. The &ldquo;accessibility&rdquo; rules prevent dangling references (in the absence of uses of certain unchecked features &mdash; see Clause <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/">13</a>).] <br /></p>

#### Language Design Principles

<MarginText>1.a_3.10.2</MarginText>
It should be possible for an access value to designate an object declared by an object declaration, or a subcomponent thereof. In implementation terms, this means pointing at stack-allocated and statically allocated data structures. However, dangling references should be prevented, primarily via compile-time rules, so long as features like Unchecked{"_"}Access and Unchecked{"_"}Deallocation are not used.<br />

<MarginText>1.b_3.10.2</MarginText>
In order to create such access values, we require that the access type be a general access type, that the designated object be aliased, and that the accessibility rules be obeyed. <br />

#### Name Resolution Rules

<MarginText>2/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00235-01"]} />
<p>For an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0100">attribute_reference</a></code> with <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0101">attribute_designator</a></code> Access (or Unchecked{"_"}Access &mdash; see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.10">13.10</a>), the expected type shall be a single access type <i>A</i> such that: <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.1/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00235-01"]} />
<ul>
<li><i>A</i> is an access-to-object type with designated type <i>D</i> and the type of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> is <i>D</i>'Class or is covered by <i>D</i>, or<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.2/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00235-01"]} />
<li><i>A</i> is an access-to-subprogram type whose designated profile is type conformant with that of the prefix. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>2.3/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00235-01"]} />
<p>[The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> of such an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0100">attribute_reference</a></code> is never interpreted as an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0095">implicit_dereference</a></code> or a parameterless <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#S0218">function_call</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#Subclause_4.1.4">4.1.4</a>).] The designated type or profile of the expected type of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0100">attribute_reference</a></code> is the expected type or profile for the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.a_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Saying that the expected type shall be a "single access type" is our "new" way of saying that the type has to be determinable from context using only the fact that it is an access type. See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.2">4.2</a> and <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>. Specifying the expected profile only implies type conformance. The more stringent subtype conformance is required by a Legality Rule. This is the only Resolution Rule that applies to the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0100">attribute_reference</a></code>. In all other cases, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> has to be resolved without using context. See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#Subclause_4.1.4">4.1.4</a>.<br />

<MarginText>2.b/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00235-01"]} />
Saying &ldquo;single access type&rdquo; is a bit of a fudge. Both the context and the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> may provide both multiple types; &ldquo;single&rdquo; only means that a single, specific interpretation must remain after resolution. We say &ldquo;single&rdquo; here to trigger the Legality Rules of <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>. The resolution of an access attribute is similar to that of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>. For example: <br />

<MarginText>2.c/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type Int{"_"}Ptr is access all Integer;{"\n"}type Char{"_"}Ptr is access all Character;{"\n"}type Float{"_"}Ptr is access all Float;{"\n"}
<MarginText>2.d/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
function Zap (Val : Int{"_"}Ptr) return Float;   -- (1){"\n"}function Zap (Val : Float{"_"}Ptr) return Float; -- (2){"\n"}function Zop return Int{"_"}Ptr;  -- (3){"\n"}function Zop return Char{"_"}Ptr; -- (4){"\n"}
<MarginText>2.e/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
Result : Float := Zap (Zop.all'Access); -- Resolves to Zap (1) and Zop (3).{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>3/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00162-01", "AI12-0406-1"]} />
<p>[The accessibility rules, which prevent dangling references, are written in terms of <i>accessibility levels</i>, which reflect the run-time nesting of <i>masters</i>. As explained in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.6#Subclause_7.6.1">7.6.1</a>, a master is the execution of a certain construct (called a <i>master construct</i>), such as a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.3#S0216">subprogram_body</a></code>. An accessibility level is <i>deeper than</i> another if it is more deeply nested at run time. For example, an object declared local to a called subprogram has a deeper accessibility level than an object declared local to the calling subprogram. The accessibility rules for access types require that the accessibility level of an object designated by an access value be no deeper than that of the access type. This ensures that the object will live at least as long as the access type, which in turn ensures that the access value cannot later designate an object that no longer exists. The Unchecked{"_"}Access attribute may be used to circumvent the accessibility rules.]<br /></p>

<MarginText>3.a/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The Unchecked{"_"}Access attribute acts as if the object was declared at library-level; this applies even when it is used as the value of anonymous access type. See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.10">13.10</a>.<br />

<MarginText>3.b/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
Subclause <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#Subclause_3.10.2">3.10.2</a>, home of the accessibility rules, is informally known as the &ldquo;Heart of Darkness&rdquo; amongst the maintainers of Ada. Woe unto all who enter here (well, at least unto anyone that needs to understand any of these rules). <br />

<MarginText>3.b.1/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>accessibility level</b> &mdash; representation of the lifetime of an entity in terms of the level of dynamic nesting within which the entity is known to exist<br />

<MarginText>4_3.10.2</MarginText>
<p>[A given accessibility level is said to be <i>statically deeper</i> than another if the given level is known at compile time (as defined below) to be deeper than the other for all possible executions. In most cases, accessibility is enforced at compile time by Legality Rules. Run-time accessibility checks are also used, since the Legality Rules do not cover certain cases involving access parameters and generic packages.]<br /></p>

<MarginText>5/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0345-1"]} />
<p>Each master, and each entity and view created by it, has an accessibility level; when two levels are defined to be the same, the accessibility levels of the two associated entities are said to be <i>tied</i> to each other. Accessibility levels are defined as follows: <br /></p>

<MarginText>6_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>The accessibility level of a given master is deeper than that of each dynamically enclosing master, and deeper than that of each master upon which the task executing the given master directly depends (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.3">9.3</a>).<br /></li>
<MarginText>7/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00162-01", "AI95-00416-01", "AI05-0235-1", "AI12-0067-1", "AI12-0089-1", "AI12-0345-1"]} />
<li>An entity or view defined by a declaration and created as part of its elaboration has the same accessibility level as the innermost master of the declaration except in the cases of renaming and derived access types described below. A formal parameter of a callable entity has the same accessibility level as the master representing the invocation of the entity. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>7.a/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This rule defines the &ldquo;normal&rdquo; accessibility of entities. In the absence of special rules below, we intend for this rule to apply. <br />

<MarginText>7.b/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01", "AI12-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>This rule defines the accessibility of all named access types, as well as the accessibility level of anonymous access types defined by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6#S0056">component_definition</a></code> Special rules exist for the accessibility level of other anonymous types. Components whose (anonymous) type is defined by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0084">access_definition</a></code> have accessibility levels corresponding to named access types defined at the same point. <br />

<MarginText>7.c/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00230-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Because accessibility level is determined by where the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0084">access_definition</a></code> is elaborated, for a type extension, the anonymous access types of components (other than access discriminants) inherited from the parent have the same accessibility as they did in the parent; those in the extension part have the accessibility determined by the scope where the type extension is declared. Similarly, the types of the nondiscriminant access components of a derived untagged type have the same accessibility as they did in the parent. <br />

<MarginText>7.d/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0235-1"]} />
<b>To be honest: </b>We use "invocation of" in the parameter case as a master is formally an execution of something. But we mean this to be interpreted statically (for instance, as the body of the subprogram) for the purposes of computing "statically deeper than" (see below). <br />

<MarginText>7.e/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0235-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Note that accessibility can differ depending on the view of an object (for both static and dynamic accessibility). For instance, the accessibility level of a formal parameter may be different than the accessibility level of the corresponding actual parameter. This occurs in other cases as well. <br />

<MarginText>7.f/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0235-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We define the (dynamic) accessibility of formal parameters in order that it does not depend on the parameter passing model (by-reference or by-copy) as that is implementation defined. Otherwise, there would be a portability issue. <br />

<MarginText>8/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0371-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>The accessibility level of a view of an object or subprogram defined by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0238">renaming_declaration</a></code> is the same as that of the renamed view, unless the renaming is of a formal subprogram, in which case the accessibility level is that of the instance.<br /></li>
<MarginText>9/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01"]} />
<li>The accessibility level of a view conversion, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code>, or parenthesized expression, is the same as that of the operand.<br /></li>
<MarginText>9.1/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0188-1", "AI12-0292-1"]} />
<li>The accessibility level of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#S0148">conditional_expression</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#Subclause_4.5.7">4.5.7</a>) is the accessibility level of the evaluated <i>dependent{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code>.<br /></li>
<MarginText>9.2/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0236-1"]} />
<li>The accessibility level of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#S0156">declare_expression</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#Subclause_4.5.9">4.5.9</a>) is the accessibility level of the <i>body{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code>.<br /></li>
<MarginText>10/4_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00318-02", "AI95-00416-01", "AI05-0234-1", "AI12-0027-1"]} />
<li>The accessibility level of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> that is used (in its entirety) to directly initialize part of an object is that of the object being initialized. In other contexts, the accessibility level of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> is that of the innermost master that evaluates the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code>. Corresponding rules apply to a value conversion (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6">4.6</a>).<br /></li>
<MarginText>10.1/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0234-1"]} />
<li>The accessibility level of the result of a function call is that of the <i>master of the function call</i>, which is determined by the point of call as follows:<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>10.2/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0234-1", "AI12-0402-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>If the result type at the point of the function (or access-to-function type) declaration is a composite type, and the result is used (in its entirety) to directly initialize part of an object, the master is that of the object being initialized. In the case where the initialized object is a coextension (see below) that becomes a coextension of another object, the master is that of the eventual object to which the coextension will be transferred.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>10.a/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01"]} />
<b>To be honest: </b>The first sentence is talking about a static use of the entire return object &mdash; a slice that happens to be the entire return object doesn't count. On the other hand, this is intended to allow parentheses and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code>s. <br />

<MarginText>10.b/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01", "AI05-0234-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>If the function is used as a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>, this bullet does not apply. Similarly, an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code> is not an initialization of an object, so this bullet does not apply. <br />

<MarginText>10.b.1/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0402-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We restrict the above rule to apply only if the function result is declared to be of a composite type. This makes sense since only results of a composite type (or of an anonymous access type, which are handled separately below) are potentially affected by the master of the function call. Note that a private type is considered composite, so this result assumes the worst for a function returning a private type. We could have made the rule more complex, depending on whether the result might be built in place, or might have an access discriminant, but we chose to keep the rule simpler. The wording says &ldquo;the result type at the point of function declaration is a composite type&rdquo;, to make it clear that this depends on the properties at the point of the declaration of the function, rather than properties that might be known at the point of call or inside the function body. <br />

<MarginText>10.3/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0234-1", "AI12-0278-1", "AI12-0390-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>If the result is of an anonymous access type and is converted to a (named or anonymous) access type, the master is determined following the rules given below for determining the master of an object created by an allocator (even if the access result is of an access-to-subprogram type);<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>10.b.2/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0278-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The conversion can be an explicit type conversion, or an implicit subtype conversion (these happen when anonymous access types are allowed to match named general access types, see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>). <br />

<MarginText>10.4/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0234-1", "AI12-0390-1"]} />
<ul>
<li><i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br /></li>
<MarginText>10.5/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0234-1", "AI12-0345-1", "AI12-0372-1"]} />
<li>If the call itself defines the result of a function <i>F</i>, or has an accessibility level that is tied to the result of such a function <i>F</i>, then the master of the call is that of the master of the call invoking <i>F</i>;<br /></li>
<MarginText>10.6/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0234-1"]} />
<li>In other cases, the master of the call is that of the innermost master that evaluates the function call.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>10.c/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00318-02", "AI95-00416-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The &ldquo;innermost master which evaluated the function call&rdquo; does not include the function call itself (which might be a master).<br />

<MarginText>10.d/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00318-02", "AI95-00416-01"]} />
We really mean the innermost master here, which could be a very short lifetime. Consider a function call used as a parameter of a procedure call. In this case the innermost master which evaluated the function call is the procedure call. <br />

<MarginText>10.d.1/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0234-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>These rules do not mention whether the result object is built-in-place (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.6">7.6</a>). In particular, in the case where building in place is optional, the choice whether or not to build-in-place has no effect on masters, lifetimes, or accessibility. <br />

<MarginText>10.d.2/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0234-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>There are several cases where the implementation may have to pass in the accessibility level of the result object on a call, to support later rules where the accessibility level comes from the master of the call:<br />

<MarginText>10.d.3/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>when the function result may have a part with access discriminants;<br /></li>
<MarginText>10.d.4/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>when the function result type is an anonymous access type;<br /></li>
<MarginText>10.d.5/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0345-1"]} />
<li>when the function result is built-in-place.<br /></li>
<MarginText>10.d.6/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0345-1"]} />
<li><i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>10.d.7/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
In particular, this implies passing a level parameter when the result type is class-wide, since descendants may add access discriminants. For most implementations this will mean that functions with controlling results will also need a level parameter. <br />

<MarginText>10.7/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0284-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>In the case of a call to a function whose result type is an anonymous access type, the accessibility level of the type of the result of the function call is also determined by the point of call as described above.<br /></li>
<MarginText>10.8/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01"]} />
<li>Within a return statement, the accessibility level of the return object is that of the execution of the return statement. If the return statement completes normally by returning from the function, then prior to leaving the function, the accessibility level of the return object changes to be a level determined by the point of call, as does the level of any coextensions (see below) of the return object.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>10.e/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We define the accessibility level of the return object during the return statement to be that of the return statement itself so that the object may be designated by objects local to the return statement, but not by objects outside the return statement. In addition, the intent is that the return object gets finalized if the return statement ends without actually returning (for example, due to propagating an exception, or a goto). For a normal return, of course, no finalization is done before returning. <br />

<MarginText>11_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>The accessibility level of a derived access type is the same as that of its ultimate ancestor.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.1/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00230-01"]} />
<li>The accessibility level of the anonymous access type defined by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0084">access_definition</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0239">object_renaming_declaration</a></code> is the same as that of the renamed view.<br /></li>
<MarginText>11.2/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0156-1"]} />
<li>The accessibility level of the anonymous access type defined by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0084">access_definition</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.5#S0184">loop_parameter_subtype_indication</a></code> is that of the loop parameter.<br /></li>
<MarginText>12/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00230-01", "AI95-00416-01"]} />
<li>The accessibility level of the anonymous access type of an access discriminant in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code>, or in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5#S0226">return{"_"}subtype{"_"}indication</a></code> of a return statement is determined as follows:<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>12.1/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>If the value of the access discriminant is determined by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0065">discriminant_association</a></code> in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code>, the accessibility level of the object or subprogram designated by the associated value (or library level if the value is null); <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>12.a/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>This deals with the following cases, when they occur in the context of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> or return statement: <br />

<MarginText>12.b/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>An <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0111">extension_aggregate</a></code> where the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0112">ancestor_part</a></code> is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code> denoting a constrained subtype;<br /></li>
<MarginText>12.c/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>An uninitialized <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> where the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> defines a constrained subtype;<br /></li>
<MarginText>12.d/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>A discriminant of an object with a constrained nominal subtype, including constrained components, the result of calling a function with a constrained result subtype, the dereference of an access-to-constrained subtype, etc. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>12.e/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0281-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> mentioned in this bullet is not necessarily the one given in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> or return statement that is determining the accessibility level; the constrained subtype might have been defined in an earlier declaration (as a named subtype).<br />

<MarginText>12.f/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1"]} />
If the value for this rule and the next one is derived from an Unchecked{"_"}Access attribute, the accessibility is library-level no matter what the accessibility level of the object is (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.10">13.10</a>). <br />

<MarginText>12.2/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0234-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>If the value of the access discriminant is determined by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0063">default_expression</a></code> in the declaration of the discriminant, the level of the object or subprogram designated by the associated value (or library level if null); <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>12.f.1/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>This covers the case of an unconstrained subcomponent of a limited type with defaulted access discriminants. <br />

<MarginText>12.3/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0004-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>If the value of the access discriminant is determined by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0109">record_component_association</a></code> in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code>, the accessibility level of the object or subprogram designated by the associated value (or library level if the value is null);<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>12.g/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>In this bullet, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> has to occur in the context of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> or return statement, while the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> of the previous bullet can occur anywhere (it doesn't have to be directly given in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> or return statement). <br />

<MarginText>12.4/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>In other cases, where the value of the access discriminant is determined by an object with an unconstrained nominal subtype, the accessibility level of the object.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>12.h/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>In other words, if you know the value of the discriminant for an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> or return statement from a discriminant constraint or an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> component association, then that determines the accessibility level; if you don't know it, then it is based on the object itself. <br />

<MarginText>12.5/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>The accessibility level of the anonymous access type of an access discriminant in any other context is that of the enclosing object.<br /></li>
<MarginText>13/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00162-01", "AI95-00254-01", "AI05-0270-1"]} />
<li>The accessibility level of the anonymous access type of an access parameter specifying an access-to-object type is the same as that of the view designated by the actual (or library-level if the actual is null). <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>13.a/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>If the value of the actual is derived from an Unchecked{"_"}Access attribute, the accessibility is always library-level (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.10">13.10</a>). <br />

<MarginText>13.1/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00254-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>The accessibility level of the anonymous access type of an access parameter specifying an access-to-subprogram type is deeper than that of any master; all such anonymous access types have this same level. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>13.b/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>These represent &ldquo;downward closures&rdquo; and thus require passing of static links or global display information (along with generic sharing information if the implementation does sharing) along with the address of the subprogram. We must prevent conversions of these to types with &ldquo;normal&rdquo; accessibility, as those typically don't include the extra information needed to make a call. <br />

<MarginText>13.2/4_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0070-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>The accessibility level of the anonymous access subtype defined by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5#S0226">return_subtype_indication</a></code> that is an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0084">access_definition</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5">6.5</a>) is that of the result subtype of the enclosing function.<br /></li>
<MarginText>13.3/4_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0148-1", "AI05-0240-1", "AI12-0070-1"]} />
<li>The accessibility level of the type of a stand-alone object of an anonymous access-to-object type is the same as the accessibility level of the type of the access value most recently assigned to the object[; accessibility checks ensure that this is never deeper than that of the declaration of the stand-alone object].<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>13.c/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>Conversions <i>into</i> the anonymous access type of a stand-alone object use a stricter (static) accessibility rule - see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6">4.6</a>; these checks are the ones referred to above. <br />

<MarginText>14/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01", "AI05-0051-1", "AI05-0253-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>The accessibility level of an object created by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> is the same as that of the access type, except for an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> of an anonymous access type (an <i>anonymous allocator</i>) in certain contexts, as follows: For an anonymous allocator that defines the result of a function with an access result, the accessibility level is determined as though the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> were in place of the call of the function; in the special case of a call that is the operand of a type conversion, the level is that of the target access type of the conversion. For an anonymous allocator defining the value of an access parameter, the accessibility level is that of the innermost master of the call. For an anonymous allocator whose type is that of a stand-alone object of an anonymous access-to-object type, the accessibility level is that of the declaration of the stand-alone object. For one defining an access discriminant, the accessibility level is determined as follows:<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>14.1/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01", "AI05-0024-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>for an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> used to define the discriminant of an object, the level of the object;<br /></li>
<MarginText>14.2/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01", "AI05-0024-1"]} />
<li>for an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> used to define the constraint in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> in any other context, the level of the master that elaborates the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code>.<br /></li>
<MarginText>14.3/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01", "AI05-0024-1"]} />
<li><i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>14.4/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01", "AI05-0024-1", "AI05-0066-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>In the first case, the allocated object is said to be a <i>coextension</i> of the object whose discriminant designates it, as well as of any object of which the discriminated object is itself a coextension or subcomponent. If the allocated object is a coextension of an anonymous object representing the result of an aggregate or function call that is used (in its entirety) to directly initialize a part of an object, after the result is assigned, the coextension becomes a coextension of the object being initialized and is no longer considered a coextension of the anonymous object. All coextensions of an object [(which have not thus been transfered by such an initialization)] are finalized when the object is finalized (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.6#Subclause_7.6.1">7.6.1</a>). <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>14.a.1/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The rules of access discriminants are such that when the space for an object with a coextension is reclaimed, the space for the coextensions can be reclaimed. Hence, there is implementation advice (see 13.11) that an object and its coextensions all be allocated from the same storage pool (or stack frame, in the case of a declared object). <br />

<MarginText>14.5/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0051-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>Within a return statement, the accessibility level of the anonymous access type of an access result is that of the master of the call.<br /></li>
<MarginText>15/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0014-1"]} />
<li>The accessibility level of a view of an object or subprogram designated by an access value is the same as that of the access type. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>15.a/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1", "AI05-0014-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>This rule applies even when no dereference exists, for example when an access value is passed as an access parameter. This rule ensures that implementations are not required to include dynamic accessibility values with all access values. <br />

<MarginText>16_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>The accessibility level of a component, protected subprogram, or entry of (a view of) a composite object is the same as that of (the view of) the composite object. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>16.1/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01", "AI05-0262-1", "AI12-0236-1", "AI12-0317-1"]} />
<p>In the above rules, the operative constituents of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4">4.4</a>) are considered to be used in a given context if the enclosing <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> is used in that context.<br /></p>

<MarginText>16.a/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>This means that constructs like parenthesized expressions, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code>s, and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#S0148">conditional_expression</a></code>s are ignored for the purposes of calculating accessibility levels, determining the master of a function call, and so on. <br />

<MarginText>17_3.10.2</MarginText>
<p>One accessibility level is defined to be <i>statically deeper</i> than another in the following cases: <br /></p>

<MarginText>18/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0406-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>For a master construct that is statically nested within another master construct, the accessibility level of the inner master construct is statically deeper than that of the outer master construct. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>18.a/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0406-1"]} />
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>18.b_3.10.2</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>If a given accessibility level is statically deeper than another, then each level defined to be the same as the given level is statically deeper than each level defined to be the same as the other level. <br />

<MarginText>18.1/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00254-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>The accessibility level of the anonymous access type of an access parameter specifying an access-to-subprogram type is statically deeper than that of any master; all such anonymous access types have this same level. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>18.c/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>This rule means that it is illegal to convert an access parameter specifying an access to subprogram to a named access to subprogram type, but it is allowed to pass such an access parameter to another access parameter (the implicit conversion's accessibility will succeed). <br />

<MarginText>19/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00254-01", "AI05-0082-1", "AI12-0406-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>The statically deeper relationship does not apply to the accessibility level of the following:<br /></li>
<MarginText>19.1/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0406-1"]} />
<li>the anonymous type of an access parameter specifying an access-to-object type;<br /></li>
<MarginText>19.2/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0406-1"]} />
<li>the type of a stand-alone object of an anonymous access-to-object type;<br /></li>
<MarginText>19.3/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0392-1", "AI12-0406-1"]} />
<li>a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.3#S0309">raise_expression</a></code>;<br /></li>
<MarginText>19.4/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0406-1"]} />
<li>a descendant of a generic formal type;<br /></li>
<MarginText>19.5/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0406-1"]} />
<li>a descendant of a type declared in a generic formal package. <br /></li>
<MarginText>19.6/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0148-1", "AI12-0406-1"]} />
<li>When the statically deeper relationship does not apply, the accessibility level is not considered to be statically deeper, nor statically shallower, than any other.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>19.a/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>In these cases, no static accessibility checks are made, and we use dynamic accessibility checks to prevent problems. <br />

<MarginText>19.7/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0142-4", "AI05-0235-1", "AI12-0089-1", "AI12-0157-1", "AI12-0277-1", "AI12-0324-1", "AI12-0345-1"]} />
<ul>
<li><i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br /></li>
<MarginText>19.8/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0051-1", "AI05-0234-1", "AI05-0235-1", "AI12-0089-1", "AI12-0157-1", "AI12-0372-1"]} />
<li>When within a function body or the return expression of an expression function, the accessibility level of the master representing an execution of the function is statically deeper than that of the master of the function call invoking that execution[, independent of how the master of the function call is determined (see above)].<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>19.b/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0235-1", "AI12-0345-1"]} />
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>19.c/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0005-1"]} />
<b>To be honest: </b>&ldquo;Function body&rdquo; includes bodies of generic functions. <br />

<MarginText>20/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0445-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>[For determining whether one level is statically deeper than another when within a generic package body, the generic package is presumed to be instantiated at the same level as where it was declared; runtime checks are required in the case of more deeply nested instantiations.] <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>20.a/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0082-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>A generic package does not introduce a new master, so it has the static level of its declaration; the rest follows from the other &ldquo;statically deeper&rdquo; rules. <br />

<MarginText>21_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>For determining whether one level is statically deeper than another when within the declarative region of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0023">type_declaration</a></code>, the current instance of the type is presumed to be an object created at a deeper level than that of the type. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>21.a_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>In other words, the rules are checked at compile time of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0023">type_declaration</a></code>, in an assume-the-worst manner. <br />

<MarginText>21.1/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0345-1"]} />
<p>Notwithstanding other rules given above, the accessibility level of an entity that is tied to that of an explicitly aliased formal parameter of an enclosing function is considered (both statically and dynamically) to be the same as that of an entity whose accessibility level is tied to that of the return object of that function.<br /></p>

<MarginText>21.b/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>This rule only applies when the level of an explicitly aliased parameter of a function is compared to that of the return object of the function. If a value designating the explicitly aliased parameter is created and stored in a stand-alone object or passed as a parameter, this special property is lost (even for the dynamic accessibility of anonymous access types in these contexts). <br />

<MarginText>21.c/5_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>When this rule applies, no dynamic accessibility check should be made, even when one would normally be part of the execution of the construct. All places where this rule applies are known at compile-time. <br />

<MarginText>22_3.10.2</MarginText>
<p>The accessibility level of all library units is called the <i>library level</i>; a library-level declaration or entity is one whose accessibility level is the library level. <br /></p>

<MarginText>22.a_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-10/AA-10.1#S0288">Library_unit_declaration</a></code>s are library level. Nested declarations are library level if they are nested only within packages (possibly more than one), and not within subprograms, tasks, etc. <br />

<MarginText>22.b/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>The definition of the accessibility level of the anonymous type of an access parameter specifying an access-to-object type cheats a bit, since it refers to the view designated by the actual, but access values designate objects, not views of objects. What we really mean is the view that &ldquo;would be&rdquo; denoted by an expression &ldquo;X.<b>all</b>&rdquo;, where X is the actual, even though such an expression is a figment of our imagination. The definition is intended to be equivalent to the following more verbose version: The accessibility level of the anonymous type of an access parameter is as follows: <br />

<MarginText>22.c_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>if the actual is an expression of a named access type &mdash; the accessibility level of that type;<br /></li>
<MarginText>22.d_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>if the actual is an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> &mdash; the accessibility level of the execution of the called subprogram;<br /></li>
<MarginText>22.e/1_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>if the actual is a reference to the Access attribute &mdash; the accessibility level of the view denoted by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>;<br /></li>
<MarginText>22.f_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>if the actual is a reference to the Unchecked{"_"}Access attribute &mdash; library accessibility level;<br /></li>
<MarginText>22.g_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>if the actual is an access parameter &mdash; the accessibility level of its type. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>22.h_3.10.2</MarginText>
Note that the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> case is explicitly mentioned in the RM95, because otherwise the definition would be circular: the level of the anonymous type is that of the view designated by the actual, which is that of the access type. <br />

<MarginText>22.i_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>A deeper accessibility level implies a shorter maximum lifetime. Hence, when a rule requires X to have a level that is &ldquo;not deeper than&rdquo; Y's level, this requires that X has a lifetime at least as long as Y. (We say &ldquo;maximum lifetime&rdquo; here, because the accessibility level really represents an upper bound on the lifetime; an object created by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> can have its lifetime prematurely ended by an instance of Unchecked{"_"}Deallocation.)<br />

<MarginText>22.j_3.10.2</MarginText>
Package elaborations are not masters, and are therefore invisible to the accessibility rules: an object declared immediately within a package has the same accessibility level as an object declared immediately within the declarative region containing the package. This is true even in the body of a package; it jibes with the fact that objects declared in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.2#S0231">package_body</a></code> live as long as objects declared outside the package, even though the body objects are not visible outside the package.<br />

<MarginText>22.k_3.10.2</MarginText>
Note that the level of the <i>view</i> denoted by X.<b>all</b> can be different from the level of the <i>object</i> denoted by X.<b>all</b>. The former is determined by the type of X; the latter is determined either by the type of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code>, or by the master in which the object was declared. The former is used in several Legality Rules and runtime checks; the latter is used to define when X.<b>all</b> gets finalized. The level of a view reflects what we can conservatively &ldquo;know&rdquo; about the object of that view; for example, due to <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6#S0162">type_conversion</a></code>s, an access value might designate an object that was allocated by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code> for a different access type.<br />

<MarginText>22.l_3.10.2</MarginText>
Similarly, the level of the view denoted by X.<b>all</b>.Comp can be different from the level of the object denoted by X.<b>all</b>.Comp.<br />

<MarginText>22.m_3.10.2</MarginText>
If Y is statically deeper than X, this implies that Y will be (dynamically) deeper than X in all possible executions.<br />

<MarginText>22.n_3.10.2</MarginText>
Most accessibility checking is done at compile time; the rules are stated in terms of &ldquo;statically deeper than&rdquo;. The exceptions are: <br />

<MarginText>22.o/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>Checks involving access parameters of an access-to-object type. The fact that &ldquo;statically deeper than&rdquo; is not defined for the anonymous access type of an access parameter implies that any rule saying &ldquo;shall not be statically deeper than&rdquo; does not apply to such a type, nor to anything defined to have &ldquo;the same&rdquo; level as such a type.<br /></li>
<MarginText>22.o.1/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0082-1"]} />
<li>Checks involving generic formal types and their descendants. This is because the actual type can be more or less deeply nested than the generic unit. Note that this only applies to the generic unit itself, and not to the instance. Any static checks needed in the instance will be performed. Any other checks (such as those in the generic body) will require a run-time check of some sort (although implementations that macro-expand generics can determine the result of the check when the generic is expanded).<br /></li>
<MarginText>22.p/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0082-1"]} />
<li>Checks involving other entities and views within generic packages. This is because an instantiation can be at a level that is more deeply nested than the generic package itself. In implementations that use a macro-expansion model of generics, these violations can be detected at macro-expansion time. For implementations that share generics, run-time code is needed to detect the error.<br /></li>
<MarginText>22.q/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00318-02", "AI95-00344-01", "AI95-00416-01"]} />
<li>Checks during function return and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code>s, for nested type extensions and access discriminants. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>22.r/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1"]} />
Note that runtime checks are not required for access discriminants (except during function returns and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code>s), because their accessibility is determined statically by the accessibility level of the enclosing object.<br />

<MarginText>22.s/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
The accessibility level of the result object of a function reflects the time when that object will be finalized; we don't allow pointers to the object to survive beyond that time.<br />

<MarginText>22.t_3.10.2</MarginText>
We sometimes use the terms &ldquo;accessible&rdquo; and &ldquo;inaccessible&rdquo; to mean that something has an accessibility level that is not deeper, or deeper, respectively, than something else. <br />

<MarginText>22.u/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00318-02", "AI95-00344-01", "AI95-00416-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>If an accessibility Legality Rule is satisfied, then the corresponding runtime check (if any) cannot fail (and a reasonable implementation will not generate any checking code) unless one of the cases requiring runtime checks mentioned previously is involved.<br />

<MarginText>22.v_3.10.2</MarginText>
Accessibility levels are defined in terms of the relations &ldquo;the same as&rdquo; and &ldquo;deeper than&rdquo;. To make the discussion more concrete, we can assign actual numbers to each level. Here, we assume that library-level accessibility is level 0, and each level defined as &ldquo;deeper than&rdquo; is one level deeper. Thus, a subprogram directly called from the environment task (such as the main subprogram) would be at level 1, and so on.<br />

<MarginText>22.w/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
Accessibility is not enforced at compile time for access parameters of an access-to-object type. The &ldquo;obvious&rdquo; implementation of the runtime checks would be inefficient, and would involve distributed overhead; therefore, an efficient method is given below. The &ldquo;obvious&rdquo; implementation would be to pass the level of the caller at each subprogram call, task creation, etc. This level would be incremented by 1 for each dynamically nested master. An Accessibility{"_"}Check would be implemented as a simple comparison &mdash; checking that X is not deeper than Y would involve checking that X {"<"}= Y.<br />

<MarginText>22.x_3.10.2</MarginText>
A more efficient method is based on passing <i>static</i> nesting levels (within constructs that correspond at run time to masters &mdash; packages don't count). Whenever an access parameter is passed, an implicit extra parameter is passed with it. The extra parameter represents (in an indirect way) the accessibility level of the anonymous access type, and, therefore, the level of the view denoted by a dereference of the access parameter. This is analogous to the implicit &ldquo;Constrained&rdquo; bit associated with certain formal parameters of an unconstrained but definite composite subtype. In this method, we avoid distributed overhead: it is not necessary to pass any extra information to subprograms that have no access parameters. For anything other than an access parameter and its anonymous type, the static nesting level is known at compile time, and is defined analogously to the RM95 definition of accessibility level (e.g. derived access types get their nesting level from their parent). Checking &ldquo;not deeper than&rdquo; is a "{"<"}=" test on the levels.<br />

<MarginText>22.y/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
For each access parameter of an access-to-object type, the static depth passed depends on the actual, as follows: <br />

<MarginText>22.z_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>If the actual is an expression of a named access type, pass the static nesting level of that type.<br /></li>
<MarginText>22.aa_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>If the actual is an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code>, pass the static nesting level of the caller, plus one.<br /></li>
<MarginText>22.bb/1_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>If the actual is a reference to the Access attribute, pass the level of the view denoted by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>.<br /></li>
<MarginText>22.cc_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>If the actual is a reference to the Unchecked{"_"}Access attribute, pass 0 (the library accessibility level).<br /></li>
<MarginText>22.dd/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>If the actual is an access parameter of an access-to-object type, usually just pass along the level passed in. However, if the static nesting level of the formal (access) parameter is greater than the static nesting level of the actual (access) parameter, the level to be passed is the minimum of the static nesting level of the access parameter and the actual level passed in. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>22.ee/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
For the Accessibility{"_"}Check associated with a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6#S0162">type_conversion</a></code> of an access parameter of an access-to-object type of a given subprogram to a named access type, if the target type is statically nested within the subprogram, do nothing; the check can't fail in this case. Otherwise, check that the value passed in is {"<"}= the static nesting depth of the target type. The other Accessibility{"_"}Checks are handled in a similar manner.<br />

<MarginText>22.ff_3.10.2</MarginText>
This method, using statically known values most of the time, is efficient, and, more importantly, avoids distributed overhead.<br />

<MarginText>22.ff.1/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0148-1"]} />
The implementation of accessibility checks for stand-alone objects of anonymous access-to-object types can be similar to that for anonymous access-to-object parameters. A static level suffices; it can be calculated using rules similar to those previously described for access parameters.<br />

<MarginText>22.ff.2/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0148-1"]} />
One important difference between the stand-alone access variables and access parameters is that one can assign a local access parameter to a more global stand-alone access variable. Similarly, one can assign a more global access parameter to a more local stand-alone access variable.<br />

<MarginText>22.ff.3/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0148-1"]} />
For these cases, it is important to note that the &ldquo;correct&rdquo; static accessibility level for an access parameter assigned to a stand-alone access object is the minimum of the passed in level and the static accessibility level of the stand-alone object itself. This is true since the static accessibility level passed in might be deeper than that of the stand-alone object, but the dynamic accessibility of the passed in object clearly must be shallower than the stand-alone object (whatever is passed in must live at least as long as the subprogram call). We do not need to keep a more local static level as accesses to objects statically deeper than the stand-alone object cannot be stored into the stand-alone object. <br />

<MarginText>22.gg_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Examples of accessibility: <br />

<MarginText>22.hh/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package body Lib{"_"}Unit is{"\n"}    type T is tagged ...;{"\n"}    type A0 is access all T;{"\n"}    Global: A0 := ...;{"\n"}    procedure P(X: in out T) is{"\n"}        Y: aliased T;{"\n"}        type A1 is access all T;{"\n"}        Ptr0: A0 := Global; -- OK.{"\n"}        Ptr1: A1 := X'Access; -- OK.{"\n"}    begin{"\n"}        Ptr1 := Y'Access; -- OK;{"\n"}        Ptr0 := A0(Ptr1); -- Illegal type conversion!{"\n"}        Ptr0 := X'Access; -- Illegal reference to Access attribute!{"\n"}        Ptr0 := Y'Access; -- Illegal reference to Access attribute!{"\n"}        Global := Ptr0; -- OK.{"\n"}    end P;{"\n"}end Lib{"_"}Unit;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>22.ii/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1"]} />
The above illegal statements are illegal because the accessibility levels of X and Y are statically deeper than the accessibility level of A0. In every possible execution of any program including this library unit, if P is called, the accessibility level of X will be (dynamically) deeper than that of A0. Note that the accessibility levels of X and Y are the same.<br />

<MarginText>22.jj/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
Here's an example involving access parameters of an access-to-object type: <br />

<MarginText>22.kk_3.10.2</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
procedure Main is{"\n"}    type Level{"_"}1{"_"}Type is access all Integer;{"\n"}
<MarginText>22.ll_3.10.2</MarginText>
    procedure P(X: access Integer) is{"\n"}        type Nested{"_"}Type is access all Integer;{"\n"}    begin{"\n"}        ... Nested{"_"}Type(X) ... -- (1){"\n"}        ... Level{"_"}1{"_"}Type(X) ... -- (2){"\n"}    end P;{"\n"}
<MarginText>22.mm_3.10.2</MarginText>
    procedure Q(X: access Integer) is{"\n"}        procedure Nested(X: access Integer) is{"\n"}        begin{"\n"}            P(X);{"\n"}        end Nested;{"\n"}    begin{"\n"}        Nested(X);{"\n"}    end Q;{"\n"}
<MarginText>22.nn_3.10.2</MarginText>
    procedure R is{"\n"}        Level{"_"}2: aliased Integer;{"\n"}    begin{"\n"}        Q(Level{"_"}2'Access); -- (3){"\n"}    end R;{"\n"}
<MarginText>22.oo_3.10.2</MarginText>
    Level{"_"}1: aliased Integer;{"\n"}begin{"\n"}    Q(Level{"_"}1'Access); -- (4){"\n"}    R;{"\n"}end Main;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>22.pp_3.10.2</MarginText>
The run-time Accessibility{"_"}Check at (1) can never fail, and no code should be generated to check it. The check at (2) will fail when called from (3), but not when called from (4).<br />

<MarginText>22.qq_3.10.2</MarginText>
Within a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0023">type_declaration</a></code>, the rules are checked in an assume-the-worst manner. For example: <br />

<MarginText>22.rr/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0298-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package P is{"\n"}    type Int{"_"}Ptr is access all Integer;{"\n"}    type Rec(D: access Integer) is limited private;{"\n"}private{"\n"}    type Rec{"_"}Ptr is access all Rec;{"\n"}    function F(X: Rec{"_"}Ptr) return Boolean;{"\n"}    function G(X: access Rec) return Boolean;{"\n"}    type Rec(D: access Integer) is{"\n"}        limited record{"\n"}            C1: Int{"_"}Ptr := Int{"_"}Ptr(D); -- Illegal!{"\n"}            C2: Rec{"_"}Ptr := Rec'Access; -- Illegal!{"\n"}            C3: Boolean := F(Rec'Access); -- Illegal!{"\n"}            C4: Boolean := G(Rec'Access);{"\n"}        end record;{"\n"}end P;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>22.ss_3.10.2</MarginText>
C1, C2, and C3 are all illegal, because one might declare an object of type Rec at a more deeply nested place than the declaration of the type. C4 is legal, but the accessibility level of the object will be passed to function G, and constraint checks within G will prevent it from doing any evil deeds.<br />

<MarginText>22.tt_3.10.2</MarginText>
Note that we cannot defer the checks on C1, C2, and C3 until compile-time of the object creation, because that would cause violation of the privacy of private parts. Furthermore, the problems might occur within a task or protected body, which the compiler can't see while compiling an object creation. <br />

<MarginText>23_3.10.2</MarginText>
<p>The following attribute is defined for a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> X that denotes an aliased view of an object: <br /></p>

<MarginText>24/1_3.10.2</MarginText>
<dt><br/>X'Access</dt>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00127-01"]} />
<dl>
<dd>{"{"}<i>8652/0010</i>{"}"} X'Access yields an access value that designates the object denoted by X. The type of X'Access is an access-to-object type, as determined by the expected type. The expected type shall be a general access type. X shall denote an aliased view of an object[, including possibly the current instance (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>) of a limited type within its definition, or a formal parameter or generic formal object of a tagged type]. The view denoted by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> X shall satisfy the following additional requirements, presuming the expected type for X'Access is the general access type <i>A</i> with designated type <i>D</i>: <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>25_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>If <i>A</i> is an access-to-variable type, then the view shall be a variable; [on the other hand, if <i>A</i> is an access-to-constant type, the view may be either a constant or a variable.] <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>25.a_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The current instance of a limited type is considered a variable. <br />

<MarginText>26/3_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00363-01", "AI05-0008-1", "AI05-0041-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>The view shall not be a subcomponent that depends on discriminants of an object unless the object is known to be constrained.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>26.a_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>This restriction is intended to be similar to the restriction on renaming discriminant-dependent subcomponents. <br />

<MarginText>26.b_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This prevents references to subcomponents that might disappear or move or change constraints after creating the reference. <br />

<MarginText>26.c_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>There was some thought to making this restriction more stringent, roughly: "X shall not denote a subcomponent of a variable with discriminant-dependent subcomponents, if the nominal subtype of the variable is an unconstrained definite subtype." This was because in some implementations, it is not just the discriminant-dependent subcomponents that might move as the result of an assignment that changed the discriminants of the enclosing object. However, it was decided not to make this change because a reasonable implementation strategy was identified to avoid such problems, as follows: <br />

<MarginText>26.d_3.10.2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>Place nondiscriminant-dependent components with any aliased parts at offsets preceding any discriminant-dependent components in a discriminated record type with defaulted discriminants.<br /></li>
<MarginText>26.e_3.10.2</MarginText>
<li>Preallocate the maximum space for unconstrained discriminated variables with aliased subcomponents, rather than allocating the initial size and moving them to a larger (heap-resident) place if they grow as the result of an assignment. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>26.f_3.10.2</MarginText>
Note that for objects of a by-reference type, it is not an error for a programmer to take advantage of the fact that such objects are passed by reference. Therefore, the above approach is also necessary for discriminated record types with components of a by-reference type.<br />

<MarginText>26.g_3.10.2</MarginText>
To make the above strategy work, it is important that a component of a derived type is defined to be discriminant-dependent if it is inherited and the parent subtype constraint is defined in terms of a discriminant of the derived type (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7">3.7</a>). <br />

<MarginText>27/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00127-01", "AI95-00363-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>{"{"}<i>8652/0010</i>{"}"} If <i>A</i> is a named access type and <i>D</i> is a tagged type, then the type of the view shall be covered by <i>D</i>; if <i>A</i> is anonymous and <i>D</i> is tagged, then the type of the view shall be either <i>D</i>'Class or a type covered by <i>D</i>; if <i>D</i> is untagged, then the type of the view shall be <i>D</i>, and either: <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>27.1/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00363-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>the designated subtype of <i>A</i> shall statically match the nominal subtype of the view; or<br /></li>
<MarginText>27.2/4_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00363-01", "AI05-0041-1", "AI12-0095-1"]} />
<li><i>D</i> shall be discriminated in its full view and unconstrained in any partial view, and the designated subtype of <i>A</i> shall be unconstrained. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>27.a_3.10.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>This ensures that the dope for an aliased array object can always be stored contiguous with it, but need not be if its nominal subtype is constrained. <br />

<MarginText>27.a.1/1_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00127-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>{"{"}<i>8652/0010</i>{"}"} An access attribute can be used as the controlling operand in a dispatching call; see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.2">3.9.2</a>.<br />

<MarginText>27.a.2/2_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00363-01"]} />
This does not require that types have a partial view in order to allow an access attribute of an unconstrained discriminated object, only that any partial view that does exist is unconstrained. <br />

<MarginText>27.a.3/4_3.10.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0095-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
