<li>For each user-defined primitive subprogram (other than a user-defined equality operator &mdash; see below) of the parent type or of a progenitor type that already exists at the place of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#S0035">derived_type_definition</a></code>, there exists a corresponding <i>inherited</i> primitive subprogram of the derived type with the same defining name. Primitive user-defined equality operators of the parent type and any progenitor types are also inherited by the derived type, except when the derived type is a nonlimited record extension, and the inherited operator would have a profile that is type conformant with the profile of the corresponding predefined equality operator; in this case, the user-defined equality operator is not inherited, but is rather incorporated into the implementation of the predefined equality operator of the record extension (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#Subclause_4.5.2">4.5.2</a>). <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>17.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>We say &ldquo;...already exists...&rdquo; rather than &ldquo;is visible&rdquo; or &ldquo;has been declared&rdquo; because there are certain operations that are declared later, but still exist at the place of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#S0035">derived_type_definition</a></code>, and there are operations that are never declared, but still exist. These cases are explained in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3#Subclause_7.3.1">7.3.1</a>.<br />

<MarginText>17.b</MarginText>
Note that nonprivate extensions can appear only after the last primitive subprogram of the parent &mdash; the freezing rules ensure this. <br />

<MarginText>17.c</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>A special case is made for the equality operators on nonlimited record extensions because their predefined equality operators are already defined in terms of the primitive equality operator of their parent type (and of the tagged components of the extension part). Inheriting the parent's equality operator as is would be undesirable, because it would ignore any components of the extension part. On the other hand, if the parent type is limited, then any user-defined equality operator is inherited as is, since there is no predefined equality operator to take its place. <br />

<MarginText>17.d/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Because user-defined equality operators are not inherited by nonlimited record extensions, the formal parameter names of = and /= revert to Left and Right, even if different formal parameter names were used in the user-defined equality operators of the parent type. <br />

<MarginText>17.e/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00401-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>This rule only describes what operations are inherited; the rules that describe what happens when there are conflicting inherited subprograms are found in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.3">8.3</a>. <br />

<MarginText>18/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00401-01", "AI05-0164-1", "AI05-0240-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>The profile of an inherited subprogram (including an inherited enumeration literal) is obtained from the profile of the corresponding (user-defined) primitive subprogram of the parent or progenitor type, after systematic replacement of each subtype of its profile (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1">6.1</a>) that is of the parent or progenitor type, other than those subtypes found in the designated profile of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0084">access_definition</a></code>, with a <i>corresponding subtype</i> of the derived type. For a given subtype of the parent or progenitor type, the corresponding subtype of the derived type is defined as follows: <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>19</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>If the declaration of the derived type has neither a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0061">known_discriminant_part</a></code> nor a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0075">record_extension_part</a></code>, then the corresponding subtype has a constraint that corresponds (as defined above for the first subtype of the derived type) to that of the given subtype.<br /></li>
<MarginText>20</MarginText>
<li>If the derived type is a record extension, then the corresponding subtype is the first subtype of the derived type.<br /></li>
<MarginText>21</MarginText>
<li>If the derived type has a new <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0061">known_discriminant_part</a></code> but is not a record extension, then the corresponding subtype is constrained to those values that when converted to the parent type belong to the given subtype (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6">4.6</a>). <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>21.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>An inherited subprogram of an untagged type has an Intrinsic calling convention, which precludes the use of the Access attribute. We preclude 'Access because correctly performing all required constraint checks on an indirect call to such an inherited subprogram was felt to impose an undesirable implementation burden.<br />

<MarginText>21.b/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0164-1"]} />
Note that the exception to substitution of the parent or progenitor type applies only in the profiles of anonymous access-to-subprogram types. The exception is necessary to avoid calling an access-to-subprogram with types and/or constraints different than expected by the actual routine. <br />

<MarginText>22/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00401-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>The same formal parameters have <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0063">default_expression</a></code>s in the profile of the inherited subprogram. [Any type mismatch due to the systematic replacement of the parent or progenitor type by the derived type is handled as part of the normal type conversion associated with parameter passing &mdash; see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#Subclause_6.4.1">6.4.1</a>.] <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>22.a/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00401-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We don't introduce the type conversion explicitly here since conversions to record extensions or on access parameters are not generally legal. Furthermore, any type conversion would just be "undone" since the subprogram of the parent or progenitor is ultimately being called anyway. (Null procedures can be inherited from a progenitor without being overridden, so it is possible to call subprograms of an interface.) <br />

<MarginText>23/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00401-01"]} />
<p>If a primitive subprogram of the parent or progenitor type is visible at the place of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#S0035">derived_type_definition</a></code>, then the corresponding inherited subprogram is implicitly declared immediately after the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#S0035">derived_type_definition</a></code>. Otherwise, the inherited subprogram is implicitly declared later or not at all, as explained in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3#Subclause_7.3.1">7.3.1</a>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>24</MarginText>
<p>A derived type can also be defined by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3#S0233">private{"_"}extension{"_"}declaration</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3">7.3</a>) or a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.5#S0325">formal{"_"}derived{"_"}type{"_"}definition</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.5#Subclause_12.5.1">12.5.1</a>). Such a derived type is a partial view of the corresponding full or actual type.<br /></p>

<MarginText>25</MarginText>
<p>All numeric types are derived types, in that they are implicitly derived from a corresponding root numeric type (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#Subclause_3.5.4">3.5.4</a> and <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#Subclause_3.5.6">3.5.6</a>).<br /></p>

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>26</MarginText>
<p>The elaboration of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#S0035">derived_type_definition</a></code> creates the derived type and its first subtype, and consists of the elaboration of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype{"_"}indication</a></code> and the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0075">record{"_"}extension{"_"}part</a></code>, if any. If the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype{"_"}indication</a></code> depends on a discriminant, then only those expressions that do not depend on a discriminant are evaluated. <br /></p>

<MarginText>26.a/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>We don't mention the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0078">interface_list</a></code>, because it does not need elaboration (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.4">3.9.4</a>). This is consistent with the handling of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0059">discriminant_part</a></code>s, which aren't elaborated either. <br />

<MarginText>27/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00391-01", "AI95-00401-01"]} />
<p>For the execution of a call on an inherited subprogram, a call on the corresponding primitive subprogram of the parent or progenitor type is performed; the normal conversion of each actual parameter to the subtype of the corresponding formal parameter (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#Subclause_6.4.1">6.4.1</a>) performs any necessary type conversion as well. If the result type of the inherited subprogram is the derived type, the result of calling the subprogram of the parent or progenitor is converted to the derived type, or in the case of a null extension, extended to the derived type using the equivalent of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0111">extension_aggregate</a></code> with the original result as the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0112">ancestor_part</a></code> and <b>null record</b> as the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0108">record_component_association_list</a></code>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>27.a/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00391-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>If an inherited function returns the derived type, and the type is a nonnull record extension, then the inherited function shall be overridden, unless the type is abstract (in which case the function is abstract, and (unless overridden) cannot be called except via a dispatching call). See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.3">3.9.3</a>. <br />

<MarginText>28</MarginText>
NOTE 1   Classes are closed under derivation &mdash; any class that contains a type also contains its derivatives. Operations available for a given class of types are available for the derived types in that class.<br />

<MarginText>29</MarginText>
NOTE 2   Evaluating an inherited enumeration literal is equivalent to evaluating the corresponding enumeration literal of the parent type, and then converting the result to the derived type. This follows from their equivalence to parameterless functions. <br />

<MarginText>30</MarginText>
NOTE 3   A generic subprogram is not a subprogram, and hence cannot be a primitive subprogram and cannot be inherited by a derived type. On the other hand, an instance of a generic subprogram can be a primitive subprogram, and hence can be inherited.<br />

<MarginText>31</MarginText>
NOTE 4   If the parent type is an access type, then the parent and the derived type share the same storage pool; there is a <b>null</b> access value for the derived type and it is the implicit initial value for the type. See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10">3.10</a>.<br />

<MarginText>32</MarginText>
NOTE 5   If the parent type is a boolean type, the predefined relational operators of the derived type deliver a result of the predefined type Boolean (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#Subclause_4.5.2">4.5.2</a>). If the parent type is an integer type, the right operand of the predefined exponentiation operator is of the predefined type Integer (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#Subclause_4.5.6">4.5.6</a>).<br />

<MarginText>33</MarginText>
NOTE 6   Any discriminants of the parent type are either all inherited, or completely replaced with a new set of discriminants.<br />

<MarginText>34/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0442-1"]} />
NOTE 7   For an inherited subprogram, the subtype of a formal parameter of the derived type can be such that it has no value in common with the first subtype of the derived type. <br />

<MarginText>34.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>This happens when the parent subtype is constrained to a range that does not overlap with the range of a subtype of the parent type that appears in the profile of some primitive subprogram of the parent type. For example: <br />

<MarginText>34.b</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type T1 is range 1..100;{"\n"}subtype S1 is T1 range 1..10;{"\n"}procedure P(X : in S1);  -- P is a primitive subprogram{"\n"}type T2 is new T1 range 11..20;{"\n"}-- implicitly declared:{"\n"}-- procedure P(X : in T2'Base range 1..10);{"\n"}--      X cannot be in T2'First .. T2'Last{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>35</MarginText>
NOTE 8   If the reserved word <b>abstract</b> is given in the declaration of a type, the type is abstract (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.3">3.9.3</a>).<br />

<MarginText>35.1/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00401-01"]} />
NOTE 9   An interface type that has a progenitor type &ldquo;is derived from&rdquo; that type. A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#S0035">derived_type_definition</a></code>, however, never defines an interface type.<br />

<MarginText>35.2/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01"]} />
NOTE 10   It is illegal for the parent type of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#S0035">derived_type_definition</a></code> to be a synchronized tagged type. <br />

<MarginText>35.a/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.1">3.9.1</a> prohibits record extensions whose parent type is a synchronized tagged type, and this subclause requires tagged types to have a record extension. Thus there are no legal derivations. Note that a synchronized interface can be used as a progenitor in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0077">interface_type_definition</a></code> as well as in task and protected types, but we do not allow concrete extensions of any synchronized tagged type. <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>36</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of derived type declarations:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>37</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type Local{"_"}Coordinate is new Coordinate;  -- two different types{"\n"}type Midweek is new Day range Tue .. Thu; -- see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#Subclause_3.5.1">3.5.1</a>{"\n"}type Counter is new Positive;             -- same range as Positive {"\n"}
<MarginText>38</MarginText>
type Special{"_"}Key is new Key{"_"}Manager.Key;  -- see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3#Subclause_7.3.1">7.3.1</a>{"\n"}  -- the inherited subprograms have the following specifications:{"\n"}  --         procedure Get{"_"}Key(K : out Special{"_"}Key);{"\n"}  --         function "{"<"}"(X,Y : Special{"_"}Key) return Boolean;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

#### Inconsistencies With Ada 83

<MarginText>38.a</MarginText>
When deriving from a (nonprivate, nonderived) type in the same visible part in which it is defined, if a predefined operator had been overridden prior to the derivation, the derived type will inherit the user-defined operator rather than the predefined operator. The work-around (if the new behavior is not the desired behavior) is to move the definition of the derived type prior to the overriding of any predefined operators.<br />

#### Incompatibilities With Ada 83

<MarginText>38.b</MarginText>
When deriving from a (nonprivate, nonderived) type in the same visible part in which it is defined, a primitive subprogram of the parent type declared before the derived type will be inherited by the derived type. This can cause upward incompatibilities in cases like this: <br />

<MarginText>38.c</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
   package P is{"\n"}      type T is (A, B, C, D);{"\n"}      function F( X : T := A ) return Integer;{"\n"}      type NT is new T;{"\n"}      -- inherits F as{"\n"}      -- function F( X : NT := A ) return Integer;{"\n"}      -- in Ada 95 only{"\n"}      ...{"\n"}   end P;{"\n"}   ...{"\n"}   use P;  -- Only one declaration of F from P is use-visible in{"\n"}           -- Ada 83;  two declarations of F are use-visible in{"\n"}           -- Ada 95.{"\n"}begin{"\n"}   ...{"\n"}   if F {">"} 1 then ... -- legal in Ada 83, ambiguous in Ada 95{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>38.d</MarginText>
The syntax for a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#S0035">derived_type_definition</a></code> is amended to include an optional <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0075">record_extension_part</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.1">3.9.1</a>).<br />

<MarginText>38.e</MarginText>
A derived type may override the discriminants of the parent by giving a new <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0059">discriminant_part</a></code>.<br />

<MarginText>38.f</MarginText>
The parent type in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#S0035">derived_type_definition</a></code> may be a derived type defined in the same visible part.<br />

<MarginText>38.g</MarginText>
When deriving from a type in the same visible part in which it is defined, the primitive subprograms declared prior to the derivation are inherited as primitive subprograms of the derived type. See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#Subclause_3.2.3">3.2.3</a>. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>38.h</MarginText>
We now talk about the classes to which a type belongs, rather than a single class.<br />

#### Extensions to Ada 95

<MarginText>38.i/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00401-01", "AI05-0190-1"]} />
A derived type may inherit from multiple (interface) progenitors, as well as the parent type &mdash; see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.4">3.9.4</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.4">Interface Types</a>&rdquo;.<br />

<MarginText>38.j/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01"]} />
A derived type may specify that it is a limited type. This is required for interface ancestors (from which limitedness is not inherited), but it is generally useful as documentation of limitedness. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>38.k/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00391-01"]} />
Defined the result of functions for null extensions (which we no longer require to be overridden - see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.3">3.9.3</a>).<br />

<MarginText>38.l/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00442-01"]} />
Defined the term &ldquo;category of types&rdquo; and used it in wording elsewhere; also specified the language-defined categories that form classes of types (this was never normatively specified in Ada 95). <br />

#### Incompatibilities With Ada 2005

<MarginText>38.m/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0096-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Added a (re)check that limited type extensions never are derived from nonlimited types in generic private parts. This is disallowed as it would make it possible to pass a limited object to a nonlimited class-wide type, which could then be copied. This is only possible using Ada 2005 syntax, so examples in existing programs should be rare. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>38.n/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0110-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Added wording to clarify that the characteristics of derived types are formally defined here. (This is the only place in the Reference Manual that actually spells out what sorts of things are actually characteristics, which is rather important.)<br />

<MarginText>38.o/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0164-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Added wording to ensure that anonymous access-to-subprogram types don't get modified on derivation. <br />

<a id="Subclause_3.4.1"></a>

## 3.4.1  Derivation Classes

<MarginText>1_3.4.1</MarginText>
<p>In addition to the various language-defined classes of types, types can be grouped into <i>derivation classes</i>. <br /></p>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>2/2_3.4.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00401-01"]} />
<p>A derived type is <i>derived from</i> its parent type <i>directly</i>; it is derived <i>indirectly</i> from any type from which its parent type is derived. A derived type, interface type, type extension, task type, protected type, or formal derived type is also derived from every ancestor of each of its progenitor types, if any. The derivation class of types for a type <i>T</i> (also called the class <i>rooted</i> at <i>T</i>) is the set consisting of <i>T</i> (the <i>root type</i> of the class) and all types derived from <i>T</i> (directly or indirectly) plus any associated universal or class-wide types (defined below). <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.a_3.4.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Note that the definition of &ldquo;derived from&rdquo; is a recursive definition. We don't define a root type for all interesting language-defined classes, though presumably we could. <br />

<MarginText>2.b_3.4.1</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>By the class-wide type &ldquo;associated&rdquo; with a type <i>T</i>, we mean the type <i>T</i>'Class. Similarly, the universal type associated with <i>root{"_"}integer</i>, <i>root{"_"}real</i>, and <i>root{"_"}fixed</i> are <i>universal{"_"}integer</i>, <i>universal{"_"}real</i>, and <i>universal{"_"}fixed</i>, respectively. <br />

<MarginText>3/5_3.4.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00230-01", "AI12-0437-1"]} />
<p>Every type is one of a <i>specific</i> type, a <i>class-wide</i> type, or a <i>universal</i> type. A specific type is one defined by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0023">type_declaration</a></code>, a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.5#S0320">formal_type_declaration</a></code>, or a full type definition embedded in another construct. Class-wide and universal types are implicitly defined, to act as representatives for an entire class of types, as follows: <br /></p>

<MarginText>3.a_3.4.1</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>The root types <i>root{"_"}integer</i>, <i>root{"_"}real</i>, and <i>root{"_"}fixed</i> are also specific types. They are declared in the specification of package Standard. <br />

<MarginText>4_3.4.1</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Class-wide types </dt>
<dl>
<dd>Class-wide types are defined for [(and belong to)] each derivation class rooted at a tagged type (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9">3.9</a>). Given a subtype S of a tagged type <i>T</i>, S'Class is the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code> for a corresponding subtype of the tagged class-wide type <i>T</i>'Class. Such types are called &ldquo;class-wide&rdquo; because when a formal parameter is defined to be of a class-wide type <i>T</i>'Class, an actual parameter of any type in the derivation class rooted at <i>T</i> is acceptable (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>).<br /></dd>
<MarginText>5_3.4.1</MarginText>
<dd>The set of values for a class-wide type <i>T</i>'Class is the discriminated union of the set of values of each specific type in the derivation class rooted at <i>T</i> (the tag acts as the implicit discriminant &mdash; see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9">3.9</a>). Class-wide types have no primitive subprograms of their own. However, as explained in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.2">3.9.2</a>, operands of a class-wide type <i>T</i>'Class can be used as part of a dispatching call on a primitive subprogram of the type <i>T</i>. The only components [(including discriminants)] of <i>T</i>'Class that are visible are those of <i>T</i>. If S is a first subtype, then S'Class is a first subtype. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>5.a_3.4.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We want S'Class to be a first subtype when S is, so that an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute{"_"}definition{"_"}clause</a></code> like &ldquo;<b>for</b> S'Class'Output <b>use</b> ...;&rdquo; will be legal. <br />

<MarginText>6/5_3.4.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00230-01", "AI12-0445-1"]} />
<dt><br/>Universal types </dt>
<dl>
<dd>Universal types are defined for [(and belong to)] the integer, real, fixed point, and access classes, and are referred to in this document as respectively, <i>universal{"_"}integer</i>, <i>universal{"_"}real</i>, <i>universal{"_"}fixed</i>, and <i>universal{"_"}access</i>. These are analogous to class-wide types for these language-defined elementary classes. As with class-wide types, if a formal parameter is of a universal type, then an actual parameter of any type in the corresponding class is acceptable. In addition, a value of a universal type (including an integer or real <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.4#S0006">numeric_literal</a></code>, or the literal <b>null</b>) is &ldquo;universal&rdquo; in that it is acceptable where some particular type in the class is expected (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>).<br /></dd>
<MarginText>7_3.4.1</MarginText>
<dd>The set of values of a universal type is the undiscriminated union of the set of values possible for any definable type in the associated class. Like class-wide types, universal types have no primitive subprograms of their own. However, their &ldquo;universality&rdquo; allows them to be used as operands with the primitive subprograms of any type in the corresponding class. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>7.a_3.4.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>A class-wide type is only class-wide in one direction, from specific to class-wide, whereas a universal type is class-wide (universal) in both directions, from specific to universal and back.<br />

<MarginText>7.b/2_3.4.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00230-01"]} />
We considered defining class-wide or perhaps universal types for all derivation classes, not just tagged classes and these four elementary classes. However, this was felt to overly weaken the strong-typing model in some situations. Tagged types preserve strong type distinctions thanks to the run-time tag. Class-wide or universal types for untagged types would weaken the compile-time type distinctions without providing a compensating run-time-checkable distinction.<br />

<MarginText>7.c_3.4.1</MarginText>
We considered defining standard names for the universal numeric types so they could be used in formal parameter specifications. However, this was felt to impose an undue implementation burden for some implementations. <br />

<MarginText>7.d_3.4.1</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>Formally, the set of values of a universal type is actually a <i>copy</i> of the undiscriminated union of the values of the types in its class. This is because we want each value to have exactly one type, with explicit or implicit conversion needed to go between types. An alternative, consistent model would be to associate a class, rather than a particular type, with a value, even though any given expression would have a particular type. In that case, implicit type conversions would not generally need to change the value, although an associated subtype conversion might need to. <br />

<MarginText>8_3.4.1</MarginText>
<p>The integer and real numeric classes each have a specific root type in addition to their universal type, named respectively <i>root{"_"}integer</i> and <i>root{"_"}real</i>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>9/5_3.4.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0325-1"]} />
<p>A class-wide or universal type is said to <i>cover</i> all of the types in its class. In addition, <i>universal{"_"}integer</i> covers a type that has a specified Integer{"_"}Literal aspect, while <i>universal{"_"}real</i> covers a type that has a specified Real{"_"}Literal aspect (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.2#Subclause_4.2.1">4.2.1</a>). A specific type covers only itself.<br /></p>

<MarginText>10/2_3.4.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00230-01", "AI95-00251-01"]} />
<p>A specific type <i>T2</i> is defined to be a <i>descendant</i> of a type <i>T1</i> if <i>T2</i> is the same as <i>T1</i>, or if <i>T2</i> is derived (directly or indirectly) from <i>T1</i>. A class-wide type <i>T2</i>'Class is defined to be a descendant of type <i>T1</i> if <i>T2</i> is a descendant of <i>T1</i>. Similarly, the numeric universal types are defined to be descendants of the root types of their classes. If a type <i>T2</i> is a descendant of a type <i>T1</i>, then <i>T1</i> is called an <i>ancestor</i> of <i>T2</i>. An <i>ultimate ancestor</i> of a type is an ancestor of that type that is not itself a descendant of any other type. Every untagged type has a unique ultimate ancestor. <br /></p>

<MarginText>10.a_3.4.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>A specific type is a descendant of itself. Class-wide types are considered descendants of the corresponding specific type, and do not have any descendants of their own.<br />

<MarginText>10.b_3.4.1</MarginText>
A specific type is an ancestor of itself. The root of a derivation class is an ancestor of all types in the class, including any class-wide types in the class. <br />

<MarginText>10.c_3.4.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The terms root, parent, ancestor, and ultimate ancestor are all related. For example: <br />

<MarginText>10.d/2_3.4.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>Each type has at most one parent, and one or more ancestor types; each untagged type has exactly one ultimate ancestor. In Ada 83, the term &ldquo;parent type&rdquo; was sometimes used more generally to include any ancestor type (e.g. RM83-9.4(14)). In Ada 95, we restrict parent to mean the immediate ancestor.<br /></li>
<MarginText>10.e_3.4.1</MarginText>
<li>A class of types has at most one root type; a derivation class has exactly one root type.<br /></li>
<MarginText>10.f_3.4.1</MarginText>
<li>The root of a class is an ancestor of all of the types in the class (including itself).<br /></li>
<MarginText>10.g_3.4.1</MarginText>
<li>The type <i>root{"_"}integer</i> is the root of the integer class, and is the ultimate ancestor of all integer types. A similar statement applies to <i>root{"_"}real</i>. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>10.h/5_3.4.1</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>ancestor of a type</b> &mdash; type itself or, in the case of a type derived from other types, its parent type or one of its progenitor types or one of their ancestors<br />Note: Ancestor and descendant are inverse relationships.<br />

<MarginText>10.i/5_3.4.1</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>descendant of a type</b> &mdash; type itself or a type derived (directly or indirectly) from it<br />Note: Descendant and ancestor are inverse relationships.<br />

<MarginText>11_3.4.1</MarginText>
<p>An inherited component [(including an inherited discriminant)] of a derived type is inherited <i>from</i> a given ancestor of the type if the corresponding component was inherited by each derived type in the chain of derivations going back to the given ancestor.<br /></p>

<MarginText>12_3.4.1</MarginText>
NOTE   Because operands of a universal type are acceptable to the predefined operators of any type in their class, ambiguity can result. For <i>universal{"_"}integer</i> and <i>universal{"_"}real</i>, this potential ambiguity is resolved by giving a preference (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>) to the predefined operators of the corresponding root types (<i>root{"_"}integer</i> and <i>root{"_"}real</i>, respectively). Hence, in an apparently ambiguous expression like <br />

<MarginText>13_3.4.1</MarginText>
1 + 4 {"<"} 7<br />

<MarginText>14_3.4.1</MarginText>
where each of the literals is of type <i>universal{"_"}integer</i>, the predefined operators of <i>root{"_"}integer</i> will be preferred over those of other specific integer types, thereby resolving the ambiguity. <br />

<MarginText>14.a_3.4.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Except for this preference, a root numeric type is essentially like any other specific type in the associated numeric class. In particular, the result of a predefined operator of a root numeric type is not &ldquo;universal&rdquo; (implicitly convertible) even if both operands were. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>14.b/2_3.4.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00230-01"]} />
Updated the wording to define the <i>universal{"_"}access</i> type. This was defined to make <b>null</b> for anonymous access types sensible.<br />

<MarginText>14.c/2_3.4.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00401-01"]} />
The definitions of ancestors and descendants were updated to allow multiple ancestors (necessary to support interfaces). <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2012

<MarginText>14.d/5_3.4.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0325-1"]} />
Updated the wording to say that universal types cover the types with the appropriate user-defined literal. <br />

---

# 3.5. Scalar Types

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5.mdx

sidebar_position:  23

# 3.5. Scalar Types

<MarginText>1</MarginText>
<p><i>Scalar</i> types comprise enumeration types, integer types, and real types. Enumeration types and integer types are called <i>discrete</i> types; each value of a discrete type has a <i>position number</i> which is an integer value. Integer types and real types are called <i>numeric</i> types. [All scalar types are ordered, that is, all relational operators are predefined for their values.]<br /></p>

#### Syntax

<MarginText>2</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>range{"_"}constraint</code><a id="S0036"></a><code> ::= </code> <b>range</b> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>range</code><a id="S0037"></a><code> ::= </code> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0102">range_attribute_reference</a></code><br />   | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0138">simple_expression</a></code> .. <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0138">simple_expression</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>These need to be <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0138">simple_expression</a></code>s rather than more general <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code>s because ranges appear in membership tests and other contexts where <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> .. <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> would be ambiguous. <br />

<MarginText>4</MarginText>
<p>A <i>range</i> has a <i>lower bound</i> and an <i>upper bound</i> and specifies a subset of the values of some scalar type (the <i>type of the range</i>). A range with lower bound L and upper bound R is described by &ldquo;L .. R&rdquo;. If R is less than L, then the range is a <i>null range</i>, and specifies an empty set of values. Otherwise, the range specifies the values of the type from the lower bound to the upper bound, inclusive. A value <i>belongs</i> to a range if it is of the type of the range, and is in the subset of values specified by the range. A value <i>satisfies</i> a range constraint if it belongs to the associated range. One range is <i>included</i> in another if all values that belong to the first range also belong to the second. <br /></p>

#### Name Resolution Rules

<MarginText>5</MarginText>
<p>For a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> containing a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0036">range_constraint</a></code>, either directly or as part of some other <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0030">scalar_constraint</a></code>, the type of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code> shall resolve to that of the type determined by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code> of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code>. For a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code> of a given type, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0138">simple_expression</a></code>s of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code> (likewise, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0138">simple_expression</a></code>s of the equivalent <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code> for a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0102">range_attribute_reference</a></code>) are expected to be of the type of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>5.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>In Ada 95, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0029">constraint</a></code>s only appear within <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code>s; things that look like constraints that appear in type declarations are called something else like <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0046">real_range_specification</a></code>s.<br />

<MarginText>5.b/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1", "AI12-0449-1"]} />
We say "the expected type is ..." or "the type is expected to be ..." depending on which reads better. They are fundamentally equivalent, and both feed into the type resolution rules of <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>.<br />

<MarginText>5.c</MarginText>
In some cases, it doesn't work to use expected types. For example, in the above rule, we say that the &ldquo;type of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code> shall resolve to ...&rdquo; rather than &ldquo;the expected type for the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code> is ...&rdquo; We then use &ldquo;expected type&rdquo; for the bounds. If we used &ldquo;expected&rdquo; at both points, there would be an ambiguity, since one could apply the rules of <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a> either on determining the type of the range, or on determining the types of the individual bounds. It is clearly important to allow one bound to be of a universal type, and the other of a specific type, so we need to use &ldquo;expected type&rdquo; for the bounds. Hence, we used &ldquo;shall resolve to&rdquo; for the type of the range as a whole. There are other situations where &ldquo;expected type&rdquo; is not quite right, and we use &ldquo;shall resolve to&rdquo; instead. <br />

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>6</MarginText>
<p>The <i>base range</i> of a scalar type is the range of finite values of the type that can be represented in every unconstrained object of the type; it is also the range supported at a minimum for intermediate values during the evaluation of expressions involving predefined operators of the type. <br /></p>

<MarginText>6.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>Note that in some machine architectures intermediates in an expression (particularly if static), and register-resident variables might accommodate a wider range. The base range does not include the values of this wider range that are not assignable without overflow to memory-resident objects.<br />

<MarginText>6.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The base range of an enumeration type is the range of values of the enumeration type. <br />

<MarginText>6.c</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>If the representation supports infinities, the base range is nevertheless restricted to include only the representable finite values, so that 'Base'First and 'Base'Last are always guaranteed to be finite.<br />

<MarginText>6.d</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>By a "value that can be assigned without overflow" we don't mean to restrict ourselves to values that can be represented exactly. Values between machine representable values can be assigned, but on subsequent reading, a slightly different value might be retrieved, as (partially) determined by the number of digits of precision of the type. <br />

<MarginText>7</MarginText>
<p>[A constrained scalar subtype is one to which a range constraint applies.] The <i>range</i> of a constrained scalar subtype is the range associated with the range constraint of the subtype. The <i>range</i> of an unconstrained scalar subtype is the base range of its type. <br /></p>

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>8</MarginText>
<p>A range is <i>compatible</i> with a scalar subtype if and only if it is either a null range or each bound of the range belongs to the range of the subtype. A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0036">range_constraint</a></code> is <i>compatible</i> with a scalar subtype if and only if its range is compatible with the subtype. <br /></p>

<MarginText>8.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Only <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0036">range_constraint</a></code>s (explicit or implicit) impose conditions on the values of a scalar subtype. The other <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0030">scalar_constraint</a></code>s, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0050">digits_constraint</a></code>s and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-J/AA-J.3#S0367">delta_constraint</a></code>s impose conditions on the subtype denoted by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code> in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code>, but don't impose a condition on the values of the subtype being defined. Therefore, a scalar subtype is not called <i>constrained</i> if all that applies to it is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0050">digits_constraint</a></code>. Decimal subtypes are subtle, because a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0050">digits_constraint</a></code> without a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0036">range_constraint</a></code> nevertheless includes an implicit <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0036">range_constraint</a></code>. <br />

<MarginText>9</MarginText>
<p>The elaboration of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0036">range_constraint</a></code> consists of the evaluation of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code>. The evaluation of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code> determines a lower bound and an upper bound. If <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0138">simple_expression</a></code>s are given to specify bounds, the evaluation of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code> evaluates these <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0138">simple_expression</a></code>s in an arbitrary order, and converts them to the type of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code>. If a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0102">range_attribute_reference</a></code> is given, the evaluation of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code> consists of the evaluation of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0102">range_attribute_reference</a></code>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>10</MarginText>
<p><i>Attributes</i><br /></p>

<MarginText>11</MarginText>
<p>For every scalar subtype S, the following attributes are defined: <br /></p>

<MarginText>12</MarginText>
<dt><br/>S'First</dt>
<dl>
<dd>S'First denotes the lower bound of the range of S. The value of this attribute is of the type of S. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>12.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Evaluating S'First never raises Constraint{"_"}Error.<br />

<MarginText>13</MarginText>
<dt><br/>S'Last</dt>
<dl>
<dd>S'Last denotes the upper bound of the range of S. The value of this attribute is of the type of S. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>13.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Evaluating S'Last never raises Constraint{"_"}Error.<br />

<MarginText>14</MarginText>
<dt><br/>S'Range</dt>
<dl>
<dd>S'Range is equivalent to the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0037">range</a></code> S'First .. S'Last.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>15</MarginText>
<dt><br/>S'Base</dt>
<dd>S'Base denotes an unconstrained subtype of the type of S. This unconstrained subtype is called the <i>base subtype</i> of the type. <br /></dd>
<MarginText>16</MarginText>
<dt><br/>S'Min</dt>
<dd>S'Min denotes a function with the following specification: <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>17</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
function S'Min(Left, Right : S'Base){"\n"}  return S'Base{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>18</MarginText>
<dl>
<dd>The function returns the lesser of the values of the two parameters. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>18.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The formal parameter names are italicized because they cannot be used in calls &mdash; see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4">6.4</a>. Such a specification cannot be written by the user because an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0100">attribute_reference</a></code> is not permitted as the designator of a user-defined function, nor can its formal parameters be anonymous. <br />

<MarginText>19</MarginText>
<dt><br/>S'Max</dt>
<dl>
<dd>S'Max denotes a function with the following specification: <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>20</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
function S'Max(Left, Right : S'Base){"\n"}  return S'Base{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>21</MarginText>
<dl>
<dd>The function returns the greater of the values of the two parameters.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>22</MarginText>
<dt><br/>S'Succ</dt>
<dd>S'Succ denotes a function with the following specification: <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>23</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
function S'Succ(Arg : S'Base){"\n"}  return S'Base{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>24</MarginText>
<dl>
<dd>For an enumeration type, the function returns the value whose position number is one more than that of the value of <i>Arg</i>; Constraint{"_"}Error is raised if there is no such value of the type. For an integer type, the function returns the result of adding one to the value of <i>Arg</i>. For a fixed point type, the function returns the result of adding <i>small</i> to the value of <i>Arg</i>. For a floating point type, the function returns the machine number (as defined in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#Subclause_3.5.7">3.5.7</a>) immediately above the value of <i>Arg</i>; Constraint{"_"}Error is raised if there is no such machine number. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>24.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>S'Succ for a modular integer subtype wraps around if the value of <i>Arg</i> is S'Base'Last. S'Succ for a signed integer subtype might raise Constraint{"_"}Error if the value of <i>Arg</i> is S'Base'Last, or it might return the out-of-base-range value S'Base'Last+1, as is permitted for all predefined numeric operations. <br />

<MarginText>25</MarginText>
<dt><br/>S'Pred</dt>
<dl>
<dd>S'Pred denotes a function with the following specification: <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>26</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
function S'Pred(Arg : S'Base){"\n"}  return S'Base{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>27</MarginText>
<dl>
<dd>For an enumeration type, the function returns the value whose position number is one less than that of the value of <i>Arg</i>; Constraint{"_"}Error is raised if there is no such value of the type. For an integer type, the function returns the result of subtracting one from the value of <i>Arg</i>. For a fixed point type, the function returns the result of subtracting <i>small</i> from the value of <i>Arg</i>. For a floating point type, the function returns the machine number (as defined in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#Subclause_3.5.7">3.5.7</a>) immediately below the value of <i>Arg</i>; Constraint{"_"}Error is raised if there is no such machine number. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>27.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>S'Pred for a modular integer subtype wraps around if the value of <i>Arg</i> is S'Base'First. S'Pred for a signed integer subtype might raise Constraint{"_"}Error if the value of <i>Arg</i> is S'Base'First, or it might return the out-of-base-range value S'Base'First&ndash;1, as is permitted for all predefined numeric operations. <br />

<dl>
<dd><i>Paragraphs 28 through 37 were moved to <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.10">4.10</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.10">Image Attributes</a>&rdquo;.</i> <br /></dd>
<MarginText>37.1/5</MarginText>

<CodeBlock language="ada">
function S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value(Arg : Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}String){"\n"}  return S'Base{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>39.3/2</MarginText>
<dl>
<dd>This function returns a value given an image of the value as a Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}String, ignoring any leading or trailing spaces.<br /></dd>
<MarginText>39.4/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0264-1"]} />
<dd>For the evaluation of a call on S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value for an enumeration subtype S, if the sequence of characters of the parameter (ignoring leading and trailing spaces) has the syntax of an enumeration literal and if it corresponds to a literal of the type of S (or corresponds to the result of S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image for a nongraphic character of the type), the result is the corresponding enumeration value; otherwise, Constraint{"_"}Error is raised. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>39.a.1/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>It's not crystal clear that Range{"_"}Check is appropriate here, but it doesn't seem worthwhile to invent a whole new check name just for this weird case, so we decided to lump it in with Range{"_"}Check. <br />

<MarginText>39.a.2/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00053-01"]} />
<b>To be honest: </b>{"{"}<i>8652/0096</i>{"}"} A sequence of characters corresponds to the result of S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image if it is the same ignoring case. Thus, the case of an image of a nongraphic character does not matter. For example, Character'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value("nul") does not raise Constraint{"_"}Error, even though Character'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image returns "NUL" for the nul character. <br />

<MarginText>39.5/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0264-1"]} />
<dl>
<dd>For the evaluation of a call on S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value for an integer subtype S, if the sequence of characters of the parameter (ignoring leading and trailing spaces) has the syntax of an integer literal, with an optional leading sign character (plus or minus for a signed type; only plus for a modular type), and the corresponding numeric value belongs to the base range of the type of S, then that value is the result; otherwise, Constraint{"_"}Error is raised.<br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>39.a.3/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>We considered allowing 'Value to return a representable but out-of-range value without a Constraint{"_"}Error. However, we currently require (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.9">4.9</a>) in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code> like "X := {"<"}numeric{"_"}literal{">"};" that the value of the numeric-literal be in X's base range (at compile time), so it seems unfriendly and confusing to have a different range allowed for 'Value. Furthermore, for modular types, without the requirement for being in the base range, 'Value would have to handle arbitrarily long literals (since overflow never occurs for modular types). <br />

<MarginText>39.6/2</MarginText>
<dl>
<dd>For the evaluation of a call on S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value for a real subtype S, if the sequence of characters of the parameter (ignoring leading and trailing spaces) has the syntax of one of the following: <br /></dd>
</dl>

<MarginText>39.9/2</MarginText>
<li>.<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.4#S0008">numeral</a></code>[<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.4#S0009">exponent</a></code>]<br /></li>
<MarginText>39.10/2</MarginText>
<li><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.4#S0012">base</a></code>{"#"}<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.4#S0013">based_numeral</a></code>.{"#"}[<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.4#S0009">exponent</a></code>]<br /></li>
<MarginText>39.11/2</MarginText>
<li><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.4#S0012">base</a></code>{"#"}.<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.4#S0013">based_numeral</a></code>{"#"}[<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.4#S0009">exponent</a></code>] <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>39.12/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0264-1"]} />
<dl>
<dd>with an optional leading sign character (plus or minus), and if the corresponding numeric value belongs to the base range of the type of S, then that value is the result; otherwise, Constraint{"_"}Error is raised. The sign of a zero value is preserved (positive if none has been specified) if S'Signed{"_"}Zeros is True.<br /></dd>

<MarginText>43.a/2</MarginText>
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>43.a.1/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00053-01"]} />
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i>{"{"}<i>8652/0096</i>{"}"} <br />

<MarginText>43.b/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>S'Wide{"_"}Value is subtly different from S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value for enumeration subtypes since S'Wide{"_"}Image might produce a different sequence of characters than S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image if the enumeration literal uses characters outside of the predefined type Wide{"_"}Character. That is why we don't just define S'Wide{"_"}Value in terms of S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value for enumeration subtypes. S'Wide{"_"}Value and S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value for numeric subtypes yield the same result given the same sequence of characters. <br />

#### Implementation Permissions

<MarginText>56/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01"]} />
<p>An implementation may extend the Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value, [Wide{"_"}Value, Value, Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image, Wide{"_"}Image, and Image] attributes of a floating point type to support special values such as infinities and NaNs.<br /></p>

<MarginText>56.a/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>The permission is really only necessary for Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value, because Value and Wide{"_"}Value are defined in terms of Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value, and because the behavior of Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image, Wide{"_"}Image, and Image is already unspecified for things like infinities and NaNs. <br />

<MarginText>56.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This is to allow implementations to define full support for IEEE arithmetic. See also the similar permission for Get in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-A/AA-A.10#Subclause_A.10.9">A.10.9</a>. <br />

<MarginText>56.1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0182-1", "AI05-0262-1", "AI05-0269-1"]} />
<p>An implementation may extend the Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value, Wide{"_"}Value, and Value attributes of a character type to accept strings of the form &ldquo;Hex{"_"}<i>hhhhhhhh</i>&rdquo; (ignoring case) for any character (not just the ones for which Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image would produce that form &mdash; see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#Subclause_3.5.2">3.5.2</a>), as well as three-character strings of the form &ldquo;'<i>X</i>'&rdquo;, where <i>X</i> is any character, including nongraphic characters. <br /></p>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>56.2/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0228-1"]} />
<p>For a scalar type, the following language-defined representation aspect may be specified with an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#Subclause_13.1.1">13.1.1</a>): <br /></p>

<MarginText>56.3/3</MarginText>
<dt><br/>Default{"_"}Value</dt>
<dl>
<dd>This aspect shall be specified by a static expression, and that expression shall be explicit, even if the aspect has a boolean type. Default{"_"}Value shall be specified only on a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0024">full_type_declaration</a></code>. <br /></dd>
</dl>
<MarginText>56.c/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The part about requiring an explicit expression is to disallow omitting the value for this aspect, which would otherwise be allowed by the rules of <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#Subclause_13.1.1">13.1.1</a>.<br />

<MarginText>56.d/3</MarginText>
This is a representation aspect in order to disallow specifying it on a derived type that has inherited primitive subprograms; that is necessary as the sizes of <b>out</b> parameters could be different whether or not a Default{"_"}Value is specified (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#Subclause_6.4.1">6.4.1</a>). <br />

<MarginText>56.e/3</MarginText>
<b>Aspect Description for </b><b>Default{"_"}Value: </b>Default value for a scalar subtype.<br />

<MarginText>56.4/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0228-1", "AI12-0427-1"]} />
<p>If a derived type inherits a boolean Default{"_"}Value aspect, the aspect may be specified to have any value for the derived type. If a derived type <i>T</i> does not inherit a Default{"_"}Value aspect, it shall not specify such an aspect if it inherits a primitive subprogram that has a parameter of type <i>T</i> of mode <b>out</b>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>56.f/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This overrides the <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#Subclause_13.1.1">13.1.1</a> rule that says that a boolean aspect with a value True cannot be changed.<br />

<MarginText>56.g/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0427-1"]} />
The second sentence is to avoid violating the rules specified in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#Subclause_6.4.1">6.4.1</a> about view conversions of <b>out</b> parameters with a specified Default{"_"}Value aspect. <br />

#### Name Resolution Rules

<MarginText>56.5/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0228-1"]} />
<p>The expected type for the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> specified for the Default{"_"}Value aspect is the type defined by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0024">full_type_declaration</a></code> on which it appears. <br /></p>

<MarginText>57</MarginText>
NOTE 1   The evaluation of S'First or S'Last never raises an exception. If a scalar subtype S has a nonnull range, S'First and S'Last belong to this range. These values can, for example, always be assigned to a variable of subtype S. <br />

<MarginText>57.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>This paragraph addresses an issue that came up with Ada 83, where for fixed point types, the end points of the range specified in the type definition were not necessarily within the base range of the type. However, it was later clarified (and we reconfirm it in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#Subclause_3.5.9">3.5.9</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#Subclause_3.5.9">Fixed Point Types</a>&rdquo;) that the First and Last attributes reflect the true bounds chosen for the type, not the bounds specified in the type definition (which might be outside the ultimately chosen base range). <br />

<MarginText>58/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0442-1"]} />
NOTE 2   For a subtype of a scalar type, the result delivered by the attributes Succ, Pred, and Value can be outside to the subtype; similarly, the actual parameters of the attributes Succ, Pred, and Image can also be outside the subtype.<br />

<MarginText>59/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI12-0020-1"]} />
NOTE 3   For any value V (including any nongraphic character) of an enumeration subtype S without a specified Put{"_"}Image (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.10">4.10</a>), S'Value(S'Image(V)) equals V, as do S'Wide{"_"}Value(S'Wide{"_"}Image(V)) and S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value(S'Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image(V)). None of these expressions ever raise Constraint{"_"}Error. <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>60</MarginText>

-10 .. 10{"\n"}X .. X + 1{"\n"}0.0 .. 2.0{"*"}Pi{"\n"}Red .. Green     -- see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#Subclause_3.5.1">3.5.1</a>{"\n"}1 .. 0           -- a null range{"\n"}Table'Range      -- a range attribute reference (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6">3.6</a>){"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

</CodeBlock>

#### Incompatibilities With Ada 83

<MarginText>63.a/1</MarginText>
S'Base is no longer defined for nonscalar types. One conceivable existing use of S'Base for nonscalar types is S'Base'Size where S is a generic formal private type. However, that is not generally useful because the actual subtype corresponding to S might be a constrained array or discriminated type, which would mean that S'Base'Size might very well overflow (for example, S'Base'Size where S is a constrained subtype of String will generally be 8 {"*"} (Integer'Last + 1)). For derived discriminated types that are packed, S'Base'Size might not even be well defined if the first subtype is constrained, thereby allowing some amount of normally required &ldquo;dope&rdquo; to have been squeezed out in the packing. Hence our conclusion is that S'Base'Size is not generally useful in a generic, and does not justify keeping the attribute Base for nonscalar types just so it can be used as a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>.<br />

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>63.b</MarginText>
The attribute S'Base for a scalar subtype is now permitted anywhere a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code> is permitted. S'Base'First .. S'Base'Last is the base range of the type. Using an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.3#S0349">attribute{"_"}definition{"_"}clause</a></code>, one cannot specify any subtype-specific attributes for the subtype denoted by S'Base (the base subtype).<br />

<MarginText>63.c</MarginText>
The attribute S'Range is now allowed for scalar subtypes.<br />

<MarginText>63.d</MarginText>
The attributes S'Min and S'Max are now defined, and made available for all scalar types.<br />

<MarginText>63.e</MarginText>
The attributes S'Succ, S'Pred, S'Image, S'Value, and S'Width are now defined for real types as well as discrete types.<br />

<MarginText>63.f</MarginText>
Wide{"_"}String versions of S'Image and S'Value are defined. These are called S'Wide{"_"}Image and S'Wide{"_"}Value to avoid introducing ambiguities involving uses of these attributes with string literals. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>63.g</MarginText>
We now use the syntactic category <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0102">range_attribute_reference</a></code> since it is now syntactically distinguished from other attribute references.<br />

<MarginText>63.h</MarginText>
The definition of S'Base has been moved here from 3.3.3 since it now applies only to scalar types.<br />

<MarginText>63.i</MarginText>
More explicit rules are provided for nongraphic characters. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 95

<MarginText>63.j/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01"]} />
The attributes Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image, Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value, and Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Width are new. Note that Wide{"_"}Image and Wide{"_"}Value are now defined in terms of Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image and Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value, but the image of types other than characters have not changed. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>63.k/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01"]} />
The Wide{"_"}Image and Wide{"_"}Value attributes are now defined in terms of Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image and Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value, but the images of numeric types have not changed. <br />

#### Inconsistencies With Ada 2005

<MarginText>63.l/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0181-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Soft hyphen (code point 173) is nongraphic in ISO/IEC 10646:2011 (and also in the 2003 version of that standard). Thus, we have given it the language-defined name <i>soft{"_"}hyphen</i>. This changes the result of Character'Image (and all of the related types and Image attributes) for this character, and changes the behavior of Character'Value (and all of the related types and Value attributes) for this character, and (in unusual circumstances), changes the result for Character'Width (and all of the related types and Width attributes). The vast majority of programs won't see any difference, as they are already prepared to handle nongraphic characters.<br />

<MarginText>63.m/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0182-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Added an Implementation Permissions to let Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value, Wide{"_"}Value, and Value accept strings in the form of literals containing nongraphic characters and "Hex{"_"}hhhhhhhh" for Latin-1 and graphic characters. These were required to raise Constraint{"_"}Error in Ada 2005. Since these attributes aren't very useful, implementations were inconsistent as to whether these were accepted, and since code that would care why the attribute failed seems unlikely, this should not be a problem in practice. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 2005

<MarginText>63.n/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0228-1"]} />
The new aspect Default{"_"}Value allows defining implicit initial values (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#Subclause_3.3.1">3.3.1</a>) for scalar types. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 2012

<MarginText>63.o/4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0124-1"]} />
<b>Corrigendum:</b> An object can be now used as the prefix of the Image attribute (as well as Wide{"_"}Image and Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image), a convenience feature already present in some implementations.<br />

<MarginText>63.p/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0020-1"]} />
All of the Image-family attributes have been moved to <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.10">4.10</a>. <br />

<a id="Subclause_3.5.1"></a>

## 3.5.1  Enumeration Types

<MarginText>1_3.5.1</MarginText>
<p>[ An <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0038">enumeration_type_definition</a></code> defines an enumeration type.] <br /></p>

#### Syntax

<MarginText>2_3.5.1</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>enumeration{"_"}type{"_"}definition</code><a id="S0038"></a><code> ::= </code><br />   (<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0039">enumeration_literal_specification</a></code> {"{"}, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0039">enumeration_literal_specification</a></code>{"}"})<br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3_3.5.1</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>enumeration{"_"}literal{"_"}specification</code><a id="S0039"></a><code> ::= </code><br />    <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.1#S0022">defining_identifier</a></code> | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0040">defining_character_literal</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>4_3.5.1</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>defining{"_"}character{"_"}literal</code><a id="S0040"></a><code> ::= </code><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>

#### Legality Rules

<MarginText>5/3_3.5.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0227-1", "AI05-0299-1"]} />
<p>The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.1#S0022">defining_identifier</a></code>s in upper case [and the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0040">defining_character_literal</a></code>s] listed in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0038">enumeration_type_definition</a></code> shall be distinct. <br /></p>

<MarginText>5.a/3_3.5.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0227-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>For character literals, this is a ramification of the normal disallowance of homographs explicitly declared immediately in the same declarative region. <br />

<MarginText>5.b/3_3.5.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0227-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>To ease implementation of the attribute Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value, we require that all enumeration literals have distinct images. <br />

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>6/3_3.5.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0006-1"]} />
<p>Each <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0039">enumeration_literal_specification</a></code> is the explicit declaration of the corresponding <i>enumeration literal</i>: it declares a parameterless function, whose defining name is the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.1#S0022">defining{"_"}identifier</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0040">defining{"_"}character{"_"}literal</a></code>, and whose result subtype is the base subtype of the enumeration type. <br /></p>

<MarginText>6.a_3.5.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This rule defines the profile of the enumeration literal, which is used in the various types of conformance. <br />

<MarginText>6.b_3.5.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The parameterless function associated with an enumeration literal is fully defined by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0038">enumeration_type_definition</a></code>; a body is not permitted for it, and it never fails the Elaboration{"_"}Check when called. <br />

<MarginText>6.c/3_3.5.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0006-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The result subtype is primarily a concern when an enumeration literal is used as the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> of a case statement, due to the full coverage requirement based on the nominal subtype. <br />

<MarginText>7_3.5.1</MarginText>
<p>Each enumeration literal corresponds to a distinct value of the enumeration type, and to a distinct position number. The position number of the value of the first listed enumeration literal is zero; the position number of the value of each subsequent enumeration literal is one more than that of its predecessor in the list.<br /></p>

<MarginText>8_3.5.1</MarginText>
<p>[The predefined order relations between values of the enumeration type follow the order of corresponding position numbers.]<br /></p>

<MarginText>9_3.5.1</MarginText>
<p>[ If the same <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.1#S0022">defining_identifier</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0040">defining_character_literal</a></code> is specified in more than one <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0038">enumeration{"_"}type{"_"}definition</a></code>, the corresponding enumeration literals are said to be <i>overloaded</i>. At any place where an overloaded enumeration literal occurs in the text of a program, the type of the enumeration literal has to be determinable from the context (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.6">8.6</a>).] <br /></p>

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>10_3.5.1</MarginText>
<p>The elaboration of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0038">enumeration_type_definition</a></code> creates the enumeration type and its first subtype, which is constrained to the base range of the type. <br /></p>

<MarginText>10.a_3.5.1</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The first subtype of a discrete type is always constrained, except in the case of a derived type whose parent subtype is Whatever'Base. <br />

<MarginText>11_3.5.1</MarginText>
<p>When called, the parameterless function associated with an enumeration literal returns the corresponding value of the enumeration type. <br /></p>

<MarginText>12_3.5.1</MarginText>
NOTE   If an enumeration literal occurs in a context that does not otherwise suffice to determine the type of the literal, then qualification by the name of the enumeration type is one way to resolve the ambiguity (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7">4.7</a>). <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>13_3.5.1</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of enumeration types and subtypes:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>14/5_3.5.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0386-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type Day        is (Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun);{"\n"}type Month{"_"}Name is (January, February, March, April, May, June, July,{"\n"}                    August, September, October, November, December);{"\n"}type Suit       is (Clubs, Diamonds, Hearts, Spades);{"\n"}type Gender     is (M, F);{"\n"}type Level      is (Low, Medium, Urgent);{"\n"}type Color      is (White, Red, Yellow, Green, Blue, Brown, Black);{"\n"}type Light      is (Red, Amber, Green); -- Red and Green are overloaded{"\n"}
<MarginText>15_3.5.1</MarginText>
type Hexa       is ('A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'F');{"\n"}type Mixed      is ('A', 'B', '{"*"}', B, None, '?', '%');{"\n"}
<MarginText>16_3.5.1</MarginText>
subtype Weekday is Day   range Mon .. Fri;{"\n"}subtype Major   is Suit  range Hearts .. Spades;{"\n"}subtype Rainbow is Color range Red .. Blue;{"\n"}                               -- the Color Red, not the Light{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>16.a_3.5.1</MarginText>
The syntax rule for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.5#S0040">defining_character_literal</a></code> is new. It is used for the defining occurrence of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code>, analogously to <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.1#S0022">defining_identifier</a></code>. Usage occurrences use the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0099">selector_name</a></code> syntactic categories.<br />

<MarginText>16.b_3.5.1</MarginText>
We emphasize the fact that an enumeration literal denotes a function, which is called to produce a value. <br />

#### Incompatibilities With Ada 2005

<MarginText>16.c/3_3.5.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0227-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Required that all enumeration literals in a type have distinct images; this might not be the case since upper case conversion can map distinct characters to the same upper case character. This can only happen for identifiers using Unicode characters first allowed by Ada 2005; moreover, the original definition of Ada 2005 was confused and appeared to require inconsistent results from the Image attribute, so implementations that allowed problematic cases are rare; the problematic cases are very rare; so it is expected that this change would only affect test programs. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>16.d/3_3.5.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0006-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Defined the result subtype of an enumeration literal to close a minor language hole. <br />

<a id="Subclause_3.5.2"></a>

## 3.5.2  Character Types

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>1_3.5.2</MarginText>
<p>An enumeration type is said to be a <i>character type</i> if at least one of its enumeration literals is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>2/5_3.5.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI05-0181-1", "AI05-0262-1", "AI05-0266-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0450-1"]} />
<p>The predefined type Character is a character type whose values correspond to the 256 code points of Row 00 (also known as Latin-1) of the ISO/IEC 10646:2020 Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP). Each of the graphic characters of Row 00 of the BMP has a corresponding <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code> in Character. Each of the nongraphic characters of Row 00 has a corresponding language-defined name, which is not usable as an enumeration literal, but which is usable with the attributes Image, Wide{"_"}Image, Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Image, Value, Wide{"_"}Value, and Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Value; these names are given in the definition of type Character in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-A/AA-A.1">A.1</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-A/AA-A.1">The Package Standard</a>&rdquo;, but are set in <i>italics</i>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.a/5_3.5.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0262-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0450-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b><i>Code point</i> is defined in ISO/IEC 10646:2020. <br />

<MarginText>3/5_3.5.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI05-0262-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0450-1"]} />
<p>The predefined type Wide{"_"}Character is a character type whose values correspond to the 65536 code points of the ISO/IEC 10646:2020 Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP). Each of the graphic characters of the BMP has a corresponding <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code> in Wide{"_"}Character. The first 256 values of Wide{"_"}Character have the same <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code> or language-defined name as defined for Character. Each of the <code>graphic{"_"}character</code>s has a corresponding <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>4/5_3.5.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI05-0262-1", "AI12-0263-1", "AI12-0450-1"]} />
<p>The predefined type Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Character is a character type whose values correspond to the 2147483648 code points of the ISO/IEC 10646:2020 character set. Each of the <code>graphic{"_"}character</code>s has a corresponding <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code> in Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Character. The first 65536 values of Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Character have the same <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code> or language-defined name as defined for Wide{"_"}Character.<br /></p>

<MarginText>5/3_3.5.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01", "AI05-0262-1"]} />
<p>The characters whose code point is larger than 16{"#"}FF{"#"} and which are not <code>graphic{"_"}character</code>s have language-defined names which are formed by appending to the string "Hex{"_"}" the representation of their code point in hexadecimal as eight extended digits. As with other language-defined names, these names are usable only with the attributes (Wide{"_"})Wide{"_"}Image and (Wide{"_"})Wide{"_"}Value; they are not usable as enumeration literals.<br /></p>

<MarginText>5.a/2_3.5.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00285-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The language-defined names are not usable as enumeration literals to avoid "polluting" the name space. Since Wide{"_"}Character and Wide{"_"}Wide{"_"}Character are defined in Standard, if the language-defined names were usable as enumeration literals, they would hide other nonoverloadable declarations with the same names in <b>use</b>-d packages.<br />

<p><i>Original Paragraphs 4 and 5 were deleted.</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>8_3.5.2</MarginText>
NOTE 1   The language-defined library package Characters.Latin{"_"}1 (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-A/AA-A.3#Subclause_A.3.3">A.3.3</a>) includes the declaration of constants denoting control characters, lower case characters, and special characters of the predefined type Character. <br />

<MarginText>8.a_3.5.2</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>The package ASCII does the same, but only for the first 128 characters of Character. Hence, it is an obsolescent package, and we no longer mention it here. <br />

<MarginText>9/5_3.5.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1", "AI12-0449-1"]} />
