The overriding declaration for P2.Op{"_"}B is not visible in Main, so the name in the call actually denotes the implicit declaration of Op{"_"}B inherited from T1.<br />

<MarginText>20.g_3.9.2</MarginText>
If a call occurs in the program text before an overriding, which can happen only if the call is part of a default expression, the overriding will still take effect for that call.<br />

<MarginText>20.h_3.9.2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>Even when a tag is not <i>statically determined</i>, a compiler might still be able to figure it out and thereby avoid the overhead of run-time dispatching. <br />

<MarginText>21_3.9.2</MarginText>
NOTE 1   The body to be executed for a call on a dispatching operation is determined by the tag; it does not matter whether that tag is determined statically or dynamically, and it does not matter whether the subprogram's declaration is visible at the place of the call.<br />

<MarginText>22/2_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00260-02"]} />
NOTE 2   This subclause covers calls on dispatching subprograms of a tagged type. Rules for tagged type membership tests are described in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#Subclause_4.5.2">4.5.2</a>. Controlling tag determination for an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code> is described in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2">5.2</a>.<br />

<MarginText>23_3.9.2</MarginText>
NOTE 3   A dispatching call can dispatch to a body whose declaration is not visible at the place of the call.<br />

<MarginText>24_3.9.2</MarginText>
NOTE 4   A call through an access-to-subprogram value is never a dispatching call, even if the access value designates a dispatching operation. Similarly a call whose <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> denotes a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0242">subprogram_renaming_declaration</a></code> cannot be a dispatching call unless the renaming itself is the declaration of a primitive subprogram. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>24.a_3.9.2</MarginText>
The concept of dispatching operations is new. <br />

#### Incompatibilities With Ada 95

<MarginText>24.b/2_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00404-01"]} />
If a dispatching operation is defined by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.5#S0242">subprogram_renaming_declaration</a></code>, and it has a controlling access parameter, Ada 2005 requires the subtype of the parameter to exclude null. The same applies to instantiations. This is required so that all calls to the subprogram operate the same way (controlling access parameters have to exclude null so that dispatching calls will work). Since Ada 95 didn't have the notion of access subtypes that exclude null, and all access parameters excluded null, it had no such rules. These rules will require the addition of an explicit <b>not null</b> on nondispatching operations that are later renamed to be dispatching, or on a generic that is used to define a dispatching operation. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 95

<MarginText>24.c/2_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00416-01"]} />
Functions that have an access result type can be dispatching in the same way as a function that returns a tagged object directly. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>24.d/3_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00127-01", "AI05-0299-1"]} />
{"{"}<i>8652/0010</i>{"}"} <b>Corrigendum:</b> Allocators and access attributes of objects of class-wide types can be used as the controlling parameter in a dispatching calls. This was an oversight in the definition of Ada 95. (See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#Subclause_3.10.2">3.10.2</a> and <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8">4.8</a>).<br />

<MarginText>24.e/2_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00117-01", "AI95-00430-01"]} />
{"{"}<i>8652/0011</i>{"}"} <b>Corrigendum:</b> Corrected the conventions of dispatching operations. This is extended in Ada 2005 to cover operations inherited from progenitors, and to ensure that the conventions of all inherited operations are the same.<br />

<MarginText>24.f/2_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00196-01"]} />
Clarified the wording to ensure that functions with no controlling operands are tag-indeterminate, and to describe that the controlling tag can come from the target of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>.<br />

<MarginText>24.g/2_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00239-01"]} />
Fixed the wording to cover default expressions inherited by derived subprograms. A literal reading of the old wording would have implied that operations would be called with objects of the wrong type.<br />

<MarginText>24.h/2_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00260-02"]} />
An abstract formal subprogram is a dispatching operation, even though it is not a primitive operation. See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6">12.6</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6">Formal Subprograms</a>&rdquo;.<br />

<MarginText>24.i/2_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01"]} />
Dispatching calls include operations implemented by entries and protected operations, so we have to update the wording to reflect that.<br />

<MarginText>24.j/2_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00335-01"]} />
A stream attribute of a tagged type is usually a dispatching operation, even though it is not a primitive operation. If they weren't dispatching, T'Class'Input and T'Class'Output wouldn't work. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>24.k/3_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0076-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Defined &ldquo;function with a controlling result&rdquo;, as it is used in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.3">3.9.3</a>.<br />

<MarginText>24.l/3_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0126-1", "AI05-0197-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Corrected holes in the definition of dynamic dispatching: the behavior for operations that are never declared and/or inherited from a progenitor were not specified. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2012

<MarginText>24.m/5_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0236-1"]} />
Added a special rule for taggedness of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#S0156">declare_expression</a></code>s, and added a pointer to the existing special rules for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#S0148">conditional_expression</a></code>s, as the list of exceptions to the usual rules appear to be exhaustive.<br />

<MarginText>24.n/5_3.9.2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0419-1"]} />
Added wording to clarify that the Put{"_"}Image attribute is a dispatching operation. Put{"_"}Image follows the model of stream-oriented attributes, and thus need to be mentioned in the same place. <br />

<a id="Subclause_3.9.3"></a>

## 3.9.3  Abstract Types and Subprograms

<MarginText>1/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01"]} />
<p>[ An <i>abstract type</i> is a tagged type intended for use as an ancestor of other types, but which is not allowed to have objects of its own. An <i>abstract subprogram</i> is a subprogram that has no body, but is intended to be overridden at some point when inherited. Because objects of an abstract type cannot be created, a dispatching call to an abstract subprogram always dispatches to some overriding body.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>1.a.1/5_3.9.3</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>abstract type</b> &mdash; tagged type intended for use as an ancestor of other types, but which is not allowed to have objects of its own<br />

#### Language Design Principles

<MarginText>1.a/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
An abstract subprogram has no body, so the rules in this subclause are designed to ensure (at compile time) that the body will never be invoked. We do so primarily by disallowing the creation of values of the abstract type. Therefore, since type conversion and parameter passing don't change the tag, we know we will never get a class-wide value with a tag identifying an abstract type. This means that we only have to disallow nondispatching calls on abstract subprograms (dispatching calls will never reach them). <br />

#### Syntax

<MarginText>1.1/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00218-03", "AI95-00348-01", "AI05-0183-1"]} />

<CodeBlock>
<code>abstract{"_"}subprogram{"_"}declaration</code><a id="S0076"></a><code> ::= </code><br />    [<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-8/AA-8.3#S0234">overriding_indicator</a></code>]<br />    <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0196">subprogram_specification</a></code> <b>is</b> <b>abstract</b><br />        [<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code>];<br />

</CodeBlock>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>1.2/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01"]} />
<p>Interface types (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.4">3.9.4</a>) are abstract types. In addition, a tagged type that has the reserved word <b>abstract</b> in its declaration is an abstract type. The class-wide type (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#Subclause_3.4.1">3.4.1</a>) rooted at an abstract type is not itself an abstract type. <br /></p>

#### Legality Rules

<MarginText>2/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01"]} />
<p>Only a tagged type shall have the reserved word <b>abstract</b> in its declaration. <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.a_3.9.3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Untagged types are never abstract, even though they can have primitive abstract subprograms. Such subprograms cannot be called, unless they also happen to be dispatching operations of some tagged type, and then only via a dispatching call.<br />

<MarginText>2.b_3.9.3</MarginText>
Class-wide types are never abstract. If T is abstract, then it is illegal to declare a stand-alone object of type T, but it is OK to declare a stand-alone object of type T'Class; the latter will get a tag from its initial value, and this tag will necessarily be different from T'Tag. <br />

<MarginText>3/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00260-02", "AI95-00348-01"]} />
<p>A subprogram declared by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0076">abstract{"_"}subprogram{"_"}declaration</a></code> or a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6#S0337">formal{"_"}abstract{"_"}subprogram{"_"}declaration</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6">12.6</a>) is an <i>abstract subprogram</i>. If it is a primitive subprogram of a tagged type, then the tagged type shall be abstract. <br /></p>

<MarginText>3.a_3.9.3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Note that for a private type, this applies to both views. The following is illegal: <br />

<MarginText>3.b_3.9.3</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package P is{"\n"}    type T is abstract tagged private;{"\n"}    function Foo (X : T) return Boolean is abstract; -- Illegal!{"\n"}private{"\n"}    type T is tagged null record; -- Illegal!{"\n"}    X : T;{"\n"}    Y : Boolean := Foo (T'Class (X));{"\n"}end P;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3.c_3.9.3</MarginText>
The full view of T is not abstract, but has an abstract operation Foo, which is illegal. The two lines marked "--<i> Illegal!</i>" are illegal when taken together. <br />

<MarginText>3.d/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00310-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We considered disallowing untagged types from having abstract primitive subprograms. However, we rejected that plan, because it introduced some silly anomalies, and because such subprograms are harmless. For example: <br />

<MarginText>3.e/1_3.9.3</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package P is{"\n"}   type Field{"_"}Size is range 0..100;{"\n"}   type T is abstract tagged null record;{"\n"}   procedure Print(X : in T; F : in Field{"_"}Size := 0) is abstract;{"\n"}  . . .{"\n"}package Q is{"\n"}   type My{"_"}Field{"_"}Size is new Field{"_"}Size;{"\n"}   -- implicit declaration of Print(X : T; F : My{"_"}Field{"_"}Size := 0) is abstract;{"\n"}end Q;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3.f_3.9.3</MarginText>
It seemed silly to make the derivative of My{"_"}Field{"_"}Size illegal, just because there was an implicitly declared abstract subprogram that was not primitive on some tagged type. Other rules could be formulated to solve this problem, but the current ones seem like the simplest.<br />

<MarginText>3.g/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00310-01"]} />
In Ada 2005, abstract primitive subprograms of an untagged type may be used to &ldquo;undefine&rdquo; an operation. <br />

<MarginText>3.h/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00260-02"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Note that the second sentence does not apply to abstract formal subprograms, as they are never primitive operations of a type. <br />

<MarginText>4/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00334-01", "AI95-00391-01", "AI05-0097-1", "AI05-0198-1"]} />
<p>If a type has an implicitly declared primitive subprogram that is inherited or is a predefined operator, and the corresponding primitive subprogram of the parent or ancestor type is abstract or is a function with a controlling access result, or if a type other than a nonabstract null extension inherits a function with a controlling result, then: <br /></p>

<MarginText>4.a/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0068-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>These rules apply to each view of the type individually. That is necessary to preserve privacy. For instance, in the following example: <br />

<MarginText>4.b/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package P is{"\n"}   type I is interface;{"\n"}   procedure Op (X : I) is abstract;{"\n"}end P;{"\n"}
<MarginText>4.c/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
with P;{"\n"}package Q is{"\n"}   type T is abstract new P.I with private;{"\n"}   -- Op inherited here.{"\n"}private{"\n"}   type T is abstract new P.I with null record;{"\n"}   procedure Op (X : T) is null;{"\n"}end Q;{"\n"}
<MarginText>4.d/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
with Q;{"\n"}package R is{"\n"}   type T2 is new Q.T with null record;{"\n"}   -- Illegal. Op inherited here, but requires overriding.{"\n"}end R;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>4.e/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
If this did not depend on the view, this would be legal. But in that case, the fact that Op is overridden in the private part would be visible; package R would have to be illegal if no overriding was in the private part.<br />

<MarginText>4.f/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
Note that this means that whether an inherited subprogram is abstract or concrete depends on where it inherited. In the case of Q, Q.Op in the visible part is abstract, while Q.Op in the private part is concrete. That is, R is illegal since it is an unrelated unit (and thus it cannot see the private part), but if R had been a private child of Q, it would have been legal. <br />

<MarginText>5/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00334-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>If the type is abstract or untagged, the implicitly declared subprogram is <i>abstract</i>. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>5.a_3.9.3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Note that it is possible to override a concrete subprogram with an abstract one. <br />

<MarginText>6/5_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00391-01", "AI12-0080-1", "AI12-0444-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>Otherwise, the subprogram shall be overridden with a nonabstract subprogram or, in the case of a private extension inheriting a nonabstract function with a controlling result, have a full type that is a null extension[; for a type declared in the visible part of a package, the overriding may be either in the visible or the private part]. Such a subprogram is said to <i>require overriding</i>. However, if the type is a generic formal type, the subprogram is allowed to be inherited as is, without being overridden for the formal type itself; [a nonabstract version will necessarily be provided by the actual type.] <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>6.a/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00228-01", "AI95-00391-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>A function that returns the parent type requires overriding for a type extension (or becomes abstract for an abstract type) because conversion from a parent type to a type extension is not defined, and function return semantics is defined in terms of conversion (other than for a null extension; see below). (Note that parameters of mode <b>in out</b> or <b>out</b> do not have this problem, because the tag of the actual is not changed.)<br />

<MarginText>6.b_3.9.3</MarginText>
Note that the overriding required above can be in the private part, which allows the following: <br />

<MarginText>6.c_3.9.3</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package Pack1 is{"\n"}    type Ancestor is abstract ...;{"\n"}    procedure Do{"_"}Something(X : in Ancestor) is abstract;{"\n"}end Pack1;{"\n"}
<MarginText>6.d_3.9.3</MarginText>
with Pack1; use Pack1;{"\n"}package Pack2 is{"\n"}    type T1 is new Ancestor with record ...;{"\n"}        -- A concrete type.{"\n"}    procedure Do{"_"}Something(X : in T1); -- Have to override.{"\n"}end Pack2;{"\n"}
<MarginText>6.e_3.9.3</MarginText>
with Pack1; use Pack1;{"\n"}with Pack2; use Pack2;{"\n"}package Pack3 is{"\n"}    type T2 is new Ancestor with private;{"\n"}        -- A concrete type.{"\n"}private{"\n"}    type T2 is new T1 with -- Parent different from ancestor.{"\n"}      record ... end record;{"\n"}    -- Here, we inherit Pack2.Do{"_"}Something.{"\n"}end Pack3;{"\n"}    {"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>6.f/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00228-01"]} />
T2 inherits an abstract Do{"_"}Something, but T2 is not abstract, so Do{"_"}Something has to be overridden. However, it is OK to override it in the private part. In this case, we override it by inheriting a concrete version from a different type. Nondispatching calls to Pack3.Do{"_"}Something are allowed both inside and outside package Pack3, as the client &ldquo;knows&rdquo; that the subprogram was necessarily overridden somewhere.<br />

<MarginText>6.g/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00391-01"]} />
For a null extension, the result of a function with a controlling result is defined in terms of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0111">extension_aggregate</a></code> with a <b>null record</b> extension part (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4">3.4</a>). This means that these restrictions on functions with a controlling result do not have to apply to null extensions.<br />

<MarginText>6.h/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00391-01"]} />
However, functions with controlling access results still require overriding. Changing the tag in place might clobber a preexisting object, and allocating new memory would possibly change the pool of the object, leading to storage leaks. Moreover, copying the object isn't possible for limited types. We don't need to restrict functions that have an access return type of an untagged type, as derived types with primitive subprograms have to have the same representation as their parent type. <br />

<MarginText>7/5_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0413-1"]} />
<p>A call on an abstract subprogram shall be a dispatching call; nondispatching calls to an abstract subprogram are not allowed. In addition to the places where Legality Rules normally apply (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3">12.3</a>), these rules also apply in the private part of an instance of a generic unit. <br /></p>

<MarginText>7.a/5_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00310-01", "AI12-0413-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>If an abstract subprogram is not a dispatching operation of some tagged type, then it cannot be called at all. In Ada 2005, such subprograms are not even considered by name resolution (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4">6.4</a>). However, this rule is still needed for cases that can arise in the instance of a generic specification where Name Resolution Rules are not reapplied, but Legality Rules are, when the equality operator for an untagged record type is abstract, while the operator for the formal type is not abstract (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.5">12.5</a>). <br />

<MarginText>7.1/5_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0189-1", "AI12-0292-1", "AI12-0320-1"]} />
<p>If the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> given in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.5#S0187">iterator_procedure_call</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.5#Subclause_5.5.3">5.5.3</a>) denotes an abstract subprogram, the subprogram shall be a dispatching subprogram.<br /></p>

<MarginText>8/5_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0073-1", "AI05-0203-1", "AI12-0437-1"]} />
<p>The type of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code>, of an object created by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#S0032">object_declaration</a></code> or an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code>, or of a generic formal object of mode <b>in</b>, shall not be abstract. The type of the target of an assignment operation (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2">5.2</a>) shall not be abstract. The type of a component shall not be abstract. If the result type of a function is abstract, then the function shall be abstract. If a function has an access result type designating an abstract type, then the function shall be abstract. The type denoted by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5#S0226">return_subtype_indication</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5">6.5</a>) shall not be abstract. A generic function shall not have an abstract result type or an access result type designating an abstract type. <br /></p>

<MarginText>8.a_3.9.3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This ensures that values of an abstract type cannot be created, which ensures that a dispatching call to an abstract subprogram will not try to execute the nonexistent body.<br />

<MarginText>8.b_3.9.3</MarginText>
Generic formal objects of mode <b>in</b> are like constants; therefore they should be forbidden for abstract types. Generic formal objects of mode <b>in out</b> are like renamings; therefore, abstract types are OK for them, though probably not terribly useful.<br />

<MarginText>8.c/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0073-1"]} />
Generic functions returning a formal abstract type are illegal because any instance would have to be instantiated with a nonabstract type in order to avoid violating the function rule (generic functions cannot be declared abstract). But that would be an implied contract; it would be better for the contract to be explicit by the formal type not being declared abstract. Moreover, the implied contract does not add any capability. <br />

<MarginText>9_3.9.3</MarginText>
<p>If a partial view is not abstract, the corresponding full view shall not be abstract. If a generic formal type is abstract, then for each primitive subprogram of the formal that is not abstract, the corresponding primitive subprogram of the actual shall not be abstract. <br /></p>

<MarginText>9.a_3.9.3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>By contrast, we allow the actual type to be nonabstract even if the formal type is declared abstract. Hence, the most general formal tagged type possible is "<b>type</b> T({"<"}{">"}) <b>is abstract tagged limited private</b>;".<br />

<MarginText>9.b_3.9.3</MarginText>
For an abstract private extension declared in the visible part of a package, it is only possible for the full type to be nonabstract if the private extension has no abstract dispatching operations. <br />

<MarginText>9.c/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00294-01"]} />
<b>To be honest: </b>In the sentence about primitive subprograms above, there is some ambiguity as to what is meant by &ldquo;corresponding&rdquo; in the case where an inherited operation is overridden.  This is best explained by an example, where the implicit declarations are shown as comments: <br />

<MarginText>9.d/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package P1 is{"\n"}   type T1 is abstract tagged null record;{"\n"}   procedure P (X : T1); -- (1){"\n"}end P1;{"\n"}
<MarginText>9.e/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
package P2 is{"\n"}   type T2 is abstract new P1.T1 with null record;{"\n"}   -- procedure P (X : T2); -- (2){"\n"}   procedure P (X : T2) is abstract; -- (3){"\n"}end P2;{"\n"}
<MarginText>9.f/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
generic{"\n"}   type D is abstract new P1.T1 with private;{"\n"}   -- procedure P (X : D); -- (4){"\n"}procedure G (X : D);{"\n"}
<MarginText>9.g/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
procedure I is new G (P2.T2); -- Illegal.{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>9.h/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
Type T2 inherits a nonabstract procedure P (2) from the primitive procedure P (1) of T1. P (2) is overridden by the explicitly declared abstract procedure P (3). Type D inherits a nonabstract procedure P (4) from P (1). In instantiation I, the operation corresponding to P (4) is the one which is not overridden, that is, P (3): the overridden operation P (2) does not &ldquo;reemerge&rdquo;. Therefore, the instantiation is illegal. <br />

<MarginText>10/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0073-1"]} />
<p>For an abstract type declared in a visible part, an abstract primitive subprogram shall not be declared in the private part, unless it is overriding an abstract subprogram implicitly declared in the visible part. For a tagged type declared in a visible part, a primitive function with a controlling result or a controlling access result shall not be declared in the private part, unless it is overriding a function implicitly declared in the visible part. <br /></p>

<MarginText>10.a_3.9.3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The &ldquo;visible part&rdquo; could be that of a package or a generic package. This rule is needed because a nonabstract type extension declared outside the package would not know about any abstract primitive subprograms or primitive functions with controlling results declared in the private part, and wouldn't know that they need to be overridden with nonabstract subprograms. The rule applies to a tagged record type or record extension declared in a visible part, just as to a tagged private type or private extension. The rule applies to explicitly and implicitly declared abstract subprograms: <br />

<MarginText>10.b_3.9.3</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package Pack is{"\n"}    type T is abstract new T1 with private;{"\n"}private{"\n"}    type T is abstract new T2 with record ... end record;{"\n"}    ...{"\n"}end Pack;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>10.c_3.9.3</MarginText>
The above example would be illegal if T1 has a nonabstract primitive procedure P, but T2 overrides P with an abstract one; the private part should override P with a nonabstract version. On the other hand, if the P were abstract for both T1 and T2, the example would be legal as is. <br />

<MarginText>11/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00260-02"]} />
<p>A generic actual subprogram shall not be an abstract subprogram unless the generic formal subprogram is declared by a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6#S0337">formal_abstract_subprogram_declaration</a></code>. The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0100">attribute_reference</a></code> for the Access, Unchecked{"_"}Access, or Address attributes shall not denote an abstract subprogram. <br /></p>

<MarginText>11.a_3.9.3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>An <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0076">abstract_subprogram_declaration</a></code> is not syntactically a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0195">subprogram_declaration</a></code>. Nonetheless, an abstract subprogram is a subprogram, and an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0076">abstract_subprogram_declaration</a></code> is a declaration of a subprogram.<br />

<MarginText>11.b/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00260-02"]} />
The part about generic actual subprograms includes those given by default. Of course, an abstract formal subprogram's actual subprogram can be abstract. <br />

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>11.1/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00348-01"]} />
<p>The elaboration of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0076">abstract_subprogram_declaration</a></code> has no effect. <br /></p>

<MarginText>12/5_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0447-1"]} />
NOTE 1   Abstractness is not inherited; a type is abstract only if the reserved word <b>abstract</b> is used in the declaration of the type extension. <br />

<MarginText>12.a_3.9.3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>A derived type can be abstract even if its parent is not. Similarly, an inherited concrete subprogram can be overridden with an abstract subprogram. <br />

<MarginText>13_3.9.3</MarginText>
NOTE 2   A class-wide type is never abstract. Even if a class is rooted at an abstract type, the class-wide type for the class is not abstract, and an object of the class-wide type can be created; the tag of such an object will identify some nonabstract type in the class. <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>14_3.9.3</MarginText>
<p><i>Example of an abstract type representing a set of natural numbers:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>15_3.9.3</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package Sets is{"\n"}    subtype Element{"_"}Type is Natural;{"\n"}    type Set is abstract tagged null record;{"\n"}    function Empty return Set is abstract;{"\n"}    function Union(Left, Right : Set) return Set is abstract;{"\n"}    function Intersection(Left, Right : Set) return Set is abstract;{"\n"}    function Unit{"_"}Set(Element : Element{"_"}Type) return Set is abstract;{"\n"}    procedure Take(Element : out Element{"_"}Type;{"\n"}                   From : in out Set) is abstract;{"\n"}end Sets;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>16/5_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0442-1", "AI12-0452-1"]} />
<p>Given the above abstract type, one can derive various (nonabstract) extensions of the type, representing alternative implementations of a set. One possibility is to use a bit vector, but impose an upper bound on the largest element representable, while another possible implementation is a hash table, trading off space for flexibility.<br /></p>

<MarginText>17.a_3.9.3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>One way to export a type from a package with some components visible and some components private is as follows: <br />

<MarginText>17.b_3.9.3</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package P is{"\n"}    type Public{"_"}Part is abstract tagged{"\n"}        record{"\n"}            ...{"\n"}        end record;{"\n"}    type T is new Public{"_"}Part with private;{"\n"}    ...{"\n"}private{"\n"}    type T is new Public{"_"}Part with{"\n"}        record{"\n"}            ...{"\n"}        end record;{"\n"}end P;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>17.c_3.9.3</MarginText>
The fact that Public{"_"}Part is abstract tells clients they have to create objects of type T instead of Public{"_"}Part. Note that the public part has to come first; it would be illegal to declare a private type Private{"_"}Part, and then a record extension T of it, unless T were in the private part after the full declaration of Private{"_"}Part, but then clients of the package would not have visibility to T. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 95

<MarginText>17.d/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00391-01"]} />
It is not necessary to override functions with a controlling result for a null extension. This makes it easier to derive a tagged type to complete a private type. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>17.e/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00345-01"]} />
Updated the wording to reflect the addition of interface types (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.4">3.9.4</a>).<br />

<MarginText>17.f/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00260-02"]} />
Updated the wording to reflect the addition of abstract formal subprograms (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.6">12.6</a>).<br />

<MarginText>17.g/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00334-01"]} />
The wording of shall-be-overridden was clarified so that it clearly applies to abstract predefined equality.<br />

<MarginText>17.h/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00348-01"]} />
Moved the syntax and elaboration rule for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0076">abstract_subprogram_declaration</a></code> here, so the syntax and most of the semantics are together (which is consistent with null procedures).<br />

<MarginText>17.i/2_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00391-01"]} />
We define the term <i>require overriding</i> to make other wording easier to understand. <br />

#### Incompatibilities With Ada 2005

<MarginText>17.j/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0073-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Added rules to eliminate holes with controlling access results and generic functions that return abstract types. While these changes are technically incompatible, it is unlikely that they could be used in a program without violating some other rule of the use of abstract types.<br />

<MarginText>17.k/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0097-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Corrected a minor glitch having to do with abstract null extensions. The Ada 2005 rule allowed such extensions to inherit concrete operations in some rare cases. It is unlikely that these cases exist in user code. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 2005

<MarginText>17.l/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0183-1"]} />
An optional <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#S0346">aspect_specification</a></code> can be used in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0076">abstract_subprogram_declaration</a></code>. This is described in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.1#Subclause_13.1.1">13.1.1</a>. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>17.m/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0198-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Clarified that the predefined operator corresponding to an inherited abstract operator is also abstract. The Ada 2005 rules caused the predefined operator and the inherited operator to override each other, which is weird. But the effect is the same either way (the operator is not considered for resolution).<br />

<MarginText>17.n/3_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0203-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Added wording to disallow abstract return objects. These were illegal in Ada 2005 by other rules; the extension to support class-wide type better opened a hole which has now been plugged. <br />

#### Incompatibilities With Ada 2012

<MarginText>17.o/5_3.9.3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0413-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Clarified that a recheck is needed in the case of an actual that is a record type with an abstract equality. This is an incompatibility as the generic boilerplate was previously omitted, meaning that such a recheck should not have been performed in the private part of an instance. Usually, this would just change an elaboration time raise of Program{"_"}Error into an error (a good thing, as the instance will never be useful), but could break a working instance if the equality usage is in a default expression that appears in the private part of the generic unit and it is never used in a call. In that case, Ada 2022 will reject the instance while it would have worked in Ada 2012. As a practical matter, it's more likely that a compiler already does the recheck in the entire instance spec, or does not do it at all; thus for many implementations there will be no practical incompatibility. <br />

<a id="Subclause_3.9.4"></a>

## 3.9.4  Interface Types

<MarginText>1/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00345-01"]} />
<p>[An interface type is an abstract tagged type that provides a restricted form of multiple inheritance. A tagged type, task type, or protected type may have one or more interface types as ancestors.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>1.a/5_3.9.4</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>interface type</b> &mdash; abstract tagged type that has no components or concrete operations except possibly null procedures<br />Note: Interface types are used for composing other interfaces and tagged types and thereby provide multiple inheritance. Only an interface type can be used as a progenitor of another type.<br />

#### Language Design Principles

<MarginText>1.b/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00345-01"]} />
The rules are designed so that an interface can be used as either a parent type or a progenitor type without changing the meaning. That's important so that the order that interfaces are specified in a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#S0035">derived_type_definition</a></code> is not significant. In particular, we want: <br />

<MarginText>1.c/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type Con1 is new Int1 and Int2 with null record;{"\n"}type Con2 is new Int2 and Int1 with null record;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>1.d/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
to mean exactly the same thing. <br />

#### Syntax

<MarginText>2/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00345-01"]} />

<CodeBlock>
<code>interface{"_"}type{"_"}definition</code><a id="S0077"></a><code> ::= </code><br />    [<b>limited</b> | <b>task</b> | <b>protected</b> | <b>synchronized</b>] <b>interface</b> [<b>and</b> <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0078">interface_list</a></code>]<br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00419-01"]} />

<CodeBlock>
<code>interface{"_"}list</code><a id="S0078"></a><code> ::= </code><i>interface{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code> {"{"}<b>and</b> <i>interface{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code>{"}"}<br />

</CodeBlock>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>4/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01"]} />
<p>An interface type (also called an <i>interface</i>) is a specific abstract tagged type that is defined by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0077">interface_type_definition</a></code>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>5/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01"]} />
<p>An interface with the reserved word <b>limited</b>, <b>task</b>, <b>protected</b>, or <b>synchronized</b> in its definition is termed, respectively, a <i>limited interface</i>, a <i>task interface</i>, a <i>protected interface</i>, or a <i>synchronized interface</i>. In addition, all task and protected interfaces are synchronized interfaces, and all synchronized interfaces are limited interfaces. <br /></p>

<MarginText>5.a/5_3.9.4</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>synchronized</b> &mdash; can be safely operated on by multiple tasks concurrently<br />Note: Synchronized is used to qualify entities, as in a synchronized interface.<br />

<MarginText>6/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01", "AI95-00443-01"]} />
<p>[A task or protected type derived from an interface is a tagged type.] Such a tagged type is called a <i>synchronized</i> tagged type, as are synchronized interfaces and private extensions whose declaration includes the reserved word <b>synchronized</b>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>6.a/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>The full definition of tagged types given in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9">3.9</a> includes task and protected types derived from interfaces. <br />

<MarginText>6.b/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The class-wide type associated with a tagged task type (including a task interface type) is a task type, because &ldquo;task&rdquo; is one of the language-defined classes of types (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2">3.2</a>). However, the class-wide type associated with an interface is <i>not</i> an interface type, as &ldquo;interface&rdquo; is <i>not</i> one of the language-defined classes (as it is not closed under derivation). In this sense, &ldquo;interface&rdquo; is similar to &ldquo;abstract&rdquo;. The class-wide type associated with an interface is a concrete (nonabstract) indefinite tagged composite type.<br />

<MarginText>6.c/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
&ldquo;Private extension&rdquo; includes generic formal private extensions, as explained in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.5#Subclause_12.5.1">12.5.1</a>. <br />

<MarginText>7/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01"]} />
<p>A task interface is an [abstract] task type. A protected interface is an [abstract] protected type. <br /></p>

<MarginText>7.a/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>The &ldquo;abstract&rdquo; follows from the definition of an interface type. <br />

<MarginText>7.b/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This ensures that task operations (like abort and the Terminated attribute) can be applied to a task interface type and the associated class-wide type. While there are no protected type operations, we apply the same rule to protected interfaces for consistency. <br />

<MarginText>8/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01"]} />
<p>[An interface type has no components.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>8.a/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>This follows from the syntax and the fact that discriminants are not allowed for interface types. <br />

<MarginText>9/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01"]} />
<p>An <i>interface{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code> in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0078">interface_list</a></code> names a <i>progenitor subtype</i>; its type is the <i>progenitor type</i>. An interface type inherits user-defined primitive subprograms from each progenitor type in the same way that a derived type inherits user-defined primitive subprograms from its progenitor types (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4">3.4</a>). <br /></p>

<MarginText>9.a/5_3.9.4</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>progenitor</b> &mdash; type given in the interface list, if any, of an interface, task, protected, or derived type definition<br />Note: A progenitor is always an interface type.<br />

#### Legality Rules

<MarginText>10/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01"]} />
<p>All user-defined primitive subprograms of an interface type shall be abstract subprograms or null procedures.<br /></p>

<MarginText>11/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01"]} />
<p>The type of a subtype named in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0078">interface_list</a></code> shall be an interface type.<br /></p>

<MarginText>12/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00345-01"]} />
<p>A type derived from a nonlimited interface shall be nonlimited.<br /></p>

<MarginText>13/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01"]} />
<p>An interface derived from a task interface shall include the reserved word <b>task</b> in its definition; any other type derived from a task interface shall be a private extension or a task type declared by a task declaration (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.1">9.1</a>).<br /></p>

<MarginText>14/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01"]} />
<p>An interface derived from a protected interface shall include the reserved word <b>protected</b> in its definition; any other type derived from a protected interface shall be a private extension or a protected type declared by a protected declaration (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.4">9.4</a>).<br /></p>

<MarginText>15/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01"]} />
<p>An interface derived from a synchronized interface shall include one of the reserved words <b>task</b>, <b>protected</b>, or <b>synchronized</b> in its definition; any other type derived from a synchronized interface shall be a private extension, a task type declared by a task declaration, or a protected type declared by a protected declaration.<br /></p>

<MarginText>15.a/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We require that an interface descendant of a task, protected, or synchronized interface repeat the explicit kind of interface it will be, rather than simply inheriting it, so that a reader is always aware of whether the interface provides synchronization and whether it may be implemented only by a task or protected type. The only place where inheritance of the kind of interface might be useful would be in a generic if you didn't know the kind of the actual interface. However, the value of that is low because you cannot implement an interface properly if you don't know whether it is a task, protected, or synchronized interface. Hence, we require the kind of the actual interface to match the kind of the formal interface (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.5#Subclause_12.5.5">12.5.5</a>). <br />

<MarginText>16/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00345-01"]} />
<p>No type shall be derived from both a task interface and a protected interface.<br /></p>

<MarginText>16.a_3.9.4</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This prevents a single private extension from inheriting from both a task and a protected interface. For a private type, there can be no legal completion. For a generic formal derived type, there can be no possible matching type (so no instantiation could be legal). This rule provides early detection of the errors. <br />

<MarginText>17/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01"]} />
<p>In addition to the places where Legality Rules normally apply (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.3">12.3</a>), these rules apply also in the private part of an instance of a generic unit. <br /></p>

<MarginText>17.a/3_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>This paragraph is intended to apply to all of the Legality Rules in this subclause. We cannot allow interface types which do not obey these rules, anywhere. Luckily, deriving from a formal type (which might be an interface) is not allowed for any tagged types in a generic body. So checking in the private part of a generic covers all of the cases. <br />

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>18/3_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI05-0070-1"]} />
<p>The elaboration of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0077">interface_type_definition</a></code> creates the interface type and its first subtype. <br /></p>

<MarginText>18.a/3_3.9.4</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>There is no other effect. An <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0078">interface_list</a></code> is made up of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code>s, which do not need to be elaborated, so the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0078">interface_list</a></code> does not either. This is consistent with the handling of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0059">discriminant_part</a></code>s. <br />

<MarginText>19/5_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00411-01", "AI12-0440-1"]} />
NOTE   Nonlimited interface types have predefined nonabstract equality operators. These can be overridden with user-defined abstract equality operators. Such operators will then require an explicit overriding for any nonabstract descendant of the interface. <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>20/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00433-01"]} />
<p><i>Example of a limited interface and a synchronized interface extending it:</i><br /></p>

<MarginText>21/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type Queue is limited interface;{"\n"}procedure Append(Q : in out Queue; Person : in Person{"_"}Name) is abstract;{"\n"}procedure Remove{"_"}First(Q      : in out Queue;{"\n"}                       Person :    out Person{"_"}Name) is abstract;{"\n"}function Cur{"_"}Count(Q : in Queue) return Natural is abstract;{"\n"}function Max{"_"}Count(Q : in Queue) return Natural is abstract;{"\n"}-- See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#Subclause_3.10.1">3.10.1</a> for Person{"_"}Name.{"\n"}
<MarginText>22/3_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0004-1"]} />
Queue{"_"}Error : exception;{"\n"}-- Append raises Queue{"_"}Error if Cur{"_"}Count(Q) = Max{"_"}Count(Q){"\n"}-- Remove{"_"}First raises Queue{"_"}Error if Cur{"_"}Count(Q) = 0{"\n"}
<MarginText>23/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
type Synchronized{"_"}Queue is{"\n"}                      synchronized interface and Queue; -- see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.11">9.11</a>{"\n"}procedure Append{"_"}Wait(Q      : in out Synchronized{"_"}Queue;{"\n"}                      Person : in     Person{"_"}Name) is abstract;{"\n"}procedure Remove{"_"}First{"_"}Wait(Q      : in out Synchronized{"_"}Queue;{"\n"}                            Person :    out Person{"_"}Name) is abstract;{"\n"}
<MarginText>24/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
...{"\n"}
<MarginText>25/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
procedure Transfer(From   : in out Queue'Class;{"\n"}                   To     : in out Queue'Class;{"\n"}                   Number : in     Natural := 1) is{"\n"}   Person : Person{"_"}Name;{"\n"}begin{"\n"}   for I in 1..Number loop{"\n"}      Remove{"_"}First(From, Person);{"\n"}      Append(To, Person);{"\n"}   end loop;{"\n"}end Transfer;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>26/5_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0442-1"]} />
<p>This defines a Queue interface defining a queue of people. (A similar design is possible to define any kind of queue simply by replacing Person{"_"}Name by an appropriate type.) The Queue interface has four dispatching operations, Append, Remove{"_"}First, Cur{"_"}Count, and Max{"_"}Count. The body of a class-wide operation, Transfer is also shown. Every nonabstract extension of Queue will provide implementations for at least its four dispatching operations, as they are abstract. Any object of a type derived from Queue can be passed to Transfer as either the From or the To operand. The two operands can be of different types in a given call.<br /></p>

<MarginText>27/5_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0440-1"]} />
<p>The Synchronized{"_"}Queue interface inherits the four dispatching operations from Queue and adds two additional dispatching operations, which wait if necessary rather than raising the Queue{"_"}Error exception. This synchronized interface can only be implemented by a task or protected type, and as such ensures safe concurrent access.<br /></p>

<MarginText>28/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00433-01"]} />
<p><i>Example use of the interface:</i><br /></p>

<MarginText>29/3_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0004-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type Fast{"_"}Food{"_"}Queue is new Queue with record ...;{"\n"}procedure Append(Q : in out Fast{"_"}Food{"_"}Queue; Person : in Person{"_"}Name);{"\n"}procedure Remove{"_"}First(Q : in out Fast{"_"}Food{"_"}Queue; {"\n"}                       Person : out Person{"_"}Name);{"\n"}function Cur{"_"}Count(Q : in Fast{"_"}Food{"_"}Queue) return Natural;{"\n"}function Max{"_"}Count(Q : in Fast{"_"}Food{"_"}Queue) return Natural;{"\n"}
<MarginText>30/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
...{"\n"}
<MarginText>31/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
Cashier, Counter : Fast{"_"}Food{"_"}Queue;{"\n"}
<MarginText>32/5_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0312-1"]} />
...{"\n"}-- Add Casey (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#Subclause_3.10.1">3.10.1</a>) to the cashier's queue:{"\n"}Append (Cashier, Casey);{"\n"}-- After payment, move Casey to the sandwich counter queue:{"\n"}Transfer (Cashier, Counter);{"\n"}...{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>33/5_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0442-1"]} />
<p>An interface such as Queue can be used directly as the parent of a new type (as shown here), or can be used as a progenitor when a type is derived. In either case, the primitive operations of the interface are inherited. For Queue, the implementation of the four inherited routines will necessarily be provided. Inside the call of Transfer, calls will dispatch to the implementations of Append and Remove{"_"}First for type Fast{"_"}Food{"_"}Queue.<br /></p>

<MarginText>34/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00433-01"]} />
<p><i>Example of a task interface:</i><br /></p>

<MarginText>35/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type Serial{"_"}Device is task interface;  -- see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.1">9.1</a>{"\n"}procedure Read (Dev : in Serial{"_"}Device; C : out Character) is abstract;{"\n"}procedure Write(Dev : in Serial{"_"}Device; C : in  Character) is abstract;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>36/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<p>The Serial{"_"}Device interface has two dispatching operations which are intended to be implemented by task entries (see 9.1).<br /></p>

#### Extensions to Ada 95

<MarginText>36.a/2_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01", "AI95-00345-01"]} />
Interface types are new. They provide multiple inheritance of interfaces, similar to the facility provided in Java and other recent language designs. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>36.b/3_3.9.4</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0070-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Corrected the definition of elaboration for an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#S0077">interface_type_definition</a></code> to match that of other type definitions. <br />

# 3. Declarations and Types

<MarginText>1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
<p>This clause describes the types in the language and the rules for declaring constants, variables, and named numbers. <br /></p>

# 4.1. Names

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1.mdx

sidebar_position:  31

# 4.1. Names

<MarginText>1</MarginText>
<p>[<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">Name</a></code>s can denote declared entities, whether declared explicitly or implicitly (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.1">3.1</a>). <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">Name</a></code>s can also denote objects or subprograms designated by access values; the results of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6#S0162">type_conversion</a></code>s or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#S0218">function_call</a></code>s; subcomponents and slices of objects and values; protected subprograms, single entries, entry families, and entries in families of entries. Finally, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>s can denote attributes of any of the foregoing.] <br /></p>

#### Syntax

<MarginText>2/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0003-1", "AI05-0139-2", "AI12-0125-3"]} />

<CodeBlock>
<code>name</code><a id="S0091"></a><code> ::= </code><br />     <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0092">direct_name</a></code>	| <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0094">explicit_dereference</a></code><br />   | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0096">indexed_component</a></code>	| <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0097">slice</a></code><br />   | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0098">selected_component</a></code>	| <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0100">attribute_reference</a></code><br />   | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6#S0162">type_conversion</a></code>	| <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#S0218">function_call</a></code><br />   | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code>	| <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code><br />   | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0104">generalized_reference</a></code>	| <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0105">generalized_indexing</a></code><br />   | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0174">target_name</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>direct{"_"}name</code><a id="S0092"></a><code> ::= </code><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.3#S0002">identifier</a></code> | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0202">operator_symbol</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>3.a/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code> is no longer a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0092">direct_name</a></code>. <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code>s are usable even when the corresponding enumeration type declaration is not visible. See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.2">4.2</a>. <br />

<MarginText>4</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>prefix</code><a id="S0093"></a><code> ::= </code><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> | <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0095">implicit_dereference</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>5</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>explicit{"_"}dereference</code><a id="S0094"></a><code> ::= </code><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>.<b>all</b><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>6</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>implicit{"_"}dereference</code><a id="S0095"></a><code> ::= </code><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code><br />

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>7/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0004-1"]} />
<p>[Certain forms of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> (<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0096">indexed_component</a></code>s, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0098">selected_component</a></code>s, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0097">slice</a></code>s, and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0100">attribute_reference</a></code>s) include a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> that is either itself a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> that denotes some related entity, or an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0095">implicit_dereference</a></code> of an access value that designates some related entity.] <br /></p>

#### Name Resolution Rules

<MarginText>8</MarginText>
<p>The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> in a <i>dereference</i> (either an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0095">implicit_dereference</a></code> or an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0094">explicit_dereference</a></code>) is expected to be of any access type. <br /></p>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>9/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0008-1"]} />
<p>If the type of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> in a dereference is some access-to-object type <i>T</i>, then the dereference denotes a view of an object, the <i>nominal subtype</i> of the view being the designated subtype of <i>T</i>. If the designated subtype has unconstrained discriminants, the (actual) subtype of the view is constrained by the values of the discriminants of the designated object, except when there is a partial view of the type of the designated subtype that does not have discriminants, in which case the dereference is not constrained by its discriminant values. <br /></p>

<MarginText>9.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>If the value of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> is the result of an access type conversion, the dereference denotes a view created as part of the conversion. The nominal subtype of the view is not necessarily the same as that used to create the designated object. See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6">4.6</a>. <br />

<MarginText>9.b</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>We sometimes refer to the nominal subtype of a particular kind of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> rather than the nominal subtype of the view denoted by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> (presuming the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> denotes a view of an object). These two uses of nominal subtype are intended to mean the same thing. <br />

<MarginText>9.c/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0008-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The last sentence was not present in Ada 95; it is necessary in Ada 2005 because general access types can designate unconstrained objects, which was not possible in Ada 95. Thus, the rules that had this effect in Ada 95 (the object being constrained by its initial value) don't work in Ada 2005 and we have to say this explicitly.<br />

<MarginText>9.d/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0008-1"]} />
The &ldquo;except&rdquo; part of the last sentence prevents privacy &ldquo;breaking&rdquo;, so that if a private type has discriminants only in the full view, they don't interfere with freely interassigning values between objects of the type, even when the objects live in the heap. <br />

<MarginText>9.e/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0008-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>Since we don't depend on whether the designated object is constrained, it is not necessary to include a constrained bit in every object that could be designated by a general access type. <br />

<MarginText>10</MarginText>
<p>If the type of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> in a dereference is some access-to-subprogram type <i>S</i>, then the dereference denotes a view of a subprogram, the <i>profile</i> of the view being the designated profile of <i>S</i>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>10.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>This means that the formal parameter names and default expressions to be used in a call whose <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> is a dereference are those of the designated profile, which need not be the same as those of the subprogram designated by the access value, since 'Access requires only subtype conformance, not full conformance. <br />

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>11/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00415-01"]} />
<p>The evaluation of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> determines the entity denoted by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>. This evaluation has no other effect for a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> that is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0092">direct_name</a></code> or a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.5#S0015">character_literal</a></code>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>12</MarginText>
<p>[The evaluation of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> that has a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> includes the evaluation of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>.] The evaluation of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> consists of the evaluation of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> or the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0095">implicit_dereference</a></code>. The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> denotes the entity denoted by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> or the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0095">implicit_dereference</a></code>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>13</MarginText>
<p>The evaluation of a dereference consists of the evaluation of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> and the determination of the object or subprogram that is designated by the value of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>. A check is made that the value of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> is not the null access value. Constraint{"_"}Error is raised if this check fails. The dereference denotes the object or subprogram designated by the value of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>. <br /></p>

#### Examples

<MarginText>14</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of direct names:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>15</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
Pi      -- the direct name of a number 	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#Subclause_3.3.2">3.3.2</a>){"\n"}Limit   -- the direct name of a constant 	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#Subclause_3.3.1">3.3.1</a>){"\n"}Count   -- the direct name of a scalar variable 	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#Subclause_3.3.1">3.3.1</a>){"\n"}Board   -- the direct name of an array variable 	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6#Subclause_3.6.1">3.6.1</a>){"\n"}Matrix  -- the direct name of a type 	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6">3.6</a>){"\n"}Random  -- the direct name of a function 	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1">6.1</a>){"\n"}Error   -- the direct name of an exception 	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.1">11.1</a>){"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>16</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of dereferences:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>17</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
Next{"_"}Car.all	-- explicit dereference denoting the object designated{"\n"}               	-- by the access variable Next{"_"}Car (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#Subclause_3.10.1">3.10.1</a>){"\n"}Next{"_"}Car.Owner 	-- selected component with implicit dereference;{"\n"}               	-- same as Next{"_"}Car.all.Owner{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>17.a</MarginText>
Type conversions and function calls are now considered names that denote the result of the operation. In the case of a type conversion used as an actual parameter or that is of a tagged type, the type conversion is considered a variable if the operand is a variable. This simplifies the description of "parameters of the form of a type conversion" as well as better supporting an important OOP paradigm that requires the combination of a conversion from a class-wide type to some specific type followed immediately by component selection. Function calls are considered names so that a type conversion of a function call and the function call itself are treated equivalently in the grammar. A function call is considered the name of a constant, and can be used anywhere such a name is permitted. See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5">6.5</a>.<br />

<MarginText>17.b/1</MarginText>
Type conversions of a tagged type are permitted anywhere their operand is permitted. That is, if the operand is a variable, then the type conversion can appear on the left-hand side of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>. If the operand is an object, then the type conversion can appear in an object renaming or as a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>. See <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6">4.6</a>. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>17.c/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01"]} />
Everything of the general syntactic form <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>(...) is now syntactically a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>. In any realistic parser, this would be a necessity since distinguishing among the various <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>(...) constructs inevitably requires name resolution. In cases where the construct yields a value rather than an object, the name denotes a value rather than an object. Names already denote values in Ada 83 with named numbers, components of the result of a function call, etc. This is partly just a wording change, and partly an extension of functionality (see Extensions heading above).<br />

<MarginText>17.d</MarginText>
The syntax rule for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0092">direct_name</a></code> is new. It is used in places where direct visibility is required. It's kind of like Ada 83's <code>simple{"_"}name</code>, but <code>simple{"_"}name</code> applied to both direct visibility and visibility by selection, and furthermore, it didn't work right for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0202">operator_symbol</a></code>s. The syntax rule for <code>simple{"_"}name</code> is removed, since its use is covered by a combination of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0092">direct_name</a></code> and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0099">selector_name</a></code>. The syntactic categories <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0092">direct_name</a></code> and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0099">selector_name</a></code> are similar; it's mainly the visibility rules that distinguish the two. The introduction of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0092">direct_name</a></code> requires the insertion of one new explicit textual rule: to forbid <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.1#S0172">statement_identifier</a></code>s from being <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0202">operator_symbol</a></code>s. This is the only case where the explicit rule is needed, because this is the only case where the declaration of the entity is implicit. For example, there is no need to syntactically forbid (say) &ldquo;X: "Rem";&rdquo;, because it is impossible to declare a type whose name is an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1#S0202">operator_symbol</a></code> in the first place.<br />

<MarginText>17.e/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0005-1"]} />
The syntax rules for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0094">explicit_dereference</a></code> and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0095">implicit_dereference</a></code> are new; this makes other rules simpler, since dereferencing an access value has substantially different semantics from <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0098">selected_component</a></code>s. We also use <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> instead of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> in the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0094">explicit_dereference</a></code> rule since that seems clearer. Note that these rules rely on the fact that function calls are now names, so we don't need to use prefix to allow function calls in front of .<b>all</b>. <br />

<MarginText>17.f</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Actually, it would be reasonable to allow any <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0141">primary</a></code> in front of .<b>all</b>, since only the value is needed, but that would be a bit radical. <br />

<MarginText>17.g</MarginText>
We no longer use the term <i>appropriate for a type</i> since we now describe the semantics of a prefix in terms of implicit dereference. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 2005

<MarginText>17.h/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0003-1"]} />
A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code> is now a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> denoting a constant view; this allows them to be used as a prefix and to be renamed as an object. They are often used to remove ambiguity from function calls, and there may be no other way to do that. Interestingly, a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6#S0162">type_conversion</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code> is already legal in these contexts, so this change mainly reduces clutter by eliminating an otherwise unneeded <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.6#S0162">type_conversion</a></code> from some expressions. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>17.i/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0008-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Added a missing rule so that most dereferences are assumed constrained (without determining whether the designated object is). This is just confirming the Ada 95 rules; Ada 2005 failed to ensure that this property was unchanged.<br />

<MarginText>17.j/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0139-2", "AI05-0299-1"]} />
Added <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0104">generalized_reference</a></code> and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0105">generalized_indexing</a></code> as types of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>; these are documented as extensions in the appropriate subclauses. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2012

<MarginText>17.k/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0125-3"]} />
Added a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0174">target_name</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#Subclause_5.2.1">5.2.1</a>) to the syntax of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code>. <br />

<a id="Subclause_4.1.1"></a>

## 4.1.1  Indexed Components

<MarginText>1_4.1.1</MarginText>
<p>[An <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0096">indexed_component</a></code> denotes either a component of an array or an entry in a family of entries. ]<br /></p>

#### Syntax

<MarginText>2_4.1.1</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>indexed{"_"}component</code><a id="S0096"></a><code> ::= </code><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>(<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> {"{"}, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code>{"}"})<br />

</CodeBlock>

#### Name Resolution Rules

<MarginText>3_4.1.1</MarginText>
<p>The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0096">indexed_component</a></code> with a given number of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code>s shall resolve to denote an array (after any implicit dereference) with the corresponding number of index positions, or shall resolve to denote an entry family of a task or protected object (in which case there shall be only one <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code>).<br /></p>

<MarginText>4_4.1.1</MarginText>
<p>The expected type for each <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> is the corresponding index type.<br /></p>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>5_4.1.1</MarginText>
<p>When the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> denotes an array, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0096">indexed_component</a></code> denotes the component of the array with the specified index value(s). The nominal subtype of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0096">indexed_component</a></code> is the component subtype of the array type. <br /></p>

<MarginText>6_4.1.1</MarginText>
<p>When the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> denotes an entry family, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0096">indexed_component</a></code> denotes the individual entry of the entry family with the specified index value.<br /></p>

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>7_4.1.1</MarginText>
<p>For the evaluation of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0096">indexed_component</a></code>, the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> and the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code>s are evaluated in an arbitrary order. The value of each <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> is converted to the corresponding index type. A check is made that each index value belongs to the corresponding index range of the array or entry family denoted by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>. Constraint{"_"}Error is raised if this check fails.<br /></p>

#### Examples

<MarginText>8_4.1.1</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of indexed components:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>9_4.1.1</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
 My{"_"}Schedule(Sat)  -- a component of a one-dimensional array	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6#Subclause_3.6.1">3.6.1</a>){"\n"} Page(10)          -- a component of a one-dimensional array	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6">3.6</a>){"\n"} Board(M, J + 1)   -- a component of a two-dimensional array	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6#Subclause_3.6.1">3.6.1</a>){"\n"} Page(10)(20)      -- a component of a component	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6">3.6</a>){"\n"} Request(Medium)   -- an entry in a family of entries	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.1">9.1</a>){"\n"} Next{"_"}Frame(L)(M, N) -- a component of a function call	(see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.1">6.1</a>){"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>10/5_4.1.1</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0452-1"]} />
<p>Distinct notations are used for components of multidimensional arrays (such as Board) and arrays of arrays (such as Page). The components of an array of arrays are arrays and can therefore be indexed. Thus Page(10)(20) denotes the 20th component of Page(10). In the last example Next{"_"}Frame(L) is a function call returning an access value that designates a two-dimensional array.<br /></p>

<a id="Subclause_4.1.2"></a>

## 4.1.2  Slices

<MarginText>1_4.1.2</MarginText>
<p>[ A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0097">slice</a></code> denotes a one-dimensional array formed by a sequence of consecutive components of a one-dimensional array. A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0097">slice</a></code> of a variable is a variable; a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0097">slice</a></code> of a constant is a constant;] a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0097">slice</a></code> of a value is a value. <br /></p>

#### Syntax

<MarginText>2_4.1.2</MarginText>

<CodeBlock>
<code>slice</code><a id="S0097"></a><code> ::= </code><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>(<code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6#S0058">discrete_range</a></code>)<br />

</CodeBlock>

#### Name Resolution Rules

<MarginText>3_4.1.2</MarginText>
<p>The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0097">slice</a></code> shall resolve to denote a one-dimensional array (after any implicit dereference).<br /></p>

<MarginText>4_4.1.2</MarginText>
<p>The expected type for the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6#S0058">discrete_range</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0097">slice</a></code> is the index type of the array type. <br /></p>

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>5_4.1.2</MarginText>
<p>A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0097">slice</a></code> denotes a one-dimensional array formed by the sequence of consecutive components of the array denoted by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>, corresponding to the range of values of the index given by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6#S0058">discrete_range</a></code>.<br /></p>

<MarginText>6_4.1.2</MarginText>
<p>The type of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0097">slice</a></code> is that of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0093">prefix</a></code>. Its bounds are those defined by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6#S0058">discrete_range</a></code>.<br /></p>

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>7_4.1.2</MarginText>
