# 7.4. Deferred Constants

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.4.mdx

sidebar_position:  63

# 7.4. Deferred Constants

<MarginText>1</MarginText>
<p>[Deferred constant declarations may be used to declare constants in the visible part of a package, but with the value of the constant given in the private part. They may also be used to declare constants imported from other languages (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-B/">Annex B</a>).] <br /></p>

#### Legality Rules

<MarginText>2/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1", "AI05-0269-1"]} />
<p>[ A <i>deferred constant declaration</i> is an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#S0032">object_declaration</a></code> with the reserved word <b>constant</b> but no initialization expression.] The constant declared by a deferred constant declaration is called a <i>deferred constant</i>. [Unless the Import aspect (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-B/AA-B.1">B.1</a>) is True for a deferred constant declaration, the] deferred constant declaration requires a completion, which shall be a full constant declaration (called the <i>full declaration</i> of the deferred constant). <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>The first sentence is redundant, as it is stated officially in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#Subclause_3.3.1">3.3.1</a>.<br />

<MarginText>2.b/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1", "AI05-0269-1"]} />
The first part of the last sentence is redundant, as no imported entity may have a completion, as stated in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-B/AA-B.1">B.1</a>. <br />

<MarginText>3</MarginText>
<p>A deferred constant declaration that is completed by a full constant declaration shall occur immediately within the visible part of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0230">package_specification</a></code>. For this case, the following additional rules apply to the corresponding full declaration: <br /></p>

<MarginText>4</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>The full declaration shall occur immediately within the private part of the same package;<br /></li>
<MarginText>5/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00385-01"]} />
<li>The deferred and full constants shall have the same type, or shall have statically matching anonymous access subtypes; <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>5.a/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00385-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>This implies that both the deferred declaration and the full declaration have to have a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0084">access_definition</a></code> rather than an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6#S0051">array_type_definition</a></code>, because each <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6#S0051">array_type_definition</a></code> would define a new type. <br />

<MarginText>6/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00385-01", "AI05-0062-1", "AI05-0262-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>If the deferred constant declaration includes a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> <i>S</i> that defines a constrained subtype, then the constraint defined by the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> in the full declaration shall match the constraint defined by <i>S</i> statically.[ On the other hand, if the subtype of the deferred constant is unconstrained, then the full declaration is still allowed to impose a constraint. The constant itself will be constrained, like all constants;]<br /></li>
<MarginText>7/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00231-01"]} />
<li>If the deferred constant declaration includes the reserved word <b>aliased</b>, then the full declaration shall also; <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>7.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>On the other hand, the full constant can be aliased even if the deferred constant is not. <br />

<MarginText>7.1/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00231-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>If the subtype of the deferred constant declaration excludes null, the subtype of the full declaration shall also exclude null. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>7.a.1/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>On the other hand, the full constant can exclude null even if the deferred constant does not. But that can only happen for a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code>, as anonymous access types are required to statically match (which includes any <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0083">null_exclusion</a></code>). <br />

<MarginText>8/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1", "AI12-0444-1"]} />
<p>[A deferred constant declaration for which the Import aspect is True can appear anywhere that an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#S0032">object_declaration</a></code> is allowed, and has no full constant declaration.]<br /></p>

<MarginText>9/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00256-01"]} />
<p>The completion of a deferred constant declaration shall occur before the constant is frozen (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.14">13.14</a>).<br /></p>

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>10/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0004-1"]} />
<p>The elaboration of a deferred constant declaration elaborates the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code>, <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0084">access_definition</a></code>, or (only allowed in the case of an imported constant) the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.6#S0051">array_type_definition</a></code>. <br /></p>

<MarginText>10.a/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0004-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>For nonimported constants, these elaborations cannot require any code or checks for a legal program, because the given <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0027">subtype_indication</a></code> has to be indefinite or statically match that of the full constant, meaning that either it is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code> or it has static constraints. If the deferred constant instead has an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0084">access_definition</a></code>, the designated subtype must be a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code>. We still say that these are elaborated, however, because part of elaboration is creating the type, which is clearly needed for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0084">access_definition</a></code>s. (A deferred constant and its full constant have different types when they are specified by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#S0084">access_definition</a></code>, although there is no visible effect of these types being different as neither can be named.) <br />

<MarginText>11</MarginText>
NOTE   The full constant declaration for a deferred constant that is of a given private type or private extension is not allowed before the corresponding <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0024">full_type_declaration</a></code>. This is a consequence of the freezing rules for types (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-13/AA-13.14">13.14</a>). <br />

<MarginText>11.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Multiple or single declarations are allowed for the deferred and the full declarations, provided that the equivalent single declarations would be allowed.<br />

<MarginText>11.b</MarginText>
Deferred constant declarations are useful for declaring constants of private views, and types with components of private views. They are also useful for declaring access-to-constant objects that designate variables declared in the private part of a package. <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>12</MarginText>
<p><i>Examples of deferred constant declarations:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>13</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
Null{"_"}Key : constant Key;      -- see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3#Subclause_7.3.1">7.3.1</a>{"\n"}
<MarginText>14/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0229-1"]} />
CPU{"_"}Identifier : constant String(1..8){"\n"}   with Import ={">"} True, Convention ={">"} Assembler, Link{"_"}Name ={">"} "CPU{"_"}ID";{"\n"}                              -- see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-B/AA-B.1">B.1</a>{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>14.a</MarginText>
In Ada 83, a deferred constant is required to be of a private type declared in the same visible part. This restriction is removed for Ada 95; deferred constants can be of any type.<br />

<MarginText>14.b</MarginText>
In Ada 83, a deferred constant declaration was not permitted to include a constraint, nor the reserved word <b>aliased</b>.<br />

<MarginText>14.c</MarginText>
In Ada 83, the rules required conformance of type marks; here we require static matching of subtypes if the deferred constant is constrained.<br />

<MarginText>14.d</MarginText>
A deferred constant declaration can be completed with a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-2/AA-2.8#S0019">pragma</a></code> Import. Such a deferred constant declaration need not be within a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1#S0230">package_specification</a></code>.<br />

<MarginText>14.e</MarginText>
The rules for too-early uses of deferred constants are modified in Ada 95 to allow more cases, and catch all errors at compile time. This change is necessary in order to allow deferred constants of a tagged type without violating the principle that for a dispatching call, there is always an implementation to dispatch to. It has the beneficial side effect of catching some Ada-83-erroneous programs at compile time. The new rule fits in well with the new freezing-point rules. Furthermore, we are trying to convert undefined-value problems into bounded errors, and we were having trouble for the case of deferred constants. Furthermore, uninitialized deferred constants cause trouble for the shared variable / tasking rules, since they are really variable, even though they purport to be constant. In Ada 95, they cannot be touched until they become constant.<br />

<MarginText>14.f</MarginText>
Note that we do not consider this change to be an upward incompatibility, because it merely changes an erroneous execution in Ada 83 into a compile-time error.<br />

<MarginText>14.g</MarginText>
The Ada 83 semantics are unclear in the case where the full view turns out to be an access type. It is a goal of the language design to prevent uninitialized access objects. One wonders if the implementation is required to initialize the deferred constant to null, and then initialize it (again!) to its real value. In Ada 95, the problem goes away. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>14.h/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
Since deferred constants can now be of a nonprivate type, we have made this a stand-alone subclause, rather than a subclause of <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3">7.3</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3">Private Types and Private Extensions</a>&rdquo;.<br />

<MarginText>14.i</MarginText>
Deferred constant declarations used to have their own syntax, but now they are simply a special case of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#S0032">object_declaration</a></code>s. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 95

<MarginText>14.j/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00385-01"]} />
Deferred constants were enhanced to allow the use of anonymous access types in them. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>14.k/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00231-01"]} />
Added matching rules for subtypes that exclude null. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>14.l/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0062-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Corrected rules so that the intent that a full constant may have a null exclusion even if the deferred constant does not is actually met. <br />

---

# 7.5. Limited Types

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.5.mdx

sidebar_position:  64

# 7.5. Limited Types

<MarginText>1/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00287-01"]} />
<p>[A limited type is (a view of) a type for which copying (such as for an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>) is not allowed. A nonlimited type is a (view of a) type for which copying is allowed.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>1.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>The concept of the <i>value</i> of a limited type is difficult to define, since the abstract value of a limited type often extends beyond its physical representation. In some sense, values of a limited type cannot be divorced from their object. The value <i>is</i> the object.<br />

<MarginText>1.b/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00318-02"]} />
In Ada 83, in the two places where limited types were defined by the language, namely tasks and files, an implicit level of indirection was implied by the semantics to avoid the separation of the value from an associated object. In Ada 95, most limited types are passed by reference, and even return-ed by reference. In Ada 2005, most limited types are built-in-place upon return, rather than returned by reference. Thus the object &ldquo;identity&rdquo; is part of the logical value of most limited types. <br />

<MarginText>1.c/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00287-01", "AI95-00419-01"]} />
<b>To be honest: </b>For a limited partial view whose full view is nonlimited, copying is possible on parameter passing and function return. To prevent any copying whatsoever, one should make both the partial <i>and</i> full views limited. <br />

<MarginText>1.d/5</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>limited type</b> &mdash; type for which copying (such as in an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>) is not allowed<br />Note: All types are either limited types or nonlimited types.<br />

<MarginText>1.e/5</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>nonlimited type</b> &mdash; type for which copying is allowed<br />

#### Legality Rules

<MarginText>2/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01"]} />
<p>If a tagged record type has any limited components, then the reserved word <b>limited</b> shall appear in its <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.8#S0066">record_type_definition</a></code>. [If the reserved word <b>limited</b> appears in the definition of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4#S0035">derived_type_definition</a></code>, its parent type and any progenitor interfaces shall be limited.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.a.1/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01", "AI12-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="proof">
<b></b>The rule about the parent type being required to be limited can be found in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4">3.4</a>. Rules about progenitor interfaces can be found in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.4">3.9.4</a>; specifically, a nonlimited interface can appear only on a nonlimited type. We repeat these rules here to gather these scattered rules in one obvious place. <br />

<MarginText>2.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This prevents tagged limited types from becoming nonlimited. Otherwise, the following could happen: <br />

<MarginText>2.b</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package P is{"\n"}    type T is limited private;{"\n"}    type R is tagged{"\n"}        record -- Illegal!{"\n"}               -- This should say &ldquo;limited record&rdquo;.{"\n"}            X : T;{"\n"}        end record;{"\n"}private{"\n"}    type T is new Integer; -- R becomes nonlimited here.{"\n"}end P;{"\n"}
<MarginText>2.c/2</MarginText>
package Q is{"\n"}    type R2 is new R with{"\n"}        record{"\n"}            Y : Some{"_"}Task{"_"}Type;{"\n"}        end record;{"\n"}end Q;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>2.d/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00230-01"]} />
If the above were legal, then assignment would be defined for R'Class in the body of P, which is bad news, given the task. <br />

<MarginText>2.1/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00287-01", "AI95-00318-02", "AI05-0147-1", "AI12-0172-1", "AI12-0236-1", "AI12-0317-1"]} />
<p>In the following contexts, an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> of a limited type is permitted only if each of its operative constituents is newly constructed (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4">4.4</a>): <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.2/2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>the initialization <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#S0032">object_declaration</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#Subclause_3.3.1">3.3.1</a>)<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.3/2</MarginText>
<li>the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0063">default_expression</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.8#S0070">component_declaration</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.8">3.8</a>)<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.4/2</MarginText>
<li>the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0109">record_component_association</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#Subclause_4.3.1">4.3.1</a>)<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.5/2</MarginText>
<li>the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> for an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0112">ancestor_part</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0111">extension_aggregate</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#Subclause_4.3.2">4.3.2</a>)<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.6/2</MarginText>
<li>an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0114">positional_array_aggregate</a></code> or the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0118">array_component_association</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#Subclause_4.3.3">4.3.3</a>)<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.7/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0127-1"]} />
<li>the <i>base{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0121">record_delta_aggregate</a></code> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#Subclause_4.3.4">4.3.4</a>) <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>2.d.1/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0127-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>We don't need to mention the <i>base{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0122">array_delta_aggregate</a></code> here, as its type cannot be limited (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#Subclause_4.3.4">4.3.4</a>), and thus neither can its <i>base{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code>. Similarly, we do not need any rules for components of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0120">delta_aggregate</a></code> nor the elements of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0123">container_aggregate</a></code>, as neither are allowed to be limited (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#Subclause_4.3.4">4.3.4</a> and <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#Subclause_4.3.5">4.3.5</a>) <br />

<MarginText>2.8/5</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.7#S0163">qualified_expression</a></code> of an initialized allocator (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8">4.8</a>)<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.9/5</MarginText>
<li>the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> of a return statement (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5">6.5</a>)<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.10/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0177-1", "AI12-0157-1"]} />
<li>the return expression of an expression function (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.8">6.8</a>)<br /></li>
<MarginText>2.11/5</MarginText>
<li>the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0063">default_expression</a></code> or actual parameter for a formal object of mode <b>in</b> (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-12/AA-12.4">12.4</a>)<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>2.e/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>All of these contexts normally require copying; by restricting the uses as above, we can require the new object to be built-in-place. <br />

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>3/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01", "AI05-0178-1"]} />
<p>A view of a type is <i>limited</i> if it is one of the following: <br /></p>

<MarginText>4/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00411-01", "AI95-00419-01"]} />
<ul>
<li>a type with the reserved word <b>limited</b>, <b>synchronized</b>, <b>task</b>, or <b>protected</b> in its definition; <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>4.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Note that there is always a &ldquo;definition&rdquo;, conceptually, even if there is no syntactic category called &ldquo;...{"_"}definition&rdquo;.<br />

<MarginText>4.b/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01"]} />
This includes interfaces of the above kinds, derived types with the reserved word <b>limited</b>, as well as task and protected types. <br />

<MarginText>5/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01", "AI05-0087-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>a class-wide type whose specific type is limited;<br /></li>
<MarginText>6/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01"]} />
<li>a composite type with a limited component;<br /></li>
<MarginText>6.1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0178-1"]} />
<li>an incomplete view;<br /></li>
<MarginText>6.2/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01"]} />
<li>a derived type whose parent is limited and is not an interface.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>6.a/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Limitedness is not inherited from interfaces; it must be explicitly specified when the parent is an interface. <br />

<MarginText>6.b/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01"]} />
<b>To be honest: </b>A derived type can become nonlimited if <b>limited</b> does not appear and the derivation takes place in the visible part of a child package, and the parent type is nonlimited as viewed from the private part or body of the child package. <br />

<MarginText>6.c/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We considered a rule where limitedness was always inherited from the parent for derived types, but in the case of a type whose parent is an interface, this meant that the first interface is treated differently than other interfaces. It also would have forced users to declare dummy nonlimited interfaces just to get the limitedness right. We also considered a syntax like <b>not limited</b> to specify nonlimitedness when the parent was limited, but that was unsavory. The rule given is more uniform and simpler to understand.<br />

<MarginText>6.d/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00419-01"]} />
The rules for interfaces are asymmetrical, but the language is not: if the parent interface is limited, the presence of the word <b>limited</b> determines the limitedness, and nonlimited progenitors are illegal by the rules in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.9#Subclause_3.9.4">3.9.4</a> if <b>limited</b> is present. If the parent interface is nonlimited, the word <b>limited</b> is illegal by the rules in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.4">3.4</a>. The net effect is that the order of the interfaces doesn't matter. <br />

<MarginText>7</MarginText>
<p>Otherwise, the type is nonlimited.<br /></p>

<MarginText>8</MarginText>
<p>[There are no predefined equality operators for a limited type.]<br /></p>

<MarginText>8.1/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0052-1"]} />
<p>A type is <i>immutably limited</i> if it is one of the following:<br /></p>

<MarginText>8.2/3</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>An explicitly limited record type;<br /></li>
<MarginText>8.3/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0217-1"]} />
<li>A record extension with the reserved word <b>limited</b>;<br /></li>
<MarginText>8.4/3</MarginText>
<li>A nonformal limited private type that is tagged or has at least one access discriminant with a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.7#S0063">default_expression</a></code>;<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>8.a/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The full type in both of these cases must necessarily be immutably limited. We need to include private types as much as possible so that we aren't unintentionally discouraging the use of private types. <br />

<MarginText>8.5/3</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>A task type, a protected type, or a synchronized interface;<br /></li>
<MarginText>8.6/3</MarginText>
<li>A type derived from an immutably limited type.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>8.b/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>An immutably limited type is a type that cannot become nonlimited subsequently in a private part or in a child unit. If a view of the type makes it immutably limited, then no copying (assignment) operations are ever available for objects of the type. This allows other properties; for instance, it is safe for such objects to have access discriminants that have defaults or designate other limited objects. <br />

<MarginText>8.c/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>A nonsynchronized limited interface type is not immutably limited; a type derived from it can be nonlimited. <br />

<MarginText>8.7/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0052-1"]} />
<p>A descendant of a generic formal limited private type is presumed to be immutably limited except within the body of a generic unit or a body declared within the declarative region of a generic unit, if the formal type is declared within the formal part of the generic unit.<br /></p>

<MarginText>8.d/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>In an instance, a type is descended from the actual type corresponding to the formal, and all rules are rechecked in the specification. Bodies are excepted so that we assume the worst there; the complex wording is required to handle children of generics and unrelated bodies properly. <br />

<MarginText>9/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00287-01", "AI95-00318-02", "AI05-0067-1", "AI12-0442-1"]} />
NOTE 1   While it is allowed to write initializations of limited objects, such initializations never copy a limited object. The source of such an assignment operation will be an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#S0218">function_call</a></code>, and such <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code>s and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#S0218">function_call</a></code>s will be built directly in the target object (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.6">7.6</a>). <br />

<MarginText>9.a/2</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>This isn't quite true if the type can become nonlimited (see below); <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#S0218">function_call</a></code>s only are required to be build-in-place for &ldquo;really&rdquo; limited types. <br />

<i>Paragraphs 10 through 15 were deleted.</i> <br />

<MarginText>16</MarginText>
NOTE 2   As illustrated in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3#Subclause_7.3.1">7.3.1</a>, an untagged limited type can become nonlimited under certain circumstances. <br />

<MarginText>16.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Limited private types do not become nonlimited; instead, their full view can be nonlimited, which has a similar effect.<br />

<MarginText>16.b</MarginText>
It is important to remember that a single nonprivate type can be both limited and nonlimited in different parts of its scope. In other words, &ldquo;limited&rdquo; is a property that depends on where you are in the scope of the type. We don't call this a &ldquo;view property&rdquo; because there is no particular declaration to declare the nonlimited view.<br />

<MarginText>16.c</MarginText>
Tagged types never become nonlimited. <br />

#### Examples

<MarginText>17</MarginText>
<p><i>Example of a package with a limited type:</i> <br /></p>

<MarginText>18</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package IO{"_"}Package is{"\n"}   type File{"_"}Name is limited private;{"\n"}
<MarginText>19</MarginText>
   procedure Open (F : in out File{"_"}Name);{"\n"}   procedure Close(F : in out File{"_"}Name);{"\n"}   procedure Read (F : in File{"_"}Name; Item : out Integer);{"\n"}   procedure Write(F : in File{"_"}Name; Item : in  Integer);{"\n"}private{"\n"}   type File{"_"}Name is{"\n"}      limited record{"\n"}         Internal{"_"}Name : Integer := 0;{"\n"}      end record;{"\n"}end IO{"_"}Package;{"\n"}
<MarginText>20</MarginText>
package body IO{"_"}Package is{"\n"}   Limit : constant := 200;{"\n"}   type File{"_"}Descriptor is record  ...  end record;{"\n"}   Directory : array (1 .. Limit) of File{"_"}Descriptor;{"\n"}   ...{"\n"}   procedure Open (F : in out File{"_"}Name) is  ...  end;{"\n"}   procedure Close(F : in out File{"_"}Name) is  ...  end;{"\n"}   procedure Read (F : in File{"_"}Name; Item : out Integer) is ... end;{"\n"}   procedure Write(F : in File{"_"}Name; Item : in  Integer) is ... end;{"\n"}begin{"\n"}   ...{"\n"}end IO{"_"}Package;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>21/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0440-1", "AI12-0452-1"]} />
<p>In the example, an outside subprogram making use of IO{"_"}Package can obtain a file name by calling Open and later use it in calls to Read and Write. Thus, outside the package, a file name obtained from Open acts as a kind of password; its internal properties (such as containing a numeric value) are not known and no other operations (such as addition or comparison of internal names) can be performed on a file name. Most importantly, clients of the package cannot make copies of objects of type File{"_"}Name.<br /></p>

<MarginText>22/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0442-1", "AI12-0452-1"]} />
<p>This example is characteristic of any case where complete control over the operations of a type is desired. Such packages serve a dual purpose. They prevent a user from making use of the internal structure of the type. They also implement the notion of an encapsulated data type where the only operations on the type are those given in the package specification.<br /></p>

<MarginText>23/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0442-1", "AI12-0452-1"]} />
<p>The fact that the full view of File{"_"}Name is explicitly declared <b>limited</b> means that parameter passing will always be by reference and function results will always be built directly in the result object (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.2">6.2</a> and <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5">6.5</a>).<br /></p>

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>26.a</MarginText>
The restrictions in RM83-7.4.4(4), which disallowed <b>out</b> parameters of limited types in certain cases, are removed. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 83

<MarginText>26.b/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0299-1"]} />
Since limitedness and privateness are orthogonal in Ada 95 (and to some extent in Ada 83), this is now its own subclause rather than being a subclause of <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3">7.3</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.3">Private Types and Private Extensions</a>&rdquo;. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 95

<MarginText>26.c/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00287-01", "AI95-00318-02"]} />
Limited types now have an assignment operation, but its use is restricted such that all uses are build-in-place. This is accomplished by restricting uses to <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code>s and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#S0218">function_call</a></code>s. <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">Aggregate</a></code>s were not allowed to have a limited type in Ada 95, which causes a compatibility issue discussed in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3">4.3</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3">Aggregates</a>&rdquo;. Compatibility issues with return statements for limited <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.4#S0218">function_call</a></code>s are discussed in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5">6.5</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5">Return Statements</a>&rdquo;. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>26.d/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00411-01", "AI95-00419-01"]} />
Rewrote the definition of limited to ensure that interfaces are covered, but that limitedness is not inherited from interfaces. Derived types that explicitly include <b>limited</b> are now also covered. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>26.e/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0052-1", "AI05-0217-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Added a definition for immutably limited types, so that the fairly complex definition does not need to be repeated in rules elsewhere in the Reference Manual.<br />

<MarginText>26.f/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1", "AI05-0299-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> The built-in-place rules are consolidated in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.6">7.6</a>, and thus they are removed from this subclause.<br />

<MarginText>26.g/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0087-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Fixed an oversight: class-wide types were never defined to be limited, even if their associated specific type is. It is thought that this oversight was never implemented incorrectly by any compiler, thus we have not classified it as an incompatibility.<br />

<MarginText>26.h/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0147-1"]} />
Allowed <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#S0148">conditional_expression</a></code>s in limited constructor contexts &mdash; we want to treat these as closely to parentheses as possible.<br />

<MarginText>26.i/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0177-1"]} />
Added wording so that expression functions can return limited entities.<br />

<MarginText>26.j/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0178-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Added incomplete views to the list of reasons for a view of a type to be limited. This is not a change as the definition already was in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.10#Subclause_3.10.1">3.10.1</a>. But it is much better to have all of the reasons for limitedness together. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 2012

<MarginText>26.k/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0172-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> A <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.3#S0309">raise_expression</a></code> can be used in an expression used in a limited context. This is harmless (no object will be created if an exception is raised instead), useful, and thus appears to have been an omission when <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-11/AA-11.3#S0309">raise_expression</a></code>s were added to the language. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2012

<MarginText>26.l/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0127-1"]} />
Added the <i>base{"_"}</i><code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0120">delta_aggregate</a></code> as a limited context. <br />

# 7.6. Assignment and Finalization

Source: https://github.com/ada-lang-io/ada-lang-io/blob/main/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.6.mdx

sidebar_position:  65

# 7.6. Assignment and Finalization

<MarginText>1</MarginText>
<p>[ Three kinds of actions are fundamental to the manipulation of objects: initialization, finalization, and assignment. Every object is initialized, either explicitly or by default, after being created (for example, by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#S0032">object_declaration</a></code> or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code>). Every object is finalized before being destroyed (for example, by leaving a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.3#S0216">subprogram_body</a></code> containing an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#S0032">object_declaration</a></code>, or by a call to an instance of Unchecked{"_"}Deallocation). An assignment operation is used as part of <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>s, explicit initialization, parameter passing, and other operations. <br /></p>

<MarginText>2</MarginText>
<p>Default definitions for these three fundamental operations are provided by the language, but a <i>controlled</i> type gives the user additional control over parts of these operations. In particular, the user can define, for a controlled type, an Initialize procedure which is invoked immediately after the normal default initialization of a controlled object, a Finalize procedure which is invoked immediately before finalization of any of the components of a controlled object, and an Adjust procedure which is invoked as the last step of an assignment to a (nonlimited) controlled object.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>2.a/5</MarginText>
<b>Term entry: </b><b>controlled type</b> &mdash; type that supports user-defined assignment and finalization<br />Note: Objects are always finalized before being destroyed.<br />

<MarginText>2.b/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00114-01", "AI95-00287-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Here's the basic idea of initialization, value adjustment, and finalization, whether or not user defined: When an object is created, if it is explicitly assigned an initial value, the object is either built-in-place from an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> or function call (in which case neither Adjust nor Initialize is applied), or the assignment copies and adjusts the initial value. Otherwise, Initialize is applied to it (except in the case of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> as a whole). An <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code> finalizes the target before copying in and adjusting the new value. Whenever an object goes away, it is finalized. Calls on Initialize and Adjust happen bottom-up; that is, components first, followed by the containing object. Calls on Finalize happen top-down; that is, first the containing object, and then its components. These ordering rules ensure that any components will be in a well-defined state when Initialize, Adjust, or Finalize is applied to the containing object. <br />

#### Static Semantics

<MarginText>3</MarginText>
<p>The following language-defined library package exists: <br /></p>

<MarginText>4/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00126-01", "AI05-0212-1", "AI12-0241-1"]} />
<CodeBlock language="ada">
{"{"}8652/0020{"}"} package Ada.Finalization{"\n"}    with Pure, Nonblocking ={">"} False is{"\n"}
<MarginText>5/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00161-01", "AI12-0399-1"]} />
    type Controlled is abstract tagged private{"\n"}       with Preelaborable{"_"}Initialization;{"\n"}
<MarginText>6/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00348-01"]} />
    procedure Initialize (Object : in out Controlled) is null;{"\n"}    procedure Adjust     (Object : in out Controlled) is null;{"\n"}    procedure Finalize   (Object : in out Controlled) is null;{"\n"}
<MarginText>7/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00161-01", "AI12-0399-1"]} />
    type Limited{"_"}Controlled is abstract tagged limited private{"\n"}       with Preelaborable{"_"}Initialization;{"\n"}
<MarginText>8/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00348-01"]} />
    procedure Initialize (Object : in out Limited{"_"}Controlled) is null;{"\n"}    procedure Finalize   (Object : in out Limited{"_"}Controlled) is null;{"\n"}private{"\n"}    ... -- not specified by the language{"\n"}end Ada.Finalization;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>8.a/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0241-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This package must allow blocking (Nonblocking ={">"} False) for compatibility. The purpose of this package is to provide a template for overriding user-defined routines; and such routines can only allow blocking if the root type does so. Users can still declare their overridding routines nonblocking if they wish. <br />

<MarginText>9/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00348-01"]} />
<p>A controlled type is a descendant of Controlled or Limited{"_"}Controlled. The predefined "=" operator of type Controlled always returns True, [since this operator is incorporated into the implementation of the predefined equality operator of types derived from Controlled, as explained in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.5#Subclause_4.5.2">4.5.2</a>.] The type Limited{"_"}Controlled is like Controlled, except that it is limited and it lacks the primitive subprogram Adjust. <br /></p>

<MarginText>9.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>We say &ldquo;nonlimited controlled type&rdquo; (rather than just &ldquo;controlled type&rdquo;;) when we want to talk about descendants of Controlled only. <br />

<MarginText>9.b</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We considered making Adjust and Finalize abstract. However, a reasonable coding convention is e.g. for Finalize to always call the parent's Finalize after doing whatever work is needed for the extension part. (Unlike CLOS, we have no way to do that automatically in Ada 95.) For this to work, Finalize cannot be abstract. In a generic unit, for a generic formal abstract derived type whose ancestor is Controlled or Limited{"_"}Controlled, calling the ancestor's Finalize would be illegal if it were abstract, even though the actual type might have a concrete version.<br />

<MarginText>9.c</MarginText>
Types Controlled and Limited{"_"}Controlled are abstract, even though they have no abstract primitive subprograms. It is not clear that they need to be abstract, but there seems to be no harm in it, and it might make an implementation's life easier to know that there are no objects of these types &mdash; in case the implementation wishes to make them &ldquo;magic&rdquo; in some way.<br />

<MarginText>9.d/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00251-01"]} />
For Ada 2005, we considered making these types interfaces. That would have the advantage of allowing them to be added to existing trees. But that was rejected both because it would cause massive disruptions to existing implementations, and because it would be very incompatible due to the "no hidden interfaces" rule. The latter rule would prevent a tagged private type from being completed with a derivation from Controlled or Limited{"_"}Controlled &mdash; a very common idiom. <br />

<MarginText>9.1/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00360-01"]} />
<p>A type is said to <i>need finalization</i> if:<br /></p>

<MarginText>9.2/2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>it is a controlled type, a task type or a protected type; or<br /></li>
<MarginText>9.3/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0092-1"]} />
<li>it has a component whose type needs finalization; or<br /></li>
<MarginText>9.4/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0013-1"]} />
<li>it is a class-wide type; or<br /></li>
<MarginText>9.5/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0026-1"]} />
<li>it is a partial view whose full view needs finalization; or<br /></li>
<MarginText>9.6/2</MarginText>
<li>it is one of a number of language-defined types that are explicitly defined to need finalization.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>9.e/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The fact that a type needs finalization does not require it to be implemented with a controlled type. It just has to be recognized by the No{"_"}Nested{"_"}Finalization restriction.<br />

<MarginText>9.f/2</MarginText>
This property is defined for the type, not for a particular view. That's necessary as restrictions look in private parts to enforce their restrictions; the point is to eliminate all controlled parts, not just ones that are visible. <br />

#### Dynamic Semantics

<MarginText>10/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00373-01"]} />
<p>During the elaboration or evaluation of a construct that causes an object to be initialized by default, for every controlled subcomponent of the object that is not assigned an initial value (as defined in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.3#Subclause_3.3.1">3.3.1</a>), Initialize is called on that subcomponent. Similarly, if the object that is initialized by default as a whole is controlled, Initialize is called on the object.<br /></p>

<MarginText>11/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00182-01", "AI95-00373-01"]} />
<p>{"{"}<i>8652/0021</i>{"}"} For an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0111">extension_aggregate</a></code> whose <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0112">ancestor_part</a></code> is a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.2#S0028">subtype_mark</a></code> denoting a controlled subtype, the Initialize procedure of the ancestor type is called, unless that Initialize procedure is abstract. <br /></p>

<MarginText>11.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>Example: <br />

<MarginText>11.b</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type T1 is new Controlled with{"\n"}    record{"\n"}        ... -- some components might have defaults{"\n"}    end record;{"\n"}
<MarginText>11.c</MarginText>
type T2 is new Controlled with{"\n"}    record{"\n"}        X : T1; -- no default{"\n"}        Y : T1 := ...; -- default{"\n"}    end record;{"\n"}
<MarginText>11.d</MarginText>
A : T2;{"\n"}B : T2 := ...;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>11.e</MarginText>
As part of the elaboration of A's declaration, A.Y is assigned a value; therefore Initialize is not applied to A.Y. Instead, Adjust is applied to A.Y as part of the assignment operation. Initialize is applied to A.X and to A, since those objects are not assigned an initial value. The assignment to A.Y is not considered an assignment to A.<br />

<MarginText>11.f</MarginText>
For the elaboration of B's declaration, Initialize is not called at all. Instead the assignment adjusts B's value; that is, it applies Adjust to B.X, B.Y, and B.<br />

<MarginText>11.f.1/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00182-01", "AI95-00373-01"]} />
{"{"}<i>8652/0021</i>{"}"} The <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0112">ancestor_part</a></code> of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0111">extension_aggregate</a></code>, {"<"}{">"} in aggregates, and the return object of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5#S0225">extended_return_statement</a></code> are handled similarly. <br />

<MarginText>12</MarginText>
<p>Initialize and other initialization operations are done in an arbitrary order, except as follows. Initialize is applied to an object after initialization of its subcomponents, if any [(including both implicit initialization and Initialize calls)]. If an object has a component with an access discriminant constrained by a per-object expression, Initialize is applied to this component after any components that do not have such discriminants. For an object with several components with such a discriminant, Initialize is applied to them in order of their <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-3/AA-3.8#S0070">component_declaration</a></code>s. For an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.8#S0164">allocator</a></code>, any task activations follow all calls on Initialize. <br /></p>

<MarginText>12.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The fact that Initialize is done for subcomponents first allows Initialize for a composite object to refer to its subcomponents knowing they have been properly initialized.<br />

<MarginText>12.b</MarginText>
The fact that Initialize is done for components with access discriminants after other components allows the Initialize operation for a component with a self-referential access discriminant to assume that other components of the enclosing object have already been properly initialized. For multiple such components, it allows some predictability. <br />

<MarginText>13</MarginText>
<p>When a target object with any controlled parts is assigned a value, [either when created or in a subsequent <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>,] the <i>assignment operation</i> proceeds as follows: <br /></p>

<MarginText>14</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>The value of the target becomes the assigned value.<br /></li>
<MarginText>15</MarginText>
<li>The value of the target is <i>adjusted.</i> <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>15.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>If any parts of the object are controlled, abort is deferred during the assignment operation. <br />

<MarginText>16/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1"]} />
<p>To adjust the value of a composite object, the values of the components of the object are first adjusted in an arbitrary order, and then, if the object is nonlimited controlled, Adjust is called. Adjusting the value of an elementary object has no effect[, nor does adjusting the value of a composite object with no controlled parts.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>16.a/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>Adjustment is never actually performed for values of an immutably limited type, since all assignment operations for such types are required to be built-in-place. Even so, we still define adjustment for all types in order that the canonical semantics is well-defined. <br />

<MarginText>16.b/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The verbiage in the Initialize rule about access discriminants constrained by per-object expressions is not necessary here, since such types are either limited or do not have defaults, so the discriminant can only be changed by an assignment to an outer object. Such an assignment could happen only before any adjustments or (if part of an outer Adjust) only after any inner (component) adjustments have completed. <br />

<MarginText>17</MarginText>
<p>For an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>,[ after the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> and <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.4#S0132">expression</a></code> have been evaluated, and any conversion (including constraint checking) has been done,] an anonymous object is created, and the value is assigned into it; [that is, the assignment operation is applied]. [(Assignment includes value adjustment.)] The target of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code> is then finalized. The value of the anonymous object is then assigned into the target of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>. Finally, the anonymous object is finalized. [As explained below, the implementation may eliminate the intermediate anonymous object, so this description subsumes the one given in <a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2">5.2</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2">Assignment Statements</a>&rdquo;.] <br /></p>

<MarginText>17.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>An alternative design for user-defined assignment might involve an Assign operation instead of Adjust: <br />

<MarginText>17.b</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
procedure Assign(Target : in out Controlled; Source : in out Controlled);{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>17.c</MarginText>
Or perhaps even a syntax like this: <br />

<MarginText>17.d</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
procedure ":="(Target : in out Controlled; Source : in out Controlled);{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>17.e</MarginText>
Assign (or ":=") would have the responsibility of doing the copy, as well as whatever else is necessary. This would have the advantage that the Assign operation knows about both the target and the source at the same time &mdash; it would be possible to do things like reuse storage belonging to the target, for example, which Adjust cannot do. However, this sort of design would not work in the case of unconstrained discriminated variables, because there is no way to change the discriminants individually. For example: <br />

<MarginText>17.f</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
type Mutable(D : Integer := 0) is{"\n"}    record{"\n"}        X : Array{"_"}Of{"_"}Controlled{"_"}Things(1..D);{"\n"}        case D is{"\n"}            when 17 ={">"} Y : Controlled{"_"}Thing;{"\n"}            when others ={">"} null;{"\n"}        end D;{"\n"}    end record;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>17.g</MarginText>
An assignment to an unconstrained variable of type Mutable can cause some of the components of X, and the component Y, to appear and/or disappear. There is no way to write the Assign operation to handle this sort of case.<br />

<MarginText>17.h</MarginText>
Forbidding such cases is not an option &mdash; it would cause generic contract model violations. <br />

<MarginText>17.1/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1", "AI12-0439-1"]} />
<p>When a function call or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> is used to initialize an object, the result of the function call or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> is an anonymous object, which is assigned into the newly-created object. For such an assignment, the anonymous object may be <i>built in place</i>, in which case the assignment does not involve any copying. Under certain circumstances, the anonymous object is required to be built in place. In particular:<br /></p>

<MarginText>17.i/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="discussion">
<b></b>We say assignment to built-in-place objects does not involve copying, which matches the intended implementation (see below). Of course, the implementation can do any copying it likes, if it can make such copying semantically invisible (by patching up access values to point to the copy, and so forth). <br />

<MarginText>17.2/3</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>If the full type of any part of the object is immutably limited, the anonymous object is built in place.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>17.j/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We talk about the full types being immutably limited, as this is independent of the view of a type (in the same way that it is for determining the technique of parameter passing). That is, privacy is ignored for this purpose.<br />

<MarginText>17.k/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1", "AI05-0067-1"]} />
For function calls, we only require building in place for immutably limited types. These are the types that would have been return-by-reference types in Ada 95. We limited the requirement because we want to minimize disruption to Ada 95 implementations and users. <br />

<MarginText>17.l/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0232-1", "AI12-0005-1"]} />
<b>To be honest: </b>This is a dynamic property and is determined by the specific type of the parts of the actual object. In particular, if a part has a class-wide type, the tag of the object might need to be examined in order to determine if build-in-place is required. However, we expect that most Ada implementations will determine this property at compile-time using some assume-the-worst algorithm in order to choose the appropriate method to implement a given call or aggregate. In addition, there is no attribute or other method for a program to determine if a particular object has this property (or not), so there is no value to a more careful description of this rule. <br />

<MarginText>17.3/3</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>In the case of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code>, if the full type of any part of the newly-created object is controlled, the anonymous object is built in place.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>17.m/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This is necessary to prevent elaboration problems with deferred constants of controlled types. Consider: <br />

<MarginText>17.m.1/3</MarginText>
<CodeBlock language="ada">
package P is{"\n"}   type Dyn{"_"}String is private;{"\n"}   Null{"_"}String : constant Dyn{"_"}String;{"\n"}   ...{"\n"}private{"\n"}   type Dyn{"_"}String is new Ada.Finalization.Controlled with ...{"\n"}   procedure Finalize(X : in out Dyn{"_"}String);{"\n"}   procedure Adjust(X : in out Dyn{"_"}String);{"\n"}{"\n"}   Null{"_"}String : constant Dyn{"_"}String :={"\n"}      (Ada.Finalization.Controlled with ...);{"\n"}   ...{"\n"}end P;{"\n"}

</CodeBlock>
<MarginText>17.m.2/3</MarginText>
When Null{"_"}String is elaborated, the bodies of Finalize and Adjust clearly have not been elaborated. Without this rule, this declaration would necessarily raise Program{"_"}Error (unless the permissions given below are used by the implementation). <br />

<MarginText>17.n/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>An <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> with a controlled part used in the return expression of a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.5#S0222">simple{"_"}return{"_"}statement</a></code> has to be built in place in the anonymous return object, as this is similar to an object declaration. (This is a change from Ada 95, but it is not an inconsistency as it only serves to restrict implementation choices.) But this only covers the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code>; a separate anonymous return object can still be used unless it too is required to be built in place.<br />

<MarginText>17.o/3</MarginText>
Similarly, an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> that has a controlled part but is not itself controlled and that is used to initialize an object also has to be built in place. This is also a change from Ada 95, but it is not an inconsistency as it only serves to restrict implementation choices. This avoids problems if a type like Dyn{"_"}String (in the example above) is used as a component in a type used as a deferred constant in package P. <br />

<MarginText>17.4/3</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>In other cases, it is unspecified whether the anonymous object is built in place.<br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>17.p/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>This is left unspecified so the implementation can use any appropriate criteria for determining when to build in place. That includes making the decision on a call-by-call basis. Reasonable programs will not care what decision is made here anyway. <br />

<MarginText>17.5/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1"]} />
<p>Notwithstanding what this document says elsewhere, if an object is built in place:<br /></p>

<MarginText>17.6/3</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>Upon successful completion of the return statement or <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code>, the anonymous object <i>mutates into</i> the newly-created object; that is, the anonymous object ceases to exist, and the newly-created object appears in its place.<br /></li>
<MarginText>17.7/3</MarginText>
<li>Finalization is not performed on the anonymous object.<br /></li>
<MarginText>17.8/3</MarginText>
<li>Adjustment is not performed on the newly-created object.<br /></li>
<MarginText>17.9/3</MarginText>
<li>All access values that designate parts of the anonymous object now designate the corresponding parts of the newly-created object.<br /></li>
<MarginText>17.10/3</MarginText>
<li>All renamings of parts of the anonymous object now denote views of the corresponding parts of the newly-created object.<br /></li>
<MarginText>17.11/3</MarginText>
<li>Coextensions of the anonymous object become coextensions of the newly-created object. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>17.q/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI12-0005-1"]} />
<b>To be honest: </b>This &ldquo;mutating&rdquo; does not necessarily happen atomically with respect to abort and other tasks. For example, if a function call is used as the ancestor part of an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0111">extension_aggregate</a></code>, then the tag of the anonymous object (the function result) will be different from the tag of the newly-created object (the ancestor part of the <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0111">extension_aggregate</a></code>). In implementation terms, this involves modifying the tag field. If the current task is aborted during this modification, the object might become abnormal. Likewise, if some other task accesses the tag field during this modification, it constitutes improper use of shared variables, and is erroneous. <br />

<MarginText>17.r/3</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="implementation-note">
<b></b>The intended implementation is that the anonymous object is allocated at the same address as the newly-created object. Thus, no run-time action is required to cause all the access values and renamings to point to the right place. They just point to the newly-created object, which is what the return object has magically &ldquo;mutated into&rdquo;.<br />

<MarginText>17.s/3</MarginText>
There is no requirement that 'Address of the return object is equal to 'Address of the newly-created object, but that will be true in the intended implementation.<br />

<MarginText>17.t/3</MarginText>
For a function call, if the size of the newly-created object is known at the call site, the object is allocated there, and the address is implicitly passed to the function; the return object is created at that address. Otherwise, a storage pool is implicitly passed to the function; the size is determined at the point of the return statement, and passed to the Allocate procedure. The address returned by the storage pool is returned from the function, and the newly-created object uses that same address. If the return statement is left without returning (via an exception or a goto, for example), then Deallocate is called.  The storage pool might be a dummy pool that represents &ldquo;allocate on the stack&rdquo;.<br />

<MarginText>17.u/3</MarginText>
The Tag of the newly-created object may be different from that of the result object. Likewise, the master and accessibility level may be different.<br />

<MarginText>17.v/3</MarginText>
An alternative implementation model might allow objects to move around to different addresses. In this case, access values and renamings would need to be modified at run time. It seems that this model requires the full power of tracing garbage collection. <br />

#### Implementation Permissions

<MarginText>18/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1"]} />
<p>An implementation is allowed to relax the above rules for <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>s in the following ways: <br /></p>

<MarginText>18.a/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1"]} />
<i>This paragraph was deleted.</i><br />

<MarginText>18.b/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1", "AI12-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>The relaxations apply only to nonlimited types, as <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-5/AA-5.2#S0173">assignment_statement</a></code>s are not allowed for limited types. This is important so that the programmer can count on stricter semantics for limited controlled types. <br />

<MarginText>19/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1", "AI12-0444-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>If an object is assigned the value of that same object, the implementation may omit the entire assignment. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>19.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>In other words, even if an object is controlled and a combination of Finalize and Adjust on the object might have a net side effect, they need not be performed. <br />

<MarginText>20/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0067-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>For assignment of a noncontrolled type, the implementation may finalize and assign each component of the variable separately (rather than finalizing the entire variable and assigning the entire new value) unless a discriminant of the variable is changed by the assignment. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>20.a</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>For example, in a slice assignment, an anonymous object is not necessary if the slice is copied component-by-component in the right direction, since array types are not controlled (although their components may be). Note that the direction, and even the fact that it's a slice assignment, can in general be determined only at run time. <br />

<MarginText>20.b/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>This potentially breaks a single assignment operation into many, and thus abort deferral (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-9/AA-9.8">9.8</a>) needs to last only across an individual component assignment when the component has a controlled part. It is only important that the copy step is not separated (by an abort) from the adjust step, so aborts between component assignments is not harmful. <br />

<MarginText>21/5</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00147-01", "AI05-0067-1", "AI12-0444-1"]} />
<ul>
<li>The implementation may avoid creating an anonymous object if the value being assigned is the result of evaluating a <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.1#S0091">name</a></code> denoting an object (the source object) whose storage cannot overlap with the target. If the source object can overlap with the target object, then the implementation can avoid the need for an intermediary anonymous object by exercising one of the above permissions and perform the assignment one component at a time (for an overlapping array assignment), or not at all (for an assignment where the target and the source of the assignment are the same object). <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>21.a/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0005-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="ramification">
<b></b>If the anonymous object is eliminated by this permission,  there is no anonymous object to be finalized and thus the Finalize call on it is eliminated.<br />

<MarginText>21.b/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00147-01", "AI05-0005-1"]} />
Note that if the anonymous object is eliminated but the new value is not built in place in the target object, that Adjust must be called directly on the target object as the last step of the assignment, since some of the subcomponents may be self-referential or otherwise position-dependent. This Adjust can be eliminated only by using one of the following permissions. <br />

<MarginText>22/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00147-01"]} />
<p>Furthermore, an implementation is permitted to omit implicit Initialize, Adjust, and Finalize calls and associated assignment operations on an object of a nonlimited controlled type provided that:<br /></p>

<MarginText>23/2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>any omitted Initialize call is not a call on a user-defined Initialize procedure, and <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>23.a/2</MarginText>
<b>To be honest: </b>This does not apply to any calls to a user-defined Initialize routine that happen to occur in an Adjust or Finalize routine. It is intended that it is never necessary to look inside of an Adjust or Finalize routine to determine if the call can be omitted. <br />

<MarginText>23.b/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>We don't want to eliminate objects for which the Initialize might have side effects (such as locking a resource). <br />

<MarginText>24/2</MarginText>
<ul>
<li>any usage of the value of the object after the implicit Initialize or Adjust call and before any subsequent Finalize call on the object does not change the external effect of the program, and<br /></li>
<MarginText>25/2</MarginText>
<li>after the omission of such calls and operations, any execution of the program that executes an Initialize or Adjust call on an object or initializes an object by an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> will also later execute a Finalize call on the object and will always do so prior to assigning a new value to the object, and<br /></li>
<MarginText>26/2</MarginText>
<li>the assignment operations associated with omitted Adjust calls are also omitted. <br /></li>
</ul>
<MarginText>27/2</MarginText>
<p>This permission applies to Adjust and Finalize calls even if the implicit calls have additional external effects. <br /></p>

<MarginText>27.a/2</MarginText>
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="reason">
<b></b>The goal of the above permissions is to allow typical dead assignment and dead variable removal algorithms to work for nonlimited controlled types. We require that &ldquo;pairs&rdquo; of Initialize/Adjust/Finalize operations are removed. (These aren't always pairs, which is why we talk about &ldquo;any execution of the program&rdquo;.) <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 83

<MarginText>27.b</MarginText>
Controlled types and user-defined finalization are new to Ada 95. (Ada 83 had finalization semantics only for masters of tasks.) <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 95

<MarginText>27.c/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00161-01"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b>Amendment </b> Types Controlled and Limited{"_"}Controlled now have Preelaborable{"_"}Initialization, so that objects of types derived from these types can be used in preelaborated packages. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 95

<MarginText>27.d/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00126-01"]} />
{"{"}<i>8652/0020</i>{"}"} <b>Corrigendum:</b> Clarified that Ada.Finalization is a remote types package.<br />

<MarginText>27.e/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00182-01"]} />
{"{"}<i>8652/0021</i>{"}"} <b>Corrigendum:</b> Added wording to clarify that the default initialization (whatever it is) of an ancestor part is used.<br />

<MarginText>27.f/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00083-01"]} />
{"{"}<i>8652/0022</i>{"}"} <b>Corrigendum:</b> Clarified that Adjust is never called on an <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code> used for the initialization of an object or subaggregate, or passed as a parameter.<br />

<MarginText>27.g/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00147-01"]} />
Additional optimizations are allowed for nonlimited controlled types. These allow traditional dead variable elimination to be applied to such types.<br />

<MarginText>27.h/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00318-02"]} />
Corrected the build-in-place requirement for controlled <code><a href="/docs/arm/AA-4/AA-4.3#S0106">aggregate</a></code>s to be consistent with the requirements for limited types.<br />

<MarginText>27.i/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00348-01"]} />
The operations of types Controlled and Limited{"_"}Controlled are now declared as null procedures (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-6/AA-6.7">6.7</a>) to make the semantics clear (and to provide a good example of what null procedures can be used for).<br />

<MarginText>27.j/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00360-01"]} />
Types that need finalization are defined; this is used by the No{"_"}Nested{"_"}Finalization restriction (see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-D/AA-D.7">D.7</a>, &ldquo;<a href="/docs/arm/AA-D/AA-D.7">Tasking Restrictions</a>&rdquo;).<br />

<MarginText>27.k/2</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI95-00373-01"]} />
Generalized the description of objects that have Initialize called for them to say that it is done for all objects that are initialized by default. This is needed so that all of the new cases are covered. <br />

#### Extensions to Ada 2005

<MarginText>27.l/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0212-1"]} />
Package Ada.Finalization now has Pure categorization, so it can be mentioned for any package. Note that this does not change the preelaborability of objects descended from Controlled and Limited{"_"}Controlled. <br />

#### Wording Changes from Ada 2005

<MarginText>27.m/3</MarginText>
<MarginInfo items={["AI05-0013-1"]} />
<Admonition type="aarm" aarm="correction">
<b></b> Eliminated coextensions from the &ldquo;needs finalization&rdquo; rules, as this cannot be determined in general in the compilation unit that declares the type. (The designated type of the coextension may have been imported as a limited view.) Uses of &ldquo;needs finalization&rdquo; need to ensure that coextensions are handled by other means (such as in No{"_"}Nested{"_"}Finalization &ndash; see <a href="/docs/arm/AA-D/AA-D.7">D.7</a>) or that coextensions cannot happen.<br />

<MarginText>27.n/3</MarginText>
